Given any recognizable and expanding morphism $\sigma$, the topological entropy of $\sigma$ is equal to the entropy of its incidence matrix. This fact can be applied to investigate the topological entropy of subshifts resulting from $\sigma$ applied to an initial data. Specifically, if the topological entropy of the initial data is unknown, yet it is finite, then the topological entropy of this resulting subshift is also finite. Conversely, if the topological entropy of the resulting subshift is finite, yet the entropy of its incidence matrix is unknown, then the entropy of its incidence matrix is also finite. Furthermore, a relationship between these entropies can be defined as a result of applying a recognizable and expanding morphism. This research builds upon the theoretical foundations established by Berstien and Kellner in 2016 and 2017. Hyperparameter tuning in AI models, especially using methods like grid search, is common. Nonetheless, these traditional techniques are not private, meaning they leak information about the model and data. As a result, researchers and practitioners cannot use them when working with sensitive or private datasets, including some that belong to individuals with whom they have no contractual relationship. In such cases, researchers and practitioners must use private hyperparameter tuning methods that minimize information disclosure. In this research, we created a novel private hyperparameter tuning method called PrivAT, which utilizes a technique called federated learning to select the best hyperparameter settings for the model. To evaluate PrivAT's effectiveness, we compared it with other private methods, including ones that utilize synthetic data, zero-shot learning, and differential privacy, and found that it performs better than the former two and similarly to the latter one, but only requires significantly less computational power than them. Furthermore, we found that PrivAT can be applied to various machine learning models, including ones that handle text, images, and audio, and to datasets of different sizes, including ones with just a few data points. Lastly, we found that PrivAT maintains the same level of accuracy as traditional hyperparameter tuning methods. The code for PrivAT is available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/HsiaoChien/PrivAT.

This study develops a comprehensive thermomechanical model to capture the structural changes in polymers, specifically shear-induced crystallization within amorphous regions. By combining viscoelastic and phase change theories, we leverage free energy frameworks to derive a macroscopic model, consisting of dual domains (amorphous and crystalline phases) that can transform into one another. We utilize gradient operators and the method of steps to obtain the second variation of the free energy, which yields the governing equations of state, phase transformation kinetics, and the mobility of the material. This model includes stress, strain, temperature, crystalline phase fraction, amorphous strain gradient, and chemical potential as key variables, and it is implemented using a computational framework based on finite elements and operator splitting. Through numerical simulations, we validate the model by replicating classic experiments, including stress-relaxation, temperature-scanning, and shear-testing, and observe excellent agreement between simulated and experimental data. Furthermore, we employ this model to investigate material degradation during cycling tests and propose a possible degradation mechanism driven by the formation of defects at phase boundaries. This study provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the thermomechanical behavior of polymers and offers a practical model for predicting material lifetimes in cyclic loading scenarios. The developed code is an initial contribution to the open community of finite dissipative dynamics models. The current code version is available at https://github.com/strategystudent/sic. Future code developments will incorporate higher-order continuum models and advanced numerical techniques. The model and code can be used as a starting point for modeling and predicting material degradation in polymers, particularly in applications involving temperature changes and cyclic loading. A differential detection system with conventional architecture can be improved by reducing errors, resulting in a coefficient detection system that utilizes the phase information more effectively. This paper presents an enhanced differential detection method that utilizes coefficient detection geometry, resulting in a 3.8 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) reduction for continuous phase modulation (CPM) signals when detecting phase information and a 6.2 dB SNR reduction when detecting phase and amplitude information. Simulation results demonstrating the performance improvement of the proposed method are presented and show that the average bit error rate (BER) performance of the proposed method is 1 dB better than conventional differential detection for CPM signals in additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. In contrast, the proposed method offers better performance than conventional differential detection in time-discrete channels and phase/frequency noisy environments. When the adiabatic constant is near 1, a system at a given pressure can be accurately described using the grand canonical ensemble, as demonstrated by the equivalence to the canonical ensemble. However, determining the compressibility within this ensemble can be challenging, leading to an exploration of alternative adiabatic constants. For the original adiabatic constant, we derived a novel expression that allows for the direct calculation of compressibility. Furthermore, we established a critical condition for validity and determined the adiabatic constant required to ensure the equivalence between canonical and grand canonical ensembles, both of which provide insights into the range where the grand canonical ensemble is viable. Numerical investigations involving a harmonic chain and the ideal gas chain have been conducted to test these findings. Additionally, the relation between the adiabatic constant and the number of particles has been examined to demonstrate the associated threats and guarantees of the ensemble equivalence with specific examples. Ultimately, our study reveals the limitations of the grand canonical ensemble and highlights the importance of rigorous validation through complementary methods. To that end, we have developed the ensemble equivalence validator (EEV) – an open-source Python tool available for other systems and ensembles – with guidelines for proper usage. The most notable advantage of the EEV lies in its ability to discern seemingly indistinguishable distributions from those that differ significantly. The implications of our research also extend to molecular dynamics simulations and other statistical mechanical simulations, where the validity of the ensemble must be scrutinized with the same intensity as the interactions, potential, and other simulation parameters. The associated metadata have been made publicly accessible to facilitate future research in this area. The proposed approach and related code can be applied to numerous statistical mechanical systems and their corresponding ensemble representations, paving the way for an automated framework that integrates ensemble validation with existing code, thereby enhancing the overall integrity of numerical simulations. If-then relation if implied by a sentence is considered a fundamental concept in natural language processing that helps achieve tasks like knowledge base completion and question answering. Most current approaches label each sentence individually, without accounting for the overall pattern of if-then relations within a text. However, it has been observed that sentences often follow a specific order, with some being conditional statements that justify others. To capture this structure, we propose an approach that employs a rich hierarchy of if-then relation types to guide the training of neural models on text data. By incorporating this structure, we significantly enhance the performance of models on tasks like sentence classification, sentence similarity, and knowledge graph completion. Furthermore, our method demonstrates a notable increase in model performance when trained on explicit if-then statements, such as CommonSenseQA. Our approach and underlying hypotheses are supported by explicit data, and it provides a framework for integrating if-then structure into various generative models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yu-Hsiao/Itnt-Tree-Graph.

To overcome these limitations, we have developed the NISQ-HHL algorithm, which reduces the required memory and mitigates the effects of noise on the quantum device. Leveraging the HHL variant that utilizes phase estimation through a unitary operator, our NISQ-HHL protocol manipulates the conditional amplitude encoding of variables, thereby minimizing the matrix inversion's impact on the quantum device's noise sensitivity. From a practical perspective, this protocol enables the successful execution of matrix inversions on noisy quantum hardware, and we demonstrate the NISQ-HHL's performance enhancements on multiple existing devices. Moreover, we illustrate the application of this protocol in a significant context, namely the computation of expected values in noisy stochastic quantum simulations. Additionally, we have made the NISQ-HHL code publicly available on GitHub, along with the related simulations conducted on real and simulated quantum devices. Furthermore, we have deposited the protocol on the NASA Quantum Classical Integration Testbeds (QCI-Tb) portal, a repository dedicated to publishing high-quality quantum-classical integration experiments and related code. Given the NISQ-HHL's versatility, we encourage the broad community to utilize and build upon this protocol. From a theoretical perspective, this protocol enables the efficient inversion of matrices within quantum circuits in the presence of noise, and we have an ongoing effort to improve its memory efficiency even further. From a practical standpoint, the NISQ-HHL algorithm has the potential to enhance the execution of the HHL variant on quantum devices, and we have observed this first-hand in the course of our experiments. Ultimately, the NISQ-HHL algorithm, the related experiments, and the associated code are all key components of our ongoing research into noise-resistant quantum algorithms and the related hardware requirements. Our linear analysis yields a $Q\bar{q}$ pair coupled to a meson-exchange core, while the nonlinear analysis shows that the Roper resonance's mass components follow a geometric rather than a linear pattern. Our results also demonstrate that the Roper resonance's density function can be accurately modeled using a nonlinear density function rather than a linear one. The Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers has been investigated, revealing a surprising decrease in scattering caused by Bismuth layers at low temperatures. The theory suggesting that interface scattering dominates the electrical transport in multilayers typically holds when the fence layers are metallic, but Bismuth's behavior requires an alternate explanation. Our study proposes that the small effective mass of Bismuth results from weak interface coupling, leading to the exclusion of Bismuth's layers from the hole-like carrier distribution, and thus, the diminished scattering with increasing Bismuth layers primarily affects the electrical transport. This hypothesis is supported by modeling showing that the effective mass of Bismuth adlayers can be highly sensitive to interface coupling, even more so than the carrier concentration. Consequently, the carrier scattering mechanism is governed by the mass distribution rather than the carrier concentration itself, and as a result, a clear anomaly in scattering is observed in these multilayers. The distinctive scattering behavior in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers may also hold promise for potential applications in thermal and spin transport studies. The general mechanism we've identified in this study is expected to be relevant to other heavy/fence layer structures and could be modulated by exsitu annealing, making it a viable option for inclusion in future device designs. Theoretical simulations have also enabled the design of improved multilayer structures, with the largest anomaly in scattering occurring in layers consisting of a heavy metal paired with either Palladium or Gold, and these structures exhibit a very low effective mass of mass anisotropy as well as unusual temperature dependencies of the Hall effect and charge transport. The anomalous scattering behavior in these multilayer structures could be influenced by exsitu annealing, offering the potential for optimized layers to be created via this method. The magnetic properties of Bismuth adlayers have also been found to be highly sensitive to interface coupling, prompting the investigation of this sensitivity in relation to various fence metals, which in turn has revealed a distinct correlation between the spin mixing parameter and the effective mass of the fence metal, thereby providing a clear understanding of the Bismuth adlayer's electronic behavior. The most intriguing aspect of this study has been the unexpected discovery that the envelope of the Hall effect in Bismuth adlayers, including the residual Hall effect in superconducting Bismuth adlayers, can be described by a Gaussian distribution, with the standard deviation of this distribution being directly related to the anisotropy of the mass of the carrier rather than the carrier concentration itself.

As WiFi fingerprint-based positioning systems become more widespread, efficiently estimating the distance between geospatially distributed data points (fingerprints) has become increasingly vital. Traditional methods rely solely on signal-strength information, but often yield inconsistent results due to WiFi signal variability. To address this challenge, we investigate the potential of incorporating contextual information from a region's layout and external data sources using machine learning techniques. Our experimental framework, set in an indoor university environment, utilizes a substantial dataset comprising 1,708 fingerprints derived from 402 unique WiFi access points. To evaluate our approach, we developed an integrated method combining graph-based distance estimation and neural network predictions, which consistently outperformed conventional metrics such as the Euclidean distance and signal-strength-based estimation methods, producing a 14.8% reduction in median distance error and a 54.4% decrease in large distance errors. Furthermore, our proposed system demonstrated flexibility and adaptability in modeling various real-world scenarios, allowing it to serve as a foundational framework for optimizing future applications. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/XiaoYi-Caizhen/GeoDistanceEstimation.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly across the electromagnetic spectrum due to the impact of powerful jets of energy. However, analyzing the long-term variations of these systems is challenging because observations from different eras may not be directly linked, which makes it difficult to understand the underlying behaviors of these complex phenomena. A novel approach called Transfer Learning for AGN Spectrum Decomposition (TL4SD) utilizes a pre-trained neural network to analyze broad-band energy spectra of AGNs, decomposing them into their fundamental components and accounting for variations in the source's strength and energy levels. By leveraging this technique, researchers can investigate the long-term behaviors of these varied systems by considering both temporal patterns and physical processes affecting the energy spectra. Utilizing this approach, a study examines the energy spectra of the AGN 3C 54 over a 15-year observation period, exploring both short-term and long-term variations in its energy distributions. The findings reveal periodic changes in the energy levels of 3C 54, along with significant shifts in the energy spectra of its jet and black hole components over an observed period of nearly two decades. The research provides a detailed analysis of the 3C 54 energy spectrum, explaining the challenges faced in studying long-term variations of these complex systems and highlighting the advantages of using TL4SD to analyze broad-band energy spectra of moving targets. The approach used in this study is generally applicable to analyzing the energy spectra of moving targets with changing energy patterns. The 3C 54 dataset demonstrates the capability of TL4SD to analyze both short-term and long-term variations in energy spectra, while the approach itself is suitable for evaluating moving target spectra across different energy levels and time periods. The research on 3C 54 also offers a useful case study for exploring the physical processes governing energy distributions in these varied systems and sheds light on the effectiveness of machine learning techniques in analyzing complex astrophysical phenomena. The interactive tool presented in the appendix of the paper is available at https://tl4sd-tool.app/. The TL4SD approach and the 3C 54 analysis are published in The Astrophysical Journal, while the original 3C 54 dataset was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Through the application of Gaussian fitting to multiple images of 21 candidates from the Palermo-Newton survey and 10 candidates from the ATLAS survey, we developed a method to assess the point spread function for each image, accounting for factors like telescope temperature, field position, and air currents. This approach allowed us to accurately model the point spread function, thereby enhancing the detection of binary asteroids in large scale surveys covering wide fields. Our analysis of selected targets from the Palermo-Newton survey, which have orbital periods likely exceeding a day, revealed that the 10 most likely binary asteroid candidates are comprised solely of one prominent component, suggesting that many such asteroids may have hidden binary companions. To analyze network peer effects, researchers often utilize exogenous changes to explicit connections within a network. However, many networks lack clear edges, making it challenging to identify how interactions between distant individuals influence each other. This issue is particularly prevalent in consumption and friendship networks that are often characterized by indirect relationships. To address this problem, the authors innovate an empirical strategy that extracts implicit edges from data on distant peer interactions, utilizing a spatial Durbin model with geographical weight matrices. By applying this method to large-scale Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) datasets containing information about respondents' geographical connections and preferences for public goods, the authors are able to recover the structure of friendship networks without prior knowledge and assess their impact on individual behavior, controlling for explicit connections. Failing to account for unobserved correlations between distant peers would lead to biased estimates of network peer effects, as demonstrated by the authors through simulated data. Furthermore, their results show that network peer effects are evident, even among physically distant individuals, and that they extend beyond observed connections, contributing significantly to behavior in areas without direct connections. Ultimately, this research on anonymous, indirect relationships in a consumption network provides a new perspective on the concept of "nearness" that underlies many peer influence models. Ultimately, it demonstrates the feasibility and utility of extracting implicit edges from data on interactions between distant individuals, offering a valuable tool for detecting hidden connections in various networks. In addition to consumption networks, the authors' approach can be applied to other settings, such as communication networks, where relationships between individuals who are not connected directly are also common, as shown in the MTurK example. In these cases, recovering the structure of connections without prior knowledge can yield a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics of peer influence. In the process, the authors also address methodological challenges associated with estimating random effects, as well as controlling for unobserved correlations between distant peers, making their approach applicable to various peer networks. From an empirical perspective, this research yields novel insights into the connections between individuals within a consumption network, while from a methodological standpoint, it introduces an innovative strategy for constructing weight matrices for spatial models based on geographical data, allowing researchers to investigate network peer effects in scenarios with unspecified edges within a network. Ultimately, it provides a framework with which the effects of network peer influence can be examined in contexts where relationships between individuals who are not directly connected exert a significant impact on behavior. The Nambu-Goldstone theorem is inherently linked to the spontaneous breaking of continuous symmetries in the mass spectrum of particles. However, the massive meson, kaon, in the kaon condensation model, appears to be an exception to this rule, thus necessitating a reinterpretation of its mass generation mechanism. We propose a novel perspective on this phenomenon by introducing a meson composite, which is coupled to a meson pair through a four-fermion interaction and arises as a result of strong interactions. We then derive a general expression for the mass of this composite, which is applicable in situations where quark and antiquark masses are asymmetric. We then apply this approach to a model based on the kaon condensation scenario, which meets the criteria of asymptotic freedom and includes a heavy composite meson with a mass anomaly that is mediated by the kaon pair. We also demonstrate that this model complies with the conditions set by the kaon condensation scenario and undergoes color screening as the density increases with time. Additionally, we examine the vector and axial-vector form factors of the heavy composite meson and determine that they behave similarly to those of the heavy composite meson without density, which is mediated by the kaon pair. We also investigate the vector and axial-vector currents and explain that the axial-vector current of the heavy composite meson is conserved, while the vector current is not, thus leading to a non-zero mass of the heavy composite meson. We also compare this approach with other methods used to calculate the mass of the heavy composite meson in the kaon condensation scenario. We also used the QCD two-point function approach to verify the consistency of our results with those obtained using the four-fermion interaction approach, which include the mass of the heavy composite meson, the kaon condensation density, as well as the vector and axial-vector form factors. We also used the finite temperature finite density QCD two-point function approach to determine the thermodynamic potentials of the heavy composite meson system at finite temperature and density. We also used the thermal dependence of the thermodynamic potentials to determine the thermal phase transition of the heavy composite meson system in the kaon condensation scenario. We also used the QCD two-point function approach to determine the momentum dependence of the thermodynamic potentials of the heavy composite meson system at finite momentum. We also used the momentum dependence of the thermodynamic potentials to determine the momentum dependence of the heavy composite meson system in the kaon condensation scenario

Researchers who use graphene as a growth substrate for epitaxial materials often encounter a problem where different materials domains form during synthesis at a single temperature. To understand this complication, researchers who grow materials on graphene typically conduct post-synthesis analyses of the resulting epitaxial layers. In contrast, this study grows ferr ferromagnetic iron germanium on graphene at various temperatures and studies the formation of domains in real-time using a combination of in situ electron microscopy and diffraction. The results show that temperatures between 450-475 degrees Celsius favor the formation of large domains of ferr iron germanium, while temperatures above 475 degrees Celsius or below 450 degrees Celsius result in smaller domains or different material compositions. The findings of this study explain previous inconsistent results and provide a straightforward method for controlling the domain structure of materials during growth. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the capability of in situ electron microscopy to directly observe the formation of domains in real-time, which can be applied to the study of other materials grown on graphene. Moreover, it has been observed that the domain structure of ferr iron germanium is not completely random, but rather follows a specific orientation with respect to the graphene substrate, which can be altered by changing the growth temperature. The exact mechanism of how the growth temperature affects the domain structure of materials grown on graphene remains unclear and requires further investigation. The outcome of this study highlights the significance of considering the domain structure of materials in the development of spin, optoelectronic and thermoelectric devices made from semiconductor materials grown on graphene. The temperature-dependent domain structure of ferr iron germanium has been successfully recreated in ex situ samples, which demonstrates the durability of this material and its potential for mass production. The study of this material has been published in the prestigious journal Nature Materials and was featured on the front page. The outcome of this research has been presented at prestigious conferences including the Materials Research Society and the American Physical Society conferences in the United States of America, as well as the International Conference on Advanced Materials at the University of Tokyo in Japan. The knowledge acquired from this study has been utilized in the development of a thermoelectric device made from iron germanium and has shown a significant improvement in performance when the domain structure is controlled. The study of this material has also been featured in the cover page of the Journal of Materials Chemistry A published in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. A significant challenge in developing effective multi-label classification models lies in acquiring large datasets with expensive annotations. To address this issue, a new sampling method called single-to-multi-label (S2M) is proposed to generate pseudo-multi-label data from existing single-label datasets. Unlike traditional methods that generate random label combinations, S2M builds on the existing annotations by creating a hierarchical relationship between categories. It utilizes a graph-based structure to identify categorizations that often co-occur and those that do not, and then employs a random walk algorithm to generate pseudo-multi-labels. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance when compared to existing approaches and baseline methods in both conventional and semi-supervised settings, and shows that using S2M sampled data yields significant gains in classification tasks using both supervised and unsupervised neural network models. Furthermore, the method is versatile and applicable to various tasks and datasets. A detailed analysis of the proposed method's components and a hypothesis on how it enhances the effectiveness of classification models are also presented. Additionally, the method's limitations and possible avenues for future improvement are discussed. Experimentation with the proposed method is demonstrated on three existing single-label datasets and three multi-label datasets that it was trained on, and it is suggested that the S2M sampling method provides a promising solution for generating pseudo-multi-label data with reduced annotation costs. The code and datasets used in the experimentation are available at https://github.com/kuangshu/S2M. The approach underlying the S2M sampling method is also applicable to real-world multi-label classification settings, and it is believed that the method can be valuable for a wide range of applications involving machine learning classification tasks. The proposed method's effectiveness is evaluated in both conventional and semi-supervised settings, and it is found that the S2M sampled data yields improved performance when compared to existing approaches and baseline methods using various evaluation metrics, and with models including DeepWalk, MLP, and BERT. The method's components and the random walk algorithm are not inherently expensive to compute, and it is anticipated that the method can be valuable for a wide range of applications involving machine learning classification tasks with large annotation costs. Medical research institutions and organizations are increasingly facing data privacy challenges when conducting studies and collecting health data from participants.  To address this issue, a new federated learning approach called FedHealth has been developed to efficiently train a wide range of machine learning models for wearable activity recognition by reducing data exchange between institutions.  Compared to standard techniques, FedHealth leads to wearable activity recognition accuracy improvements of 8% and 3% for classifying individual activities and complex scenarios, respectively.  Beyond activity recognition, FedHealth also demonstrates the ability to accurately classify simple and complex medical conditions from electronic health records with increased precision of 15% and 10%, respectively.  The effectiveness of FedHealth is attributed to 1) a newly proposed local step regulation strategy that reduces data exchange while maintaining model performance, 2) a data regularization technique that prevents degradation of the local model, and 3) a new approach for estimating participant data completeness.  The FedHealth framework and algorithms have been publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/liyouse/FedHealth.  The code has been successfully used in real-world applications and presents opportunities for future research.  A hypothetical scenario where hospital districts compete to provide accurate health data is also presented.  The feasibility and advantages of FedHealth have been validated through real-world deployments and emerging opportunities are discussed. Portfolio management strategies for cloud computing resources are influenced by optimization techniques, and researchers are continually developing more effective methods to utilize machine learning. Utility optimization and multi-objective optimization are two prominent approaches that can be used separately or in combination to enhance portfolio management. This study employs a mixed integer non-linear programming model to maximize productivity and minimize costs in cloud computing resources. Utility and multi-objective optimization frameworks are applied to improve the model's performance. However, these optimization methods require precise computational power and extensive memory, which can be challenging to achieve efficiently even with cloud computing resources. To overcome this limitation, the researchers propose using the MOEA framework on a generic optimization approach. The resulting method is tested on a representative dataset consisting of 1000 instances, each representing a set of cloud computing resources with distinct characteristics. The evaluation criteria include the number of instances optimized, the difference in productiveness, the cost savings, and the computational time required. The proposed method demonstrates a significant advantage over the traditional utility optimization approach, showcasing the effectiveness of machine learning in cloud computing portfolio management. The research highlights the importance of model precision, the choice of optimization approach, and the machine learning algorithm used, which significantly impact the effectiveness of the method. The study also emphasizes the potential applications of this research in real-world scenarios, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform, by presenting a cloud portfolio management system as an open-source platform. The system enables users to generate and manage portfolios of virtual machines based on open-source software, which can be downloaded from GitHub. The study suggests that machine learning enhances the efficiency of utility optimization, reduces the computational time required, and increases the effectiveness of cloud computing resources portfolio management. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the traditional utility optimization approach, supporting the claim that machine learning can be a powerful tool in portfolio management, even without prior knowledge of the problem domain. The research contributes to the development of cloud computing resources portfolio management using machine learning, provides actionable insights for industry leaders, and presents the associated code and data on popular open-source platforms. The efficiency of an interview scheduling algorithm is directly impacted by the method used to assign candidates to panels, a task known as panel creation. This paper tackles the bi-criteria problem of finding the best panel configuration from a set of possible combinations, taking into account both the number of panels required and the number of candidates involved. To effectively solve this problem, we develop a grid-based approach that leverages a linear ordering of candidates, ensuring that the most versatile individuals are assigned to crucial panels. A key component of our algorithm involves determining a linear ordering of candidates, which we achieve by calculating a score that reflects each individual's level of versatility. This score is calculated as the number of panels they are eligible to participate in, with higher scores indicating greater versatility. Our algorithm is designed to operate in a polynomial time complexity of $O(|E| \cdot |V|^{3.5})$, where $|E|$ represents the number of eligible candidate combinations and $|V|$ represents the total number of candidates. This algorithmic solution can be further improved using a more efficient scoring function that reduces the time complexity to $O(|E| \cdot |V|^2)$. This paper also includes a comprehensive experimental study conducted on real-world data sets, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. This research is particularly relevant to recruitment processes, but the algorithmic solution presented can be applied to any problem involving the assignment of candidates to panels. This is because the natural properties of such problems - in particular, the bi-criteria nature of finding the most versatile candidates for key panels - are inherent and not specific to the recruitment context. This makes the algorithmic contribution a valuable general solution that can be adapted to a wide range of applications sharing these common properties. This paper has been submitted to the journal Algorithmica and is currently under review. The asymmetric production of leptoquark pairs in an electron-proton or a positron-proton collider has been overlooked in previous research. We investigate this process for both photon-exchange and scalar leptoquark types, considering various leptoquark combinations and identifying the most promising ones for detection. Due to the asymmetric nature of the process, only specific leptoquark charges are produced, which can be both beneficial and limiting. Nevertheless, our findings indicate that certain leptoquark pairs, such as the second generation $SU(2)$ doublet and single leptoquark, could be viable objects for study with existing experiments like ATLAS and CMS, albeit under certain energy and luminosity conditions. Additionally, we analyze the opportunities presented by the LHeC and future electron-proton colliders. A proposed analysis utilizes leptoquark decay into electrons and quarks. A generic cut-based selection strategy is introduced, and optimization of kinematic variables is suggested for enhanced sensitivity. Although the asymmetric leptoquark production faces significant background competition, particularly from minijet events, it remains a viable research path with scope for improving the current standard model sensitivity. A leptoquark mass reach function is presented and demonstrated to offer relevant information for future experiments and potential advances in the field. Ultimately, the research highlights the importance of experimentally verifying leptoquark properties through comprehensive analysis of their production, decay, and interference patterns. A proposed dataset estimation method is also outlined, along with a discussion of potential risks and advantages associated with leptoquark physics research. A companion code is available for public use at https://www.github.com/LeptoQuarkPheno/asymmetricLQ. For the suitable leptoquark combinations, the main advantages, limitations, and future directions of the asymmetric production process in hadronic colliders are summarized in a table. A proposed strategy for further experimentation with leptoquarks is also presented in a table listing suitable leptoquark charges, scattering processes, quark and lepton flavors, and relevant particle properties. A comprehensive theoretical and experimental analysis of leptoquark properties is illustrated in a flow chart. A suggested research plan for leptoquark physics is depicted in a mind map. A leptoquark mass reach table is also presented for the ATLAS and CMS experiments and proposed for the LHeC and future electron-proton colliders. A proposed experiment design method is also discussed, along with a code availability statement. A paper appendix is also presented with additional figures

We determine the largest intersection of two metric balls in a Cayley graph based on the Hamming distance, which is particularly important for correcting up to $d$ errors in a $q$-ary code of length $n$. This intersection's volume helps us understand the Cayley graph's structure and is closely related to its diameter. Previously studied cases for $n \leq 4$ with certain constraints on the errors and distance have specific formulas for the intersection's volume. For the Cayley graph $\Sigma_n^q$, with the Hamming distance and up to $d$ errors, we find that its volume can be expressed as $\binom{n}{d} \cdot (q-1)^d$ for $d \leq n$. This formula also applies to graphs with distances greater than $d$ equal to $n$ and provides new insights into those specific cases studied earlier. Furthermore, this formula enables us to calculate the diameter of $\Sigma_n^q$ as $2d$ for $d < n$, and $n$ for $d \geq n$. It is observed that the volume of the intersection remains constant for distances greater than $d$ and equal to $n$, which suggests that the Cayley graph with the Hamming distance and up to $d$ errors has a specific structure that can be useful for code correction. This structure allows us to efficiently find the shortest path between two points in the graph. This research on the Cayley graph's structure can be applied to a broader context of graph distances and provides a meaningful contribution to the understanding of code correction. It is noted that the terms "error" and "distance" are used interchangeably in this research, which refers to the number of steps required to transform one code word into another in the Cayley graph based on the Hamming distance. It is also pointed out that the most efficient algorithm for finding the shortest path in the Cayley graph is already well known, but the research provides additional insights into the graph's structure for specific values of errors and distance. Our analysis focuses on approximate analytic expressions for the sensitivity of PTA experiments, specifically in determining the achievable astrophysical foreground from extended sources, as an alternative to other methods that utilize simulations. We evaluated the precision of these approximate formulas in comparison to more nuanced approaches, considering various factors such as data integration intervals, noise levels, and specific PTA projects. Our study reveals that approximate formulas generally offer accurate results for optimal sensitivity calculations but tend to overestimate the achievable sensitivity for more stringent criteria, with the difference becoming more pronounced over time. Furthermore, we observed that the accuracy of these approximate formulas becomes less reliable as the threshold for signal-to-noise ratio increases. Given the complexity of these sources and the limitations of actual PTA data, we conclude that the use of approximate formulas represents a viable and efficient approach, with some slight overestimation of sensitivity in more demanding scenarios. Our study also includes a descriptive analysis of the optimal array properties and specific PTA projects, highlighting their differing sensitivity to certain astrophysical signals. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the practical value of approximate formulas in the context of PTA experiments, filled with real-world complications, and serves as a useful benchmark for any more sophisticated methods developed in the future. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SaulI/pta_sensitivity. Our study was conducted in preparation for the Square Kilometre Array Phase 5 PTA project proposals. In evaluating the detectability of ECRB signals from the EGRET catalog, we found that the optimal PTA project would likely target the entire Northern Sky, utilizing up to 2048 antennas with dish diameters of 0.75 metres, and devoting 7 days to data integration, with a 256-bit floating-point sampling rate of 80 Hz. With this setup, the most sensitive PTA project to Northern Sky ECRB signals would likely achieve a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 30 within a 5-year observation period. Our code can be easily adapted to evaluate other PTA projects and proposals. Our research highlights the limitations of PTA experiments in relation to extended astrophysical sources and highlights the importance of accurately estimating foreground noise in the design of future PTA projects. This research examines the ASEP system to explore the statistics of a third class of particles that can move through the system. All particles interact by following the standard ASEP rules, except when a third class particle encounters a block, it is always absorbed and a block of the same length is created at a random location. We find that the average position of a third class particle, relative to its initial position, follows a parabolic equation and results in the particle being blocked indefinitely, on average, in a time proportional to its position. This leads to a velocity distribution for the particle, which, over time, becomes uniformly distributed across all possible velocities. As time increases, the area occupied by the third class particles takes on a specific shape, forming a parabola, and, on a logarithmic scale, appears as a straight line. This is evident when considering the time it takes for a third class particle to move from one end of the system to the other, which, on a logarithmic scale, follows a normal distribution. This behavior differs from the results seen with a single class of particles, where the time it takes to move from one end of the system to the other follows a power law distribution. This research builds upon the findings of [7, 8] which analyzed the system with only two classes of particles. This work demonstrates that even with three classes of particles, the system adheres to the COCP behavior, which provides evidence that this behavior is robust and versatile. This research has been validated through extensive simulations, with 10^7 steps for each data point, and with various system sizes, to ensure the results are not influenced by finite time or system size effects. This work has been published in the journal Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment, with the paper title "Three-sided asymmetric exclusion process: Investigating the cohomulant class phase transitions" and the paper code [75]. This research has also been presented at the conference MPA-MPM 2023, with the paper code [74]. This project focuses on developing a method for fitting differential models to data generated from a wide range of applications, including those within epidemiology, by utilizing a natural framework of biological plausibility as a key component for model fitting. Although differential models effectively capture the underlying patterns of data, they can be challenging to fit precisely due to the model's stability issues. As a result, researchers often resort to varying the original problem to make the model more solvable, often by removing the component of biological plausibility or requiring the model to have smoothness properties that are not necessarily necessary for its biological significance. Our proposed approach prioritizes biological feasibility while employing a second component to minimize the discrepancy between the model and observed data. By splitting the differential operator into a part that is solvable and a solvable complement, we are able to treat this new component using standard optimization methods. This approach results in a model that not only meets biological standards but also is capable of accommodating complex datasets with noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this method by applying it to a model used in the study of disease transmission, and show that it is able to match the performance of more challenging models that require smoothness constraints. Moreover, our method is a viable solution for a broad range of problems that involve fitting differential models to data generated from various sources and scenarios. We also provide a detailed analysis of the method's computational costs and provide recommendations for optimizing the solution. Additionally, we provide a version of the method that is specifically designed for a model used in the study of a particular disease transmission scenario, and make both the code and model datasets available for download. Our research creates a viable effective model to describe a crucial atom-molecule conversion process in a one-dimensional pendular system, governed by the Yang-Chen-Wang Hamiltonian. By employing the non-rigid pendulum model, we gain a clearer understanding of the underlying dynamics and the emergence of instability. Our findings indicate that the non-rigid pendulum model accurately replicates the behavior of its rigid counterpart in both the molecular beam regime and the overpopulated atomic condition. Furthermore, we discover that the non-rigid pendulum model exhibits a sudden increase in oscillation amplitude in the atomic beam regime, which we believe is a sign of a threshold for atom-molecule conversion. In addition, we observe that the non-rigid pendulum model displays dimer-dimer interactions leading to atom-molecule conversion, as well as the onset of noise-induced instability in the intermolecular interaction regime. Our effective model enables us to identify the onset of atom-molecule conversion and the associated non-equilibrium condensate phase, which we believe will be crucial for understanding recent experimental observations involving noise-induced instability in pendular systems. Our results demonstrate that the non-rigid pendulum model offers a useful platform for exploring the dynamics of pendular systems in the presence of atom-molecule conversions and disorder-induced driving forces. Our findings also reveal that the non-rigid pendulum model can emulate the dynamics of multiple pendula, which we believe will provide a new perspective on this well-known but intricate phenomenon. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems involves managing storage partitions, as they require for written data to be precisely located on the DNA molecule. To address this issue, a method that utilizes the design of primer pairs has been proposed, resulting in a system where data is easily identifiable on the molecule without the need for additional information. To further enhance system efficiency, a concept called "de-coded physical layout" was introduced, allowing for easy retrieval of data from the molecule. To demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, a program was developed that utilizes a microcontroller to encode and decode data, as well as a mixer that blends DNA molecules for the storage and recombination tools for data retrieval. To evaluate the proposed method, an assessment metric called "search efficiency" was created, resulting in a report on a 10-hour experiment where data was stored in DNA and successfully recovered after multiple attempts. This experiment provided valuable insights into areas such as data storage duration and the effectiveness of varying primer pairs. To facilitate widespread adoption, a DNA data storage system was proposed that utilizes a unique address system called "sequence addresses" that is distinct from conventional addressing methods, offering a promising solution for future large-scale applications. To accelerate the development of DNA data storage systems, a software framework called "Codex" was created that simplifies the design of such systems by providing a set of reusable codes for various system components, allowing developers to focus on innovative ideas rather than repetitive code. To address scalability concerns in DNA data storage systems, a concept called "hierarchical encoding" was introduced, enabling the construction of large-scale systems by combining multiple encodings, as well as a system that utilizes this approach called "Codex Tree" which can support a vast number of addresses after encoding, although it requires additional DNA molecules for this support. To further enhance the Codex Tree system, a method called "fractal encoding" was created that reduces the required number of DNA molecules by incorporating a recursive encoding method, offering a scalable solution for future large-scale applications. To evaluate the Codex Tree system, a performance assessment metric called "encoding density" was developed, resulting in a report on an experiment conducted over ten days, lasting nearly a year, where encoding densities were recorded for varying tree depths and branch lengths, yielding a codex tree model that can support up to 450 addresses per molecule with a storage duration of a year, as well as a smaller codex tree model supporting over 100 addresses per molecule with a storage duration of ten years. Accurate representation of riverbed geometry is crucial for modeling water flow and quality. Despite advancements in geophysical imaging, many rivers, especially in tropical regions, require alternative methods to understand their substrates. A new method, termed Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA), is developed to map riverbeds using flow velocity data and incorporates a variance reduction technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA). By leveraging spatial relationships and approximating the covariance matrix, PCGA enhances the geostatistical approach for making bathymetric estimates. The effectiveness of PCGA was demonstrated on the Orinoco River in Venezuela, where it successfully applied to a $10\times10$ meter section of water using 21 flow velocity measurements and resulted in a bathymetric estimate with a 5% reduction in standard deviation compared to the original data. Further analysis showed that PCGA consistently outperformed traditional geostatistical methods, thus presenting a valuable tool for efficient and accurate riverbed mapping. Recently, a significant amount of research has been focused on enhancing image quality by generating High Dynamic Range (HDR) images from two low-lightness images. These studies often rely on deep learning models to estimate exposure levels and produce HDR images. However, integrating artificial neural networks generally requires substantial amounts of comprehensive data, complicating its implementation for various real-world applications. This research proposes two novel methods, one convolutional neural network-based and the other based on artificial neural networks without a convolutional structure, for estimating exposure levels and producing HDR images. Both schemes successfully reduce the complexity and require less data for training, making them more versatile. Utilizing the Demosaicing-HDR estimation framework, experiments with real-world images demonstrate the efficacy of these proposed schemes, showing a significant improvement in produced HDR images when compared to existing exposure estimation methods. Additionally, both models exhibit robust performance when applied to various real-world scenarios. Experimental data, algorithm codes, and implementation guidelines are available at https://github.com/HengTang89/EDSNR-Net. Furthermore, an evaluation of the proposed schemes is provided at https://github.com/HengTang89/Evaluation-Code. Both repositories are publicly accessible.

Causal deep learning methods aim to incorporate causal knowledge into neural networks, but the diversity of these techniques makes it challenging to assess their limitations and possible areas of research. This study organizes various causal deep learning methods from multiple fields using a framework that categorizes them based on problems and techniques. We evaluated 70 papers from prominent conferences and journals using this framework, highlighting potential research gaps and highlighting the need for more rigorous testing of existing methods. Additionally, we propose a way to assess the validity of conclusions drawn from papers about the Seattle dataset. This study is an extension of our previous work presented at IJCAI 2023. We invite researchers to engage with our framework and the ongoing research, expressing the hope that it will contribute to the advancement of causal deep learning. This extended version of the work is available at https://causal-dl.org/. We encourage readers to explore the content there and provide feedback to the community. The Madsen-Weiss theorem, a significant result in topology, was originally proven by the duo Madsen and Weiss using harmonic integration. However, I have successfully reinterpreted their theorem utilizing the b-principle, specifically through the application of the standard embedding theorem combined with the stability theorems of Harer-Miller and Madsen-Weiss. This reinterpretation reveals a connection between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the target space of the harmonic sphere bundle, thereby establishing a more general form of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The latter is characterized by a specific integral of the harmonic sphere bundle, which is shown to be injective and surjective under certain conditions, thereby mirroring the original Madsen-Weiss theorem. The standard embedding theorem plays a crucial role in this interpretation by providing a necessary framework, while the integration of the harmonic sphere bundle bundle arises as a natural parameter space. The reexamination of the Madsen-Weiss theorem through the lens of the b-principle and the stability theorems of Harer-Miller and Madsen-Weiss offers novel geometric and cohomological inferences that are either unrelated to the original proof or have not been explicitly stated before. The current understanding of the Madsen-Weiss theorem embodies a broader vision where the interplay of the standard embedding theorem, stability theorems, the b-principle, and the harmonic integration theory could provide an integrated and far-reaching generalization of the Madsen-Weiss theorem itself. The research on the Madsen-Weiss theorem has been made more precise by the discovery of several of its subformulations, any of which could potentially be more accessible to the application of the b-principle. The most notable of these subformulations is the representation of the target space of the harmonic sphere bundle as the integral of the harmonic sphere bundle, which has been found to be connected to the Reidemeister torsion, therefore offering an innovative interpretation of this crucial topological invariant. The examination of the Madsen-Weiss theorem has also led to a more general understanding of the integration of the harmonic sphere bundle, which is shown to be a natural parameter space characterized by the standard embedding theorem, therefore providing a more integrated and far-reaching generalization of Harer-Miller's stability theorem. The most groundbreaking finding from this research is the connection between the harmonic sphere bundle integral and the Reidemeister torsion, which was unknown before the current investigation. The study focuses on analyzing how the BDDC performance relies on key parameters in a general setting, and additional insights are gained from a more specific context involving finite elements. The main results are composed of three key findings. Firstly, a lower bound for the smallest eigenvalue of the BDDC operator is established, and this lower limit can be expressed in terms of the smallest eigenvalues of the individual subdomain inverses and the intersection inverses. Secondly, an upper limit for the largest eigenvalue of the BDDC operator is determined, and this upper limit also has a defined relationship with the eigenvalues of the subdomain and intersection inverses. Thirdly, a condition is identified that ensures the convergence of the BDDC method is guaranteed, and this condition is linked to the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of the BDDC operator. The significance of these results becomes apparent in the final section, where the investigation into a specific finite element scenario reveals that the largest possible value of the condition number of the BDDC operator can be determined and, in turn, influences the overall performance of the preconditioner. The research presented here extends and generalizes the specific findings obtained in the study presented in [25]. The techniques and methods introduced here are aimed at being useful in the design and improvement of the BDDC method, particularly in regards to achieving balanced subdomains and improving the overall effectiveness of the preconditioner. The study presented here also offers a solid foundation for the development of cooperative-coarse methods that combine BDDC with other cooperative-coarse techniques, such as Neumann-Neumann and A-FEM, and provides a framework for analyzing these methods. A key assumption of Gaussian diffusion models is that the diffusing system can be characterized by an overall average, independent of the specific initial conditions. However, this assumption is overly broad and doesn't account for situations with correlated or heterogeneous starting points. In this study, we apply a Gaussian diffusion model to investigate systems that begin from a fixed, broad distribution of initial positions. We demonstrate mathematically that such diffusions deviate from the standard Gaussian assumption, resulting in skewness and kurtosis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the effects of correlations among starting points can be viewed as heterogeneous sampling from the average, encompassing situations with both uniform and non-uniform spreading patterns. In addition, we analyze the progression of mean squared displacement, which ultimately conforms to a power law, and derive the associated scaling exponent analytically. Notably, this exponent depends solely on the moment of highest order that is well-defined, offering a way to extract moments from noisy, curved data curves. The benefits of this approach are illustrated using curved data curves generated artificially as well as real-world examples of nanoscale random walks within bulk semiconductors. The developed method is accessible via a user-friendly online tool available at [www.gaussianwalk.org](http://www.gaussianwalk.org). The approach provides a useful strategy for extracting underlying statistical properties from random processes and bulk materials science. The associated data and software are available at [https://github.com/awillig/gaussian_walk](https://github.com/awillig/gaussian_walk). We studied the interplay between self-phase and cross-phase modulation in a loop resonator with identically counterpropagating light modes. Our analysis showed that cross-phase modulation exceeds self-phase modulation by a factor of $\Delta k^2$ when the frequency difference between the modes is large, where $\Delta k$ is the mismatch coefficient. Conversely, self-phase modulation dominates cross-phase modulation by a factor of $2$ when the mismatch is negligible. To validate our findings, we conducted an experiment using a fiber loop resonator and a coherent light source, varying the speed of the counterpropagating modes through changes in fiber optic temperature controls. Our results matched theoretical predictions, demonstrating the distinction between self- and cross-phase modulation in loop resonators. This distinction makes fiber loop resonators suitable for creating robust optical switches based on phase modulation. To achieve this, we proposed a design modification to eliminate the self-phase modulation entirely, thus maximizing the effect of cross-phase modulation. Consequently, we demonstrated an optical switch in a fiber loop resonator with counterpropagating modes, powered by a 2.5 kW laser, capable of generating optical switches with up to 30 dB extinction ratio at speeds of 10 km/s. This performance can be further improved by modifying the resonator to use single-mode fibers with different optical properties. By doing so, we propose the feasibility of constructing large-scale optical switches powered by high-powered coherent light sources. In addition to optical switches, we illustrate the applicability of cross-phase and self-phase modulation in fiber loop resonators to coherent laser spectroscopy, demonstrating the distinction between self- and cross-phase modulation through accurate measurement of frequency shifts during the process. These measurements are crucial for developing this technique further. Ultimately, our study paves the way for leveraging phase modulation in fiber loop resonators in various applications that require precise control over laser frequency fluctuations. These applications include coherent laser spectroscopy, optical switches, and temperature control systems for fiber optic components. Reinforcement learning algorithms are constantly evolving, and the need for methods to systematically modify the curriculum they follow is increasing. A well-curated sequence of tasks can offer a wealth of information about an algorithm's ability to adapt to novel situations. In this study, a straightforward approach is taken to assess the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to adapt to changing curricula by systematically modifying the tasks they need to complete. In contrast to existing evaluations that focus on sudden and extreme changes, this research explores the impact of gradual and controlled changes in the curriculum. A key aspect of this research involves developing a specific metric to measure the curvature of task changes, building on the idea that the difference between two tasks is meaningful only if it represents a significant change for the algorithm. In the experiments conducted, a controlled approach is employed to modify the curriculum for a range of tasks, including both simple synthetic tasks and more complex real-world environments like Minecraft. The results obtained provide valuable insights into the performance of different reinforcement learning algorithms in the face of changing curricula. In particular, the experiments reveal that algorithms that leverage curriculum adaptation successfully are capable of performing just as well as possible in an ever-changing curriculum of the most challenging tasks, even with limited observation of the curriculum's changes. In contrast, algorithms that are less robust to changes in the curriculum tend to perform significantly better when the curriculum changes more gradually, even with the presence of external distractions. The experiments conducted demonstrate the applicability of this evaluation method to a broad range of tasks and algorithms and provide a useful framework for assessing the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to adapt to changing curricula based on explicit feedback from the environment. Process behavior can change significantly in response to various events, making it crucial to analyze processes that evolve over time. Our proposed approach, called the Decoupled Contextual Reachability (DCR) approach, facilitates the analysis of processes with temporal context by utilizing reachability graphs. A process with context is considered safe if its corresponding reachability graph, after accounting for timing constraints, does not contain harmful states. The DCR approach generates a compact and standardized set of context situations that influence process behavior, allowing for its prediction and further analysis. Unlike existing methods that only consider recent past events, the DCR approach also takes into consideration past events that have lasting effects on process behavior, known as contextual footprints. These footprints, combined with the current context, determine the process's future behavior. Our approach and the Baek and Lee's method share a common underlying structure, but they differ in model assumptions and computational complexity. Through benchmark tests and a real-world application, our approach demonstrates improved performance in terms of model size, computational efficiency, and accuracy in predicting process behavior. Furthermore, it provides a more comprehensive understanding of process behavior by uncovering implicit temporal relationships and contextual dependencies. We observed a significant discrepancy in NUV-r colors for the two most massive galaxies within the X-ray luminous groups from the CIG sample, using data from GALEX. Both galaxies with higher masses than approximately one billion solar masses and low central black hole masses exhibit the same NUV-r color, between 4.0 and 4.5, indicating a lack of Balmer peaks in their spectra and suggesting little to no starlight from young stellar populations. This pattern holds true for galaxies within groups that have low central black hole masses and high sauce densities. We propose that these galaxies, despite being massive, lack central supermassive black holes and have isothermal stellar populations, yet the NUV-r color remains unchanged, even when considering different total stellar masses. We also noticed that NUV-r color remains steady, not showing any significant change with total stellar mass. Additionally, we observed a notable decrease in NUV-r color for galaxies with lower masses than approximately one billion solar masses, despite these galaxies already having smaller NUV-r color values. We interpreted this as evidence of a transition phase for galaxies with massive populations, fueled by ongoing star consumption and central black hole growth. We also looked at individual galaxies with low mass and NUV-r color and found similar characteristics, including low central black hole masses and NUV-r colors indicating little to no young stellar populations, yet these galaxies lack the same population characteristics as the most massive galaxies. We suggested that these individual galaxies are also undergoing a transition phase, but with more advanced star consumption and central black hole growth. We also compared our NUV-r color data with other observations, including from SDSS, which show similar NUV-r color Disparities for galaxies with higher masses than approximately one billion solar masses, although the difference is less pronounced than in the CIG sample. We proposed an explanation for this difference as a result of different observation methods, with tighter NUV-r color constraints in the CIG sample due to stricter criteria for galaxy selection. We also looked at the relationship between NUV-r color and the absolute magnitudes of the galaxies in the CIG sample, finding no correlation, whereas we observed a negative correlation in the CIG sample with central black hole masses above 5x10^8 solar masses. Neural machine translation has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks in part to the widespread use of LSTMs and self-learning encoders. Meanwhile, research into neural text generation for non-native languages has been less common, particularly with respect to generating official languages using dialects. This paper presents a novel approach to text generation in a new language using a source language, building on the characteristics of successful neural translation models. We put our approach to use in a practical application, creating a system that generates written Hindi from spoken dialects, and the results show it can effectively replace traditional approaches. Furthermore, our model exhibits promising performance in other tasks, such as text classification and sentiment analysis, and can be fine-tuned to generate text in a dialect different from the one it was originally trained on. This leads to a significant improvement in generating official languages using dialects, as demonstrated by an increase of 21.0% in metric scores for sentiment analysis in one such case. This technique has far-reaching implications, given the widespread use of dialects on social media platforms. To facilitate replication, we have open-sourced our model and associated data sets. This research has the potential to be expanded upon, given the limited amount of work done in the field of neural text generation in new languages using a source language. The rapid evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and changing healthcare guidelines pose significant challenges in allocating limited ICU resources effectively, particularly in the early stages of the pandemic.  A critical issue arises when deciding which patients to admit to limited ICU beds, as the data available initially is often incomplete and lacks diagnostic information. This imbalance causes standard sampling techniques to often prioritize overly common classifications, neglecting rarer and rarer ones. To address this, we present Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), a method that adapts the distribution of sampled negative relationships to mirror the frequency of proposed objects, thereby balancing the distribution of sampled negative relationships. When combined with positive samples, BNPS facilitates the detection of visual relationships by providing a more inclusive set of negative examples and a more precise model by reducing the imbalance between positive and negative samples. Experimental evaluations on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset reveal improved results for our approach, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in several metrics. Galaxies forming in the early universe are subject to gravitational influences that can deviate significantly from idealized, isolated formation models. A computational study employs hydrodynamic simulations to analyze the accretion streams feeding a 10 billion solar mass galaxy and 10-20 million years old. The framework used is a nested approach with a cosmological simulation spanning the appropriate scale and a higher-resolution merger tree for the galaxy's central black hole. A mesh-based, inviscid hydrodynamic model then simulates the flow of accretion streams towards the galaxy. The study identifies distinct patterns of accretion and identifies areas of streaming gas that miss the galaxy and instead collide with nearby galaxies, influencing galaxy evolution through both mergers and rejected accretion. The galactic central black hole grows through disk accretion, with the disk forming in areas of strong stellar winds within the galaxy. The study shows that the standard stellar initial mass function suppresses the formation of massive stars and black holes in the galaxy's center. The study also finds that the galaxy's bulge builds through the consumption of streaming gas and star-forming gas within the galaxy, rather than outside contributions. The study demonstrates that galaxies forming in the early universe are self-sufficient, with the necessary elements to build their own bulge, rather than relying on major mergers. The study suggests that the bulge formation through streaming gas leads to the creation of metal-poor, globular cluster populations in the galaxy. The study implies that the galactic central black hole growth is slowed by the absence of major mergers, resulting in a less massive black hole than in isolated galaxy formation simulations. The study provides a computational explanation for observed relationships between black hole mass and bulge mass or stellar population age. The study includes a comparison with the FUSE and HST observations of the Tidal Tail Galaxy ESO 338-09, which shows evidence of suppressed star formation and a depleted central black hole, consistent with being caused by a large amount of gas that missed the galaxy during its formation. The study also includes a computational examination of the conditions under which galaxies forming in the early universe are subject to major mergers, rather than rejecting accretion streams, finding that this typically requires galaxies with central black holes already 10-100 times more massive than the solar mass black hole in ESO 338-09. The study suggests that the observed properties of ESO 338-09, including its small size, lack of bulge, and central black hole mass, result from rejected accretion

A highly intense X6 solar flare along with widespread coronal mass ejections affected the Earth's magnetic field on November 7th, 2004. This event caused significant disturbances in the upper atmosphere of the Earth and led to the formation of bright clouds of certain chemicals at low altitudes over the Antarctic. Researchers used data from the CONCORDASEV2 instrument to study the effects of this event on the chemistry of the lower atmosphere. They found that the flare led to the formation of a 10km thick cloud of meteors (or a "cloud of polar mesosphere summer jets") at an altitude of 86km, a phenomenon previously observed during the solar maximum of 1999-2002. However, the majority of the cloud formed at an altitude of 80-85km, which is unusual according to previous observations. Additionally, the chemical composition of the upper atmosphere changed more rapidly than usual, with an increase of 20% in the amount of oxygen and a decrease of 30% in the amount of nitrogen. This was followed by a slowdown in atmospheric circulation and temperature increases of up to 40 degrees Kelvin in the polar cap and up to 20 degrees Kelvin in the inner regions. This event also led to the disappearance of polar night time clouds and the formation of new clouds in the inner regions, which took around 14 days to return to their normal state. Moreover, the flare caused a temporary halt in the degradation of the upper atmosphere, with the loss of 1km per month in the height of the 86km cloud layer instead of the usual 2km per month. This event provided a unique opportunity to observe the effects of a strong solar flare on the upper atmosphere of the Antarctic and the resulting changes in the chemistry and temperature of the 80-100km altitude range. It also offered insights into the causes of the changes observed in the upper atmosphere during the 1999-2002 solar maximum, which included increased formation of clouds at high altitudes, changes in the temperature and chemistry of the upper atmosphere, a slowdown in atmospheric circulation, and a halt in the degradation of the upper atmosphere. It was suggested that the main cause of these changes was the increased energy from the Sun interacting with the upper atmosphere rather than the direct effect of solar flares. However, the November 2004 event showed that solar flares can have a significant impact on the chemistry of the upper atmosphere at low altitudes and may also affect the lower atmosphere. KIC 9267654 is a star in the lower part of the subgiant branch with a slow and twisted rotation profile. To understand the unusual rotation pattern, several hypotheses are proposed, including the possibility of it being influenced by external sources such as a close companion, a planetary system, or tidal interactions with a initially rapidly rotating star. Alternatively, the rotation profile could be the result of internal processes, such as mass transfer from a rapidly rotating planet or small close companion during stellar evolution, or it could be attributed to a rotationally induced anisotropic mass loss. To further investigate, observations of chemical abundance patterns and search for planetary companions through precise dynamical measurements are suggested. The study of KIC 9267654 provides a unique example of how external and internal sources of interaction with a star can reveal itself through the analysis of rotation profile. The research is also an indication of how precise photometric and spectroscopic data can be used to discover similar phenomena in the future surveys of planetary systems and stellar interactions. The method presented in this research can be applied to other stars with irregular rotation patterns, such as the one observed in KIC 9267654, which are expected to be found with the help of future surveys like PLATO and TESS.
