Fake news has been a rising concern on social media platforms, and the rapid dissemination it can cause makes identifying it a pressing issue. To combat the spread of false information, our proposed model, MetaFEND, leverages a multi-task framework that combines the benefits of both sentiment classification and fact-checking to enhance the detection of fake news. Within the framework, we introduce a hierarchical structure where the overall credibility assessment guides fact-checking, and incorporate a sentiment analysis component that identifies the emotional content of the content, thereby capturing the creator's intended effect. Utilizing a deep learning approach, we switch to a feature-rich representation based on neural networks, and conduct extensive experiments on the RealNews-2020 and FCDS datasets to demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over existing methods. Additionally, we analyze the metadata influence and the difficulty level of instances on model performance. Our proposed MetaFEND model has been successfully applied to instances where the true label is unknown, leading to a new benchmark in the community. Our code and datasets are available for public use at https://github.com/liuwenqing MetaFEND.

This research investigates a one-dimensional transport equation with periodic conditions, characterized by a nonlocal flux and no dissipation. The solution's behavior is examined under specific conditions: it starts with odd, smooth data and there is no initial disturbance beyond a certain wavelength. The solution's development reveals an infinite growth of the solution's norm over a finite period of time. The time frame is specifically shown to be $\min\left(\frac{2\sigma}{c},\frac{\pi^2}{cL}\right)$, where $\sigma$ represents the distance between discontinuities, $c$ denotes the velocity, and $L$ indicates the period. The study also demonstrates that the solution experiences an infinite growth rate within this time frame, as predicted by the power law $\|u\| \simeq (\frac{1}{2}\min\left(2\sigma, \pi L\right)c)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(1-t_0)^{-1}$, where $t_0$ equals $\min\left(\frac{2\sigma}{c},\frac{\pi^2}{cL}\right)$. The research on the equation also reveals that even initial data that are not smooth will result in solutions that grow infinitely fast. The current study expands upon previous work done on a similar transport equation with local flux, where it was shown that even initial data with certain properties will lead to solutions that grow infinitely fast. The corresponding result from the previous work was proven under the condition that the velocity of transport satisfies $|c| < \frac{\pi^2}{L}$, where $L$ represents the period. The research on the original problem includes an additional transport equation with nonlocal flux and dissipation, as well as a corresponding smooth solution problem. The study further explores the behavior of a specific solution problem with even initial data that are not smooth, and reveals that the solution will exhibit infinite growth over a finite period of time. The time frame for this growth is characterized as $\min\left(\frac{2\sigma}{c+ \sqrt{c^2+4\beta}},\frac{\pi^2}{c+ \sqrt{c^2+4\beta}}\right)$, where the original equation includes a dissipation term $\beta$, velocity $c$, and distance between discontinuities $\sigma$. Along with establishing the concept of a quaternary GCA pair, our investigation involved identifying existing (23,12,1) Golay screens and testing their ability to form a quaternary GCA pair. Our study revealed that out of the 15 possible permutations of points within a (23,12,1) Golay screen, only 7 of them can be part of a quaternary GCA pair, while the other 8 are not feasible. Furthermore, our analysis facilitated the establishment of a connection between the permutation of points within a (23,12,1) Golay screen and the array pairs that can be created from them. Additionally, our screening process provided a foundation for exploring other array pairs that can be created using a (23,12,1) Golay screen. Perhaps most significantly, our work revealed that a quaternary GCA pair can be conceptualized as a combination of two array pairs that are complementary in three dimensions, and our analysis allowed us to define the conditions under which a set of 16 points in 3-D space can be considered a trinary GCA pair. Recovering a system's underlying structure from observations and probabilistic inference is challenging, especially when the system changes over time. Our research introduces a novel method, called Probabilistic Structure Learning from Time Series (PSLTs), which enables us to recover a system's underlying structure using time series observations and a single observation from a different system instance that shares the same structure. Unlike traditional approaches, PSLTs does not require access to the new system's parameters or observations beyond a initial sample. Our algorithm utilizes a greedy approach with a priority function to prioritize node selection for the underlying structure, and we prove that it recovers the correct structure in a linear time complexity of O(n). We also introduce a new evaluation metric called the Structure Coverage Ratio (SCR) to assess the learned structure's accuracy and present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of PSLTs in various scenarios, including systems with changing parameters and non-linear relationships. Our research and the proposed algorithm are applicable to various domains, including complex physiological systems, such as the human body, for which a linear structure can be determined to inform data collection via a treatment or experiment. We also provide an implementation of the algorithm and evaluation metrics in the form of an algorithmic package called PSLETS available online. This package enables users to reproduce our results and incorporate the algorithm into their own projects. We further outline potential future directions for the algorithm and associated evaluations. This paper introduces a concept it terms "partitional structures" on stable homotopy groups, represented as elements of a graded polynomial ring constructed from the rationalised Morava $E$-theory theory. These partitional structures, which can be viewed as invariants of finite localised field theories, are then employed to develop an Adams-Novikov spectral sequence, with connections to the classical sequence established by Adams, Novikov, and Leroux. Furthermore, the partitional structures facilitate the determination of stable homotopy groups for certain locally coloured finite neighbourhoods of the point in the stable homotopy category. This category is equivalent to the category of finite localised field theories. This partitional structure framework can be extended to the Morava $E$-theory theory itself, leading to a more sophisticated Adams-Novikov spectral sequence. This sequence, in turn, gives rise to a pattern of vanishing phenomena, with implications for the coefficients of the Morava $E$-theory theory itself. This leads to a deeper understanding of the relationships between the Morava $E$-theory theory, the Steenrod algebra, and the GL_2 action on elliptic formal group laws. This knowledge is further utilised to analyze various invariants, including the rank, Hilbert 90 rank, and Atiyah-Singer $\alpha$-genus rank of the Morava $E$-theory theory. This analysis reveals that all these invariants remain constant throughout the family of elliptic formal group laws, despite changes in the genus. This phenomenon is explained by the partitional structure's relationship with the global Galois group action on the Morava $E$-theory theory. This leads to a prediction that the rank of the Morava $E$-theory theory will remain invariant under the action of the absolute Galois group, with implications for its potential to contribute to the vanishing of the cohomology of the absolute Galois group over fields of characteristic two. This possibility is particularly noteworthy, given the difficulty in determining the cohomology of the absolute Galois group $\pi_1(\mathbb{Z})$ in this characteristic. This difficulty arises because the standard approaches, relying on local methods, have proved unproductive due to the limitations of local methods in characteristic two. This paper proposes an alternative approach, grounded in homotopy theory, with the potential to shed light on the cohomology of the absolute Galois group in characteristic two. A region of interest (ROI) is a confined section of an image where a pathologic change is likely to occur, and accurately labeling this region within an image can be a challenging and time-consuming task, especially for 3D medical images. These images are complex and have a high dimensionality, making them difficult to analyze using conventional image analysis techniques. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become a crucial component in analyzing these images by facilitating the efficient extraction of important features from raw input data. When employed in a shallow architecture, CNNs can effectively identify and outline areas of interest within an image by leveraging their ability to recognize patterns and shapes. This paper presents a novel approach to automatically segment ROIs in 3D medical images using a shallow architecture that incorporates CNNs and encourages the model to focus on the most critical areas of the image by introducing a class-balanced learning technique that emulates the behavior of human annotators. By leveraging this approach, we enhance our understanding of the relationships between ROI segmentation and classification and provide a framework for evaluating the reliability of ROIs that have been automatically segmented. This approach also facilitates the creation of a robust and accurate model for automatically segmenting ROIs in 3D medical images, as demonstrated by our empirical results showing that this approach can successfully apply our technique to various types of 3D medical images, including lung nodule segmentation. This approach has the added benefit of generating a reliable proxy label that can be used to train a deep architecture, thereby providing a seamless pathway from the collection of raw 3D medical images to the training of a deep architecture that can analyze these images. This approach can be applied to various types of 3D medical images, including those with complex segments, such as whole-body MRI scans. This paper also highlights the advantages of using a shallow architecture that incorporates CNNs over other machine learning techniques, demonstrating that our approach can efficiently reduce label drift when the model is transferred to different annotators and provide a more accurate proxy label when compared to other techniques, demonstrating the effectiveness and versatility of this novel approach. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at the Conference of Medical Image Analysis. These new categories comprise all possible combinations of two distinct, non-identical element sets and come equipped with a designated distance metric. A key feature of these graphs is that they contain a central infinite path on a distance of 3 from any starting point. The Group Lasso algorithm from [10] has been effectively applied to reduce model complexity by grouping and penalizing variables. We have developed a Convex Integer programming method based on the Group Lasso algorithm, which extends variable selection to both continuous and categorical data. This new method, named CICGLasso, precisely implements the Group Lasso technique and accurately handles categorical variables by employing a smoothing function. We have tested CICGLasso on datasets featuring both categories and continuity, and have compared its performance to existing methods such as elastic-net and power-variational function. Our results indicate that CICGLasso excels in variable selection and classification accuracy across these datasets. Moreover, we have made CICGLasso accessible through a user-friendly interface via the R programming language. This new method and associated results are poised to enhance variable selection and classification techniques for a broad spectrum of statistical applications. The underlying code has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/hosseinjahedi/CICGLasso. The associated R package can be downloaded from CRAN at the following address: https://cran.r-project.org/package=CICGLasso. A worked example has been provided below to ensure the ease of use for researchers and practitioners. We have a vision that this new method and associated code will serve as a foundation for the development of more advanced machine learning techniques involving variable selection. A potential extension to the current method involves combining the Group Lasso technique with the network formulation proposed in [7]. We have an ongoing project that aims to integrate the proposed method with the mentioned network formulation, and we are confident that this integration will result in the development of new learning techniques that are more sophisticated. The associated code has the potential to serve as a starting point for the implementation of these advanced learning techniques. We have an ongoing project that is focused on combining the Group Lasso technique with the network formulation proposed in [7], and we are confident that this combination will lead to the development of more advanced learning techniques. Recent advances in natural language processing are largely driven by large language model pretraining, and our research strives to understand the fundamentals of this paradigm by examining one of its core assumptions: that models trained on factual knowledge triples retain relevant information for a wide range of question-answering tasks. To investigate this assumption, we compared the performance of models pretrained on knowledge graphs consisting of factual triples against those trained on traditional text-based data for 13 question-answering tasks and 2 evaluation metrics. Although models trained on knowledge graphs frequently achieved higher performance than their text-trained counterparts, the disparity was more pronounced for tasks involving entities not previously encountered in the training data. Our detailed analysis of 5,000 triple-training instances and 20,000 text-based training instances for the Natural Language Inference task revealed that models pretrained on knowledge graphs are more resistant to noise, while models trained on knowledge graphs and text-based data for the same metric showed a high correlation of 0.75. Our research provides a framework for evaluating model performance based on their ability to generalize to unencountered entities and offers a straightforward method for enhancing model performance by incorporating relevant knowledge graphs. Our code and models are available for public use at https://github.com/TallGuy84/llm-eval. This paper introduces a novel algorithm that refines line joins in vector graphics, specifically line joins at corners and fans, which are critical in creating visually appealing drawings. Our approach modifies the original algorithm by Gooden to produce the desired shape of line joins and combines it with a point-inflation technique to achieve more accurate results. Unlike traditional methods, our algorithm ensures that the intersection points of lines are precisely located at the centers of the desired shape, resulting in simplified code and enhanced readability of drawings. Our proposed method demonstrates improved rendering of line joins at corners and fans, eliminating the need for additional scaling operations, which are now unnecessary due to the precise placement of intersection points. Furthermore, our algorithm facilitates the inflation of points, which is essential for high-resolution rendering, despite the risk of it causing unexpected corner effects in certain cases. We have tested our algorithm using popular vector graphics libraries and real-world examples to validate its efficacy and efficiency. Our algorithm has been publicly available as part of the Apache Commons Mathematics Library since the release of Apache Commons Math version 3.6 in 2023. We have also included a sample application demonstrating the practical use of our algorithm in the Apache Commons Mathematics website. Our algorithm has been employed in several real-world applications, including the rendering of paths in SVG images and the generation of plots in mathematics education software. We have compared our algorithm with existing approaches, including the standard technique used in PostScript, which results in line joins that are offset by half the width of line strokes, and the algorithm used in SVG, which produces line joins that are also offset, although to a lesser extent than PostScript. Our proposed method offers improved performance, achieving line joins that are precisely centered, whereas existing methods produce line joins that are always offset from the desired center, although the extent of the offset varies. We have also tested our algorithm against various test cases to validate its efficacy, including fan-shaped line joins, corner line joins, inflated points, point-inflation edges, and nested line joins. Our algorithm has been found to be highly efficient, requiring minimal computational resources, which is crucial for its practical use in real-world applications involving large datasets and complex geometries. We have compared our algorithm with a range of existing approaches, including the proposed algorithm by Gooden, which our method is based on, and the standard technique used in PostScript, which is widely used but has significant limitations. Our proposed method has several advantages over these existing approaches, including its simplicity, efficiency, and the precise placement of intersection points, which eliminates the need for additional scaling

A novel speech enhancement method known as the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) is proposed, consisting of a time-domain and a frequency-domain sub-network that cooperate to improve speech quality in noisy environments. The frequency-domain sub-network uses a complex-valued extension of the Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN) to efficiently handle short-term frequency variations, while the time-domain sub-network leverages a deep recurrent structure to effectively manage long-term time variations. The unique collaboration of the two sub-networks occurs through a dual-path architecture, facilitating the exchange of spatial and temporal frequency information, and ultimately yielding a higher quality speech signal with lower computational requirements than existing time and frequency domain speech enhancement methods. Experimental evaluations conducted on the deep noise removal dataset demonstrate the DPCRN's ability to produce higher quality speech signals with a score improvement of 0.136 in the PESQ metric and a decrease of 1.157 in the SSD metric, compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the DPCRN shows a reduced model size and a speed-up of 3-4 times in real-time processing, making it a highly efficient and effective speech enhancement technique. The DPCRN code will be made publicly available. Word Sense Disambiguation relies heavily on speech enhancement, and the proposed method contributes a significant improvement to this domain as well. The proposed DPCRN model stands out due to its domain-agnostic nature, and it achieves the current state-of-the-art performance on several datasets, including the widely-used WSD dataset from Wikipedia, where it demonstrates a 5.3% increase in F1-score over the current record. The model's versatility is demonstrated by applying it to tasks and datasets it has not been trained on, and the validity of its unique architecture is supported by competitive performance in speech enhancement tasks compared to widely-used baselines, despite being relatively simple. When the model is simplified to a planar setup with horizontal periodicity, the convective flow's dynamics can be further reduced to a one-dimensional problem where the heat flux is controlled by the fluid's velocity and the temperature difference between its upper and lower boundaries. According to this model, the heat flux should increase proportionally to the square root of the temperature gradient, consistent with earlier observations in Rayleigh-Bénard convection experiments involving air. When applied to convective flows within a spherical shell, the model predicts specific patterns of heat transport, including the phenomenon known as the supercritical heat flux plateau, which has been observed in experiments using liquid metals in spherical containers. Notably, the model also predicts that the plateau's upper bound is determined by the ratio of the fluid's velocity to the temperature contrast between the inner and outer boundaries, rather than the radius of the sphere, as seen in experiments with liquid metals. In addition, the model indicates that the plateau's lower bound is governed by the ratio of the fluid's viscosity to the temperature contrast between the inner and outer boundaries, which has not been previously documented. We investigate the formation of multipartite entanglement among atoms in a cavity system, incorporating both classical and quantum communications. An initial cavity entanglement with an unconnected atom serves as a generator for multipartite entanglement among multiple detached atoms via classical information. Using the Yang-Chen-Wang method, we derive an approximate generalized dynamical equation for the system's entanglement, analyzing the generation and degradation of entanglement among the atoms. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which Bell-state entanglement among all atoms can be genuinely created and analyze its evolution over time. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effects of various parameters on entanglement formation, offering potential applications in quantum networks. Additionally, we propose an autonomous scheme for quantum memory based on this cavity system, enabling self-entanglement of an arbitrary amount of memory atoms via a single cavity. Numerical experiments with real-system data from a superconducting cavity also validate our theoretical findings either approximately or exactly, depending on the complexity of the system. This research paves the way for the development of quantum memories and networks that can withstand both abrupt changes in the environment and gradual degradation over time. This robust entanglement generation and maintenance mechanism is compatible with various quantum platforms, including trapped ions and nitrogen-vacancy centers. This work is relevant to the development of reliable quantum memories and networks that can maintain entanglement in the presence of decoherence caused by both slow and sudden environmental changes. This research is applicable to different quantum systems, such as trapped ions and nitrogen-vacancy centers, and provides insights into the conditions necessary for genuine multipartite entanglement among distant atoms connected through a cavity. This cavity system can serve as a self-sustaining quantum memory for an arbitrary number of detached atoms, offering a potential design for future quantum networks. Social media feedback monitoring relies heavily on analyzing tens of thousands of tweets daily.
These tweets are primarily classified into positive, negative, or neutral sentiment types.
To achieve this efficiently, a proposed system utilizes a long short-term memory (LSTM) network
to classify a single day's worth of tweets (around 50,000 in number) by sending it a compressed
file of just 1.92 megabytes.
The system starts with an unoptimized approach to classify individual tweets, which yields a
fifty-point sentiment intensity annotation.
This involves training an LSTM network on around 5000 randomly selected tweets with annotated
sentiment scores.
To classify all tweets belonging to a given day, the system trains an LSTM network on the
previous day's processed data, which results in a compressed model of about 384 kilobytes.
This model is capable of processing new tweets at a cost of 0.00042 dollars per tweet.
The system's efficacy is demonstrated through a trial on around 20,000 tweets with annotated
sentiment scores, which yields a 79 percent accuracy rate in classification and a 21 percent
margin of error in calculating the sentiment intensity.  A 22 percent accuracy gain and a
26 percent margin of error gain are achieved when using the LSTM network with aspect-based
sentiment annotation.  A trial on around 50,000 unannotated tweets shows a 78 percent accuracy
in classification and a 22 percent margin of error in calculating the sentiment intensity. 
The system demonstrates a significant reduction in data costs, along with the LSTM network's
ability to adapt to changing language patterns over time.  The code for this project is

The non-linear Yang-Mills field theory is used to investigate the impact of a non-linear charge parameter on black holes in the presence of an electromagnetic field. This study examines how a non-linear charge parameter affects the shadow radius and thermal profile of black holes. A numerical method is introduced to solve the non-linear Yang-Mills equations, and it is observed that the non-linear charge leads to an increase in the shadow radius and a change in the thermal profile of the black hole. These findings are further confirmed through an analytical approach to the linearised case. The effect of the non-linear charge on the shadow radius is found to be significant at low accretion rates, and it is found that the non-linear charge can cause a switch from the Monopole-Hot-Dense (MHD) to the Monopole-Cold-Dense (MCD) phase. The MCD phase is characterised by a lower temperature and higher density than the MHD phase, and it is associated with the emergence of two nearly symmetric dark matter bars within the black hole accretion disk. The impact of the non-linear charge parameter on the MCD phase is further examined through the power spectrum analysis of the density fluctuations within the black hole environment. The effect of the non-linear charge parameter on the shadow radius is confirmed to be significant at high accretion rates, and it is found that the most likely value of the non-linear charge parameter is in the range $0.01\leq\alpha \leq 0.1$. The algorithms used in this study are simple and efficient, and they can be applied to the solution of various non-linear equations. The power spectrum analysis used in this study provides a clear understanding of the non-linear charge parameter's effect on the black hole environment. The research in this study can be further extended in several ways, such as investigating the impact of a non-linear charge parameter on rotating black holes, exploring the relationship between the non-linear charge parameter and the non-linear Yang-Mills equation, and examining the effect of a non-linear charge parameter on black holes in the presence of a non-linear dilaton field. We show that the resulting Wigner function exhibits unusual properties, including the appearance of entanglement that isn't present in the original system. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the measures of which types of non-classical behavior emerge during this process. The surge in video streaming for immersive technologies like VR and AR highlights a significant issue: predicting users' future eye movements within videos. By rapidly adjusting viewport predictions, applications can minimize lag and ensure an immersive experience. Various factors influence viewport predictions, including users' past interactions, video content itself. Our study introduces a novel approach that leverages video subtitles to enhance viewport prediction accuracy. Following the development of a subtitle-based viewport prediction model and evaluating it using multiple scenarios, our results show that incorporating subtitles into the model increases accuracy by up to $5.8\times$ for non-personalized predictions and $2.5\times$ for personalized predictions, compared to excluding subtitles. Furthermore, our data reveal that personalization boosts prediction accuracy by an order of magnitude, suggesting that viewers' individual preferences significantly impact eye movements. To demonstrate the practical applications of this approach, we implemented our method in a VR video streaming application. The results from user testing with this application revealed a significant reduction in user complaints about image freezing, a 36.7% decrease in user complaints about an uncomfortable VR experience, and a 20% increase in user satisfaction with the VR experience. In summary, our approach to incorporating subtitles into viewport predictions offers a straightforward, content-based solution that enhances the immersive video streaming experience. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/QianHobbs/Viewport-Prediction-with-Subtitles.

Our newly developed perimeter-tronized exact finite-dimensional description of average and thermal states, referred to as PEPOs, has been built upon a basic understanding of the universal principles behind gauge-theoretical representations of quantum systems. Our research reveals that by utilizing PEPOs, the approximate representation of thermal states and time evolution can be achieved while minimizing the required bond dimension, but this advantage comes at the cost of increasing the number of degrees of freedom in proportion to the square of the number of systems making up the whole, rather than a direct proportion as seen in previously established methods. Additionally, the investigation into average time evolution operators reveals that most of the operator's essential characteristics can be accurately replicated using a truncated bond dimension that scales linearly with the number of systems, although it must be much larger than the scaling required for the corresponding single-system operator. A newly introduced metric is also presented, offering a means to quantify the distinction between an exact and approximate representation of an operator. The advantages of PEPOs are further highlighted by demonstrating that the entanglement spectrum remains largely unaffected when approximating both single-system and multi-system operators. The newly developed methodology is demonstrated through the creation of a specific PEPO implementation tailored to a Heisenberg chain, including both its individual units and the resulting multi-system operator, which are then compared to their exact counterparts. The resulting approximation's effectiveness is evaluated through various metrics, including both the scaling of its bond dimension and its degree of faithfulness to the original entanglement spectrum. The developed PEPO framework is found to be highly adaptable, allowing for the creation of customized implementations that can match the complexity of even the most intricate quantum systems with broad applicability demonstrated through the concrete example of a Heisenberg dimer chain. The Heisenberg dimer chain implementation is notably notable for its intricate unitary operators on $4$-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The theory of approximate periodic equations arises in the study of approximate periodic solutions to a given partial differential equation. These equations take the form of a partial differential equation with periodic terms and an error term. The concept was first introduced by N. N. Pavel in 1971. However, the proven theorem contained an error. In 2019, L. R. Johnson and S. N. Antman provided a correction by developing a method to approximate periodic solutions to a non-linear Euler-Bernoulli beam equation. The current work builds upon their findings and contributes a method to approximate solutions to a non-linear Euler-Bernoulli beam equation with a decoupling property called the Taylor property. This method involves two steps: first applying Taylor-based analysis to obtain an approximate periodic equation, and then using canonical surfaces to further decouple the approximate periodic equation, allowing for the approximation of solutions to the original equation. The solutions to the approximate equation come from the approximate solutions to the original equation and its decoupling, while the remaining term is shown to be negligible. The resulting approximation preserves its same differentiability properties. The process also includes an explicit formula for the error term. The combined approach of using Taylor-based analysis and canonical surfaces assists in overcoming the limitations of both methods, allowing for the approximation of solutions to a wide range of non-linear Euler-Bernoulli beam equations with the Taylor property, even in cases where the decoupling property is not strong. The current work also provides an error estimate for the approximation, as well as an explicit formula for the error term. The formula demonstrates that the error term has the same differentiability properties as the approximate solutions. The process has implications for the approximation of solutions to other non-linear partial differential equations with approximate periodic terms. For a meson, we've established a direct relationship between this distribution and the charge density, thus making it necessary to consider infrared renormalons present in counterterms. Given that counterterms contribute significantly to the large-distance behavior of the gluon distribution, especially in its perturbative series, this leads to significant uncertainty in its estimation. A study on the impact of infrared renormalons on the gluon distribution's uncertainty, particularly for a meson, is the focus of this paper. We investigated the interference between surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly at the interface between a metal and a magnetophotonic crystal, written in air, structured with a 500 nm period in one direction and varying periods in the other. The presence of a Rayleigh anomaly resulted in a sharp minimum in reflectance spectra. By adjusting the crystal's period, the minima shifted and showed multiple spikes in the vicinity of the surface plasmon resonance. When the surface plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly hybridized, the spikes intensified and displayed the same energy splitting as the surface plasmon resonance. This effect was more pronounced perpendicular to the metal's surface and showed a significant increase in the imaginary part of the surface plasmon's permittivity. As a result, the surface plasmon's resonance widened and the magnitude of the spikes diminished with increased imaginary part. Nonetheless, the spikes' energy splitting remained nearly the same and the dimensionless magneto-optical activity in the surface plasmon resonance increased by approximately one order of magnitude compared to a smooth metal surface. Additionally, the dimensionless magneto-optical activity in the spikes exceeded the surface plasmon resonance's activity by almost two orders of magnitude and demonstrated a notable increase in the surface plasmon's anomalous dispersion in the vicinity of the surface plasmon resonance. Therefore, this investigation demonstrated that the surface plasmon's interference with a Rayleigh anomaly can significantly enhance the magneto-optical activity at the metal/magnetophotonic crystal interface. Moreover, the spikes' unique features suggest that they could be applicable in thin-film sensors, while the surface plasmon's anomalous dispersion may find use in nonlinear optics. Hence, this research proposes a simple method to enhance the magneto-optical activity in surface plasmons by adjusting the crystal's period. Furthermore, it reveals the potential of surface plasmon/Rayleigh anomaly interference in creating sensitive chemical sensors and implementing nonlinear optical effects. Given the right conditions, this investigation also suggests that surface plasmon/Rayleigh anomaly interference could result in surface plasmon hybridization beyond the limit of surface plasmon resonance broadening by the laser's beam width, which would enable the study of surface plasmon hybridization in thin films using a broadband light source. Ultimately, this research paves the way for exploring surface plasmon/Rayleigh anomaly interference in various configurations and materials. Knowledge distillation is a significant technique for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic a pre-trained high-capacity network. The traditional method requires access to the original network's output, which is often prohibited in practice due to costs associated with sending large amounts amounts of data. To overcome this limitation, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation was introduced, where a student network is trained to match the classification decisions of a vocabulary-based teacher network without using the teacher's output. However, this approach has limitations since it relies on data to infer the teacher's softmax outputs, which can be inaccurate, especially in cases where the input is far from the data distribution. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a new method called sparse knowledge distillation, which reduces the number of data points required for estimating the teacher's softmax outputs and thereby improves the accuracy of decision-based black-box knowledge distillation. Experimental evaluations on multiple networks and datasets show that the proposed method achieves better performance compared to existing approaches that employ larger datasets for estimation. Additionally, the proposed method is complementary to existing knowledge distillation techniques, offering potential applications in multi-step knowledge distillation tasks. The code for this work is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/Sparse_KD. The proposed method has the potential to accelerate deep neural networks while preserving their accuracy, which is critical in age-related AI applications requiring minimal data and model updates. The most relevant examples include smart homes, autonomous vehicles, and wearable health technology. The efficiency of the proposed method has been demonstrated in tasks such as mobile face recognition, where the ResNet-50 model was trained on just 0.5 million images for classification among 51 classes, achieving a performance boost of 12.21% in terms of the mean average precision (MAP) and reducing the model's size by 60 times for a precision of 90%. An analysis of $B$ meson decays into two neutral $K$ mesons is performed using 349 inverse femtobarns of LHCb data. Given a solvable group G and a multiplicity-free module M, we establish the compatibility of the composition factor lattice of submodules of M with its underlying poset structure. Additionally, for a specific class of groups, namely those with a normal nilpotent subgroup whose factor group is nilpotent, we demonstrate the reconstructibility of the submodule lattice of M, thereby extending a previous result by Haigh. Our research also incorporates an analysis of how the composition factor lattice of submodules of a module influences the stability of its underlying poset structure when considered within the context of automorphisms of the group. A notable case study is our examination of the conditions under which the posemanticity of the composition factor lattice of a module is equivalent to the posemanticity of its underlying poset structure. We conclude by reviewing some notable results on the posemanticity of group actions, drawn from recent studies by Duran and Haigh. Our primary aim in this research is to expand upon key concepts and results, while also presenting an array of novel findings. We have achieved this by incorporating a diverse range of methodologies, including the use of normal covers of groups. Our studies have notable implications for our understanding of the posemanticity of group actions, particularly within the context of solvable groups. We have also discovered that for a given group G and a module M, the composition factor lattice of submodules of M is not, in general, stable under the action of automorphisms of G. Our research has, however, identified specific conditions under which this stability can be achieved. We have further established that for certain types of groups, known as extended star groups, the composition factor lattice of submodules of a module M is posemantically invariant for any module M. We have also established a connection between the composition factor lattice of submodules of a module M and the posemanticity of the action of a group G on M, particularly in the context of solvable groups. We have achieved this by utilizing certain covering groups of solvable groups. We have further investigated the properties of covering groups of solvable groups, particularly with regards to their star properties. We have also examined the relationship between the composition factor lattice of submodules of a module M and the posemanticity of the action of a group G on M, particularly in the context of extended star groups. We have achieved this by considering certain normal covers of groups. We have further explored the properties of normal covers of groups, particularly with regards to their star properties.

We propose Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire expertise in multiple tasks via mutual imitation. In this approach, two agents with complementary abilities engage in an interactive process, with the more skilled agent serving as the teacher and the other as the student, and they take turns participating in tasks and providing each other with imitation guidance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Co-Imitation Learning by adapting it into a Data-Intensive Multi-Task RL framework, where agents learn multiple skills with the assistance of reward signals and shared contextual data. Through theoretical analysis and experimental results, we show that Co-Imitation Learning can significantly reduce data requirements and achieve superior performance compared to traditional methods that rely on expert demonstrations. Our approach also allows for seamless integration with existing reinforcement learning techniques, and we validate its performance across multiple benchmark tasks and realistic simulation environments. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenyuDong/VirtualCoI2D.

This research investigates how different bias values in the polarized cutoff rate affect a sequential decoder's performance. A systematic approach is developed to analyze how the average probability of the decoder making an error is impacted by the bias. Our primary finding indicates that the average error probability is directly proportional to the bias, specifically $\frac{R_b(R_c)}n$ in binary symmetric channels. To further illustrate the effect of bias, we calculate the conditionally polarized cutoff rate required to achieve a specific error probability, which is found to be proportional to the square root of this error probability. Numerical examples demonstrate the applicability of these results in practice. The study also reveals that the optimal bias value minimizes the average error probability and is proportional to the conditionally polarized cutoff rate, specifically $\frac{R_b(R_c)}2$ in binary symmetric channels. This research provides a framework for extending its analysis to other channel models and decoding schemes. The proposed approach can be extended to investigate other performance metrics, such as the decoder's throughput in sequential schemes. The importance of carefully selecting the bias value is emphasized, as it can significantly impact the decoder's performance, particularly in scenarios with limited channel knowledge. The study's findings can be applied to various applications, including those mentioned above, and provides a foundation for exploring its extensions. The developed approach is particularly useful for analyzing decoding schemes employing channel state information, sequential coding schemes, and hybrid arithmetic decoding methods. Quantum information flow between an open system and its surroundings can move in both directions, from the system to the environment and vice versa. In our analysis, a quantum hybrid model is used to illustrate how information can be shared between the system and its environment. By defining a new quantum hybrid process, we can achieve bidirectional information flow between the system and its environment. Furthermore, we determine the achievable rate of information transfer from the environment to the system and establish an essential condition for obtaining information from the system. Additionally, we can obtain both the system and its corresponding classical information from a previous state of the environment. An application to a scenario involving a sender, a system, an encoder, an channel, a decoder, and a receiver is also considered. This involves determining the maximum amount of information that can be acquired by the receiver from the system and how it affects the system's ability to function correctly. Finally, some possible future research opportunities are identified. This study is an extension of our previous work presented at QICR2022. We establish that p/q-recognisable subsets of (Z_p^d) are equivalent to those defined by a regular language based on a finite automaton in (Z_p^d). Additionally, our study extends this finding to (N_p^d) by demonstrating that q/p-recognisable subsets of (N_p^d) are also identifiable using a regular language based on a finite automaton in (N_p^d). Furthermore, these regular languages can be charaterised using a specific type of algebraic formula known as a rational expression, thereby showing that p/q-recognisable subsets of (N_p^d) are rational. A substantial contribution of our research involves providing a precise definition for subsets of (N_p^d) that are recognised by a finite automaton and subsequently establishing its equivalent form defined by a rational expression. Moreover, our investigation demonstrates that a subset of (N_p^d) identified by a finite automaton comprises subsets of the form (a_N \cdot B_p^d), where a_N is a non-zero integer and B_p^d represents the set of p-adic numbers below a specific bound. Finally, our study highlights the distinction between (N_p^d) recognised by a finite automaton and (N_p^d) defined by a rational expression, as the latter includes more extensive subsets, including those that are not comprised of a single non-zero integer. Our research also delves into the relationship between p/q-recognisable subsets of (Z_p^d) and those of (N_p^d), revealing that they share a common set of recognised subsets, which we have termed the diagonal definable subset. Our study concludes with the exploration of the dimensions of the minimal automata that can be used to identify the diagonal definable subset of (N_p^d). Our research builds upon the foundations established by Bertrand in his study of p-adic automata. Our research also draws from the theories developed by Cluckers and Denef in their investigation of a version of the Tarski-Seidenberg theorem as well as the research conducted by Macintyre into the theory of real and complex numbers defined by polynomial inequalities. Our study additionally draws from the research conducted by van den Dries into the theory of real numbers defined by polynomial inequalities as well as the research conducted by the Wisconsin group into the theory of real numbers and forms defined by polynomial inequalities. Our research also draws from the findings presented in the book titled "Introduction to the theory of locally compact fields"

We demonstrate that the $e$-positive properties of chromatic symmetric functions can be characterized via restrictions on Dyck paths, showing that each of these functions corresponds to a subset of paths that end on a specific level and satisfy certain conditions, and this level is indicative of the parameter $e$. This level can be computed using a simple step-wise procedure, and it confirms the $e$-positive status of various classes of chromatic symmetric functions, including those related to Stanley's $e$-positivity result. Furthermore, we establish an inequality between the $e$-level and the standard rank of these functions, and this rank can be achieved for certain instances, including those related to Stanley's result. Additionally, we examine relationships between the $e$-level and other rank-like indices, such as the Hilbert depth and the weak Hilbert depth of ideals associated with these functions. We also provide examples and illustrative diagrams to facilitate understanding of these concepts. We expect that further exploration of the $e$-level will reveal more insights into its properties and behaviors. We investigated the dynamic behavior of Ising spins arranged in a specific geometric configuration - each spin is connected to three neighbors - using a random regular graph with three edges per node, a model that exhibits unique thermal properties. By applying an external magnetic field in a cyclic manner and monitoring the spin configurations, we observed how the hysteresis loop changes its shape. Our study focused on the effects of temperature on the hysteresis loop and measured how the scalar order parameter's hysteresis cycle area changes with temperature. Notably, we found that the loop's area remains relatively stable over a broad temperature range, exhibiting a sharp increase or decrease only at extreme temperatures, and displaying a distinctive broad plateau. This plateau phase was found to be influenced by the temperature at which the hysteresis loop begins to form, rather than the temperature at which it reverses. Additionally, we analyzed a special temperature condition where the hysteresis loop's area reaches a minimum value before returning to its initial state, and discovered that at this specific temperature, the energy landscape's roughness reaches its most intricate state, characterized by a unique pattern of spin configurations where the external field's influence is opposed by the interactions between the spins themselves. Our research also explored the loop's area in relation to another scalar order parameter, one that tracks the rate of spin configuration changes, and found that it exhibits a more pronounced shift in behavior at higher temperatures, while the plateau phase remains largely unaffected. Finally, we compared our findings to a different magnetic hysteresis model, the infinite-range Ising model, and found that the two exhibit distinct differences in their hysteresis loop behavior. Our studies were conducted using Monte Carlo simulations that involved attempting up to nine different spin configuration changes for each spin at once. Our research was conducted in a 201-step Monte Carlo simulation cycle for each set of conditions, and the conditions themselves involved temperatures between 0.25 and 0.75, and edge connections between 1 and 3 per node, the latter two of which ensured the graphs remained random and regular. Our results can be used to describe the behavior of hysteresis loops in magnetic materials that have frustrated spin interactions at the atomic level, and may also provide insights into other phenomena that exhibit hysteresis in the presence of frustration. Recent studies near the Sun have revealed the energetic requirements for solar particles to reach certain distances, particularly within the inner heliosphere, and these needs are significantly higher than those observed at 1 AU, varying greatly and in a non-uniform distribution. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers examined the energetic necessities for solar electrons to reach as close to the Sun as 0.05 AU through numerical simulations, using data from three recent solar events and accounting for uncertainties in necessary energy estimates. The resulting distributions, although initially symmetrical and later becoming asymmetrical, showed that the lowest energetic requirements occurred near the Sun, with a peak that shifted towards higher energies in accordance with a power law, with related indices varying significantly. These results are compared to previous simulations of similar events, with some variation in peak energy indices but similar patterns, and the importance of considering uncertainty in necessary energy estimates is highlighted, affecting the distribution shape and thus the need for future observations to be extensive and precise. The energy distributions also passed tests for symmetry and Gaussian distribution, with the exception of the most recent event analyzed, which showed a more complex distribution. The investigation emphasizes the value of accessing closer heliocentric distances for solar and heliospheric research, with current limitations hindering a deeper understanding of the inner heliosphere due to the difficulties of accurately measuring energy necessities for solar particles at such distances. The study's findings are also crucial for developing more effective remote sensing techniques of the inner heliosphere, and it is proposed that future missions could be designed to more easily access this crucial area of research, encompassing distances within 0.1 to 1 AU. The research is further significant in its implications for understanding future flare-driven space environment effects on both human technology and living organisms in deep space. The study's newly developed model for simulating solar electron interactions also offers a valuable tool for addressing related key queries, such as the ability to model energy distributions with different levels of precision, the impact of considering uncertainty in necessary energy estimates, and the value of accessing closer heliocentric distances for solar and heliospheric research. The model has been made available for use by the scientific community via the open-source code available on GitHub, along with the associated data for the three events analyzed, which are valuable resources for future research into the inner heliosphere. The study's key conclusions are further relevant to the design of future space missions that will explore the inner heliosphere and the Sun, and it is proposed that such missions should prioritize accessibility to heliocentric distances within 0.

Cross-language emotion recognition allows a model to recognize emotions in a language it hasn't been trained on, by leveraging a different language it is familiar with. This proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance in two cross-language emotion recognition tasks, using English to recognize emotions in another language, and using a source language to recognize emotions in a target language when data for the target language is limited. By utilizing a rich set of text features and integrating a data-driven approach to select the most relevant text for classification, the model significantly reduces the gap between the source and target languages. As a result, it exceeds the performance of comparison models by a significant margin in two tasks, including one where the classification of emotions in the target language is based on English text. This proposed model also applies to single-language emotion recognition, and it performs better than current state-of-the-art models in several metrics, following rigorous experimental procedures that include conducting robustness and ablation experiments to validate its performance. A code for this model is available online at this link https://github.com/zhong-jianyi/CLRER.

Re-examining the behavior of planar shock waves with high adiabatic index, a phenomenon not widely recognized has been identified. For the simplest such shock, with symmetrical polar jets, a singularities-filled region exists around the origin, and an infinite number of closed curves of constant density arise. These results contrast previous findings, which revealed a smoothly changing density near the origin. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that when the adiabatic power exceeds a specific critical level, the shock wave's behavior becomes increasingly complex, with multiple dense rings forming and eventually undergoing an infinite period of expansion and collapse. The research has been expanded to include triangular jets, revealing that the shock waves' behaviors are characterized by an infinite number of closed curves of constant density and can be transformed into a rotating, high-speed jet. A notable discovery in this case is the formation of a dense ring around the origin, which after a prolonged period of time expands to infinity and is consumed by the shock wave, only to have the process repeat infinitely. The investigation has been applied to two specific configurations: one with polar jets and the other with bipolar outflows. The latter has been found to exhibit a specific behavior where the shock waves' behaviors are characterized by two closed curves of constant density, which after an infinite period of time expand to infinity and are consumed by the shock wave, also repeating infinitely. The research has also been expanded to include bipolar outflows with different jet powers, which has revealed that the shock waves' behaviors are indeed non-stationary, but become stationary under a specific power ratio, where the density around the origin remains constant. It has also been discovered that under this specific power ratio, the shock waves' behaviors can be transformed into a rotating, high-speed jet, which was initially unknown. The investigation has been further expanded to include bipolar outflows with the same jet powers, which has revealed that the shock waves' behaviors are indeed non-stationary, but become stationary under a certain condition, where the density around the origin changes smoothly, matching previous findings. This study develops a detailed analysis of B meson decay rate predictions within two beyond-SM quark sector extensions of the SM: the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks. Unlike the general approach of referring to low-energy constants to describe decay rates, both Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed scenarios provide explicit expressions for $B$ decay amplitudes. We have calculated B meson decay amplitudes for $B\rightarrow J/\psi \gamma$, $B\rightarrow \phi \phi$, $B\rightarrow \ell^+\ell^-$, $B\rightarrow K^* \bar{K}^{*}$ and $B\rightarrow \pi \pi$ using both approaches, and compared them with existing predictions from the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed papers. Additionally, we have fitted the parameters of both scenarios to data from $B\rightarrow J/\psi \gamma$ decays, and used the resulting values to predict rates and ratios for the other decay processes. Furthermore, we have calculated corrections to decay amplitudes within the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert scenario due to the $D$-term and the anomalous ZZZ and $\gamma \gamma Z$ vertices. We have also considered the impact of these corrections on predictions for $B\rightarrow \ell^+\ell^-$, $B\rightarrow J/\psi \ell^+\ell^-$ and $A_{CP}(B^0\rightarrow J/\psi \omega)$. We have compared our results with experimental measurements from BaBar, DELPHI, D0, CDF, LHCb and the B-factory experiments, and have identified potential for discoveries in rare B meson decay processes with rare quark interactions at the LHC and in the upcoming Phase II of the B-factory experiments. We have also outlined possible approaches for determining decay rate parameters in the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks using experimental data from forward detectors in the LHC. We have further analyzed the sensitivity of LHCb and the B-factory experiments in the Phase II to rare quark interactions and have prioritized the most promising processes for further study. Finally, we have considered the potential for direct detection of excited quarks in the LHC and the B-factory experiments with forward detectors in the Phase II

We develop a method to generate one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum non-singular potentials based on the harmonic oscillator, using the polynomial Heisenberg algebra, and show that these potentials result in exactly solvable systems. We achieve this by introducing an algebraic structure consisting of the ladder operators, the carrier operator, and its partner, which we then utilize to establish relationships between these operators and the carrier operator's power. Consequently, this connection allows us to derive the carrier operator's eigenvalue equation, and by substituting the potential-dependent effective Hamiltonian, we obtain the precise expression for the potential in terms of the carrier operator. This approach enables us to create a variety of exact solutions, including those with polynomial, rational, and logarithmic forms. Furthermore, we apply this method to develop novel solutions for the Mie potential, the Poschl-Teller potential, the SU(1,1) kernel potential, and the Waller potential. Additionally, we demonstrate that all previously reported one-dimensional supersymmetric quantum non-singular potentials are to be the harmonic oscillator potential or its conjugate. Additionally, we establish the energy spectrum for each potential and demonstrate that they comply with the Witten index. We also introduce algebraic structures for two- and three-dimensional non-singular potentials based on the harmonic oscillator. Nonetheless, these two-dimensional potentials fail to yield meaningful physical results. By contrast, the three-dimensional algebraic structure yields novel solutions for the Poschl-Teller potential and the Waller potential. We also introduce an alternative approach to generate the Mie potential, its conjugate, and the SU(1,1) kernel potential in one, two, and three dimensions. Lastly, we introduce a four-dimensional algebraic structure consisting of the ladder operators, the carrier operator, and its partner, which results in novel solutions for the Poschl-Teller potential and the Waller potential. By contrast, the Mie potential and its conjugate arise in one and two dimensions only. We also introduce a massless Dirac fermion algebra in one dimension based on the Heisenberg algebra, which we utilize to generate a 1D supersymmetric quantum non-singular potential, and show that this potential complies with the Witten index. Additionally, we introduce a massive Dirac fermion algebra in one dimension based on the Heisenberg algebra, which we utilize to generate a 1D supersymmetric quantum non-singular potential, and show that this potential also complies with the Witten index. Furthermore, we introduce a massive Dirac fermion algebra in three dimensions

In the analysis of a novel algorithm for computing the Lyapunov exponent from sparse data, a general method for estimating the dimension of sparse vectors has been developed, building on the Poincaré recurrence time distribution. This leads to the introduction of a Markov-dependent version of the Lyapunov exponent, which is then used to create an autonomous generator with a dimension matching its observation density. Additionally, this dimension can be adjusted to control the system's complexity, resulting in the tight bonding of the system's Lyapunov exponent between 0 and a value that indicates system complexity. This complexity can be visualized in various forms. The approach presents a blend of techniques from dimensional analysis, Markov modeling, and chaotic system dynamics. Our detection network achieves outstanding results on the FFSDC Dataset, a large-scale and publicly available deepfake detection data set, surpassing the performance of several state-of-the-art methods, including attention-based, graph-based, and spatial-based networks. Moreover, we clarify the relationship between the braid group action on the base $\hat{\Delta}$ and the quantum dimension weights, showing that they both result from the same action of the braid group, and finally, we establish an explicit expression for the quantum dimension weights in terms of the classical invariant defined by Kirillov-Reshetikhin. In order to enhance the efficiency of businesses, they are increasingly relying on prediction models to automate decision-making tasks. However, the effectiveness of these models is not constant throughout the process and can change significantly at different stages. This variation raises important implications for businesses and allows them to prioritize areas of high uncertainty. A key limitation of existing methods for predicting discrete outcomes is that they treat the problem as if the input data has a fixed and unchanging structure, which enables them to focus solely on estimating probabilities. In contrast, the performance of these models can be affected by the phase of the process, which means additional information about the current stage is necessary to enhance the accuracy of the predictions. To address this challenge, a novel machine learning model is presented that takes into consideration the impact of process stages on model performance and scales seamlessly to handle large datasets. When put to use on real-world data, it demonstrates a substantial improvement in prediction accuracy. The effect that process stages have on model performance is found to be highly complex and nuanced, meaning it cannot be captured by simple models. As a result, a robust approach is proposed that uses multi-dimensional feature vectors to describe model performance at different stages of the process. To achieve efficiency and handle large amounts of data, the proposed model uses a parameter-reduced technique that maintains feature integrity while minimizing computational costs. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through a practical application involving a large telecommunications company, where it delivers notable gains in prediction accuracy when comparing it to existing models that do not consider process stages. A clear and concise overview of the problem and proposed solution can be found in Section 1. The theoretical foundation and a detailed description of the model's design are presented in Section 2. The experimental methodology and results from testing the model on real-world data are discussed in Section 3. Possible applications and methodologies for mitigating process stage effects on model performance are explored in Section 4. Finally, the paper concludes with the results and suggests potential areas for future research in Section 5. The paper's appendices can be found in Section 6. Researchers analyzed a particularly long-duration and intense X-ray flare from the Pleiades star Taurus using extensive observations from the $XMM-Newton$ spacecraft. The data covered almost its entire duration, allowing for a detailed examination of the flare's evolution across multiple energy bands. By comparing the line broadening of hydrogen spectra with the overall energy distribution, they found that high-energy radiation softened significantly towards the end of the flare, which they attributed to a massive cloud of hot gas being cleared by a strong wind powered by the flare. Further analysis revealed that the line broadening of the hydrogen spectra and the overall energy distribution followed distinct patterns of evolution. By modeling the plasma conditions, they mapped the spatial distribution of the hot gas, which revealed a distinctive structure with an inner dense region with temperatures varying from 20 to 40 million Kelvin, surrounded by an outer more massive region with temperatures ranging from 5 to 20 million Kelvin. The large and cool outer region, which they suggested might be a stellar wind giant, was seen in several other Pleiades stars. By integrating the energy spectra, they calculated the total energy released during the flare, which ranked among the top 10 most energetic flares observed on solar analogs. The unique data set provided insights into the physical processes underlying the flare, showing that the energy release accelerated towards the end, with the line broadening of the hydrogen spectra and the overall energy distribution exhibiting distinct temporal evolution patterns. The extensive observation allowed them to examine the temporal evolution of the flare, finding that the energy release accelerated towards the end, the line broadening of the hydrogen spectra and the overall energy distribution exhibited distinct evolution patterns, and the soft X-ray energy distribution and the line broadening of the hydrogen spectra followed separate paths of evolution. The detailed analysis of the energy bands showed that the low-energy X-ray energy distribution and the line broadening of the hydrogen spectra followed separate paths of evolution, the energy release accelerated towards the end, and the simple model was confirmed by comparing the calculated with the observed energy spectra at different stages. The study also compared the flare to the highest energy flares observed on the Sun, finding that the Taurus X-1 flare ranked among the top 10 most energetic flares observed on solar analogs, and the duration was exceptional, lasting nearly twice as long as the largest solar flares. The unique data set also enabled them to examine the effects of the flare on the surrounding stellar atmosphere, finding that the extreme UV and optical emission during the initial stage suppressed the light from the cool outer atmosphere

Unlike previous approaches, our technique, titled Temporal-Periodic Coordinate (TPC), succeeds in maintaining robustness without employing data augmentation techniques or regularization methods. In the assessment of twisting sensations from a single view, TPC yields superior performance compared to existing point cloud learning methods, achieving the best result of 94.5% on the challenging ModelCIFAR4 dataset. The temporal-dependent and periodic-dependent coordinates are designed in a way that they remain invariant to twisting transformations with a specific period, thereby enhancing the robustness of the model. Our proposed method provides a concise and efficient solution for improving the robustness of point cloud models against twisting sensations from limited views. The RPA method has been successfully applied to investigate the pole structures associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. Using the Los Alamos RPA code and a macroscopic RPA approach, researchers have extracted the RPA poles from the spectral function to analyze the complex RPA pole landscape around the real axis. A study of the 10.75 MeV elastic scattering data from the Saclay facility has allowed for a precise extraction of RPA pole weights. These results are consistent with RPA predictions and reveal that the most prominent component of the electric dipole strength distribution, located in the energy range between 10-13 MeV, results from a mixture of single-particle transitions primarily involving 1p-1f orbitals and is associated with RPA poles that have relatively large real parts and relatively small imaginary parts. In contrast, the lower energy component, between 7-10 MeV, which dominates the E1 strength distribution, is composed of single-particle transitions mainly affecting the 1f-2p orbital shell and is attributed to RPA poles with smaller real parts and larger imaginary parts. This distinction is supported by a shell model RPA calculation using the JSH interaction and is reflected in the relative weights of the RPA poles in the Saclay pole spectrum. These findings clarify the RPA pole origin and provide a framework for understanding the complex RPA pole landscape, especially in relation to scattering strengths associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the RPA formalism and its application to other nuclei. In addition, it highlights the significance of examining the RPA pole spectrum in its entirety when analyzing RPA results from codes like the Los Alamos RPA code. In the process, it has also become evident that the RPA code itself plays a crucial role in determining the pole spectrum, with the default choice of RPA interaction hampering the recovery of certain RPA pole weights. Consequently, it is necessary to employ a more nuanced approach that takes into account the complexities of the RPA formalism itself. In the end, this study demonstrates that the RPA pole spectrum contains substantially more detailed and precise information about the pole structures associated with scattering strengths than previously understood, and as such, it is essential to thoroughly examine the RPA formalism and the associated codes to ensure a comprehensive comprehension of the underlying physics. This study explores the application of the Koopman operator framework to analyze nonlinear dynamical systems with localized observations. By utilizing a hierarchical learning model, we can extract global representations from nonlinear dynamics, even when the system is partially observed. This approach enables us to capture the behavior of invariant manifolds within the system's state space, extending previous work that was limited to the context of partial observations. We further develop a method to assign probabilities to the occurrence of specific invariant modes, which can be utilized for controlled system exploration. To facilitate the Koopman operator framework, we provide a algorithm that can approximate the Koopman operator from localized data, even in the presence of significant amounts of noise. This operator approximation method is based on a regularized linear inverse method and is robust to noisy data. We demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of this method by applying it to various examples of nonlinear dynamical systems. This research paves the way for the Koopman operator framework to be used in learning-based control systems. This is because the proposed algorithm generates a usable operator approximation from experimental data that can be obtained in a robust manner. This approximation can be utilized as part of the system dynamics in a learning-based control context. This is achieved by combining the Koopman operator with a model-free policy via linear program dynamic game methods. We provide both theoretical and experimental evidence to support this novel control system and validate its effectiveness by applying it to a controlled quadrotor drone system. This quadrotor drone system is a complex nonlinear dynamical system that is notorious for its sensitive response to rapid position changes. To overcome this challenge, we develop a control system that safely explores the system's state space by learning to identify the invariant modes of the system and selecting the most suitable modes to enter based on a reward function that prioritizes stable motion. This quadrotor drone system example demonstrates the practical applicability of the proposed method and the Koopman operator framework to a real-world context. This context involves a controlled quadrotor drone system that is considered a complex nonlinear dynamical system. This system is challenging to control, especially when navigating unexplored environments. To successfully control this system, we develop a method that combines the Koopman operator framework, a hierarchical learning model, and a controlled system explorer. This method enables the system to safely explore its environment by learning from its experiences. Neural text generation performance can be enhanced by improving sentence representations. A novel approach called SparseGAN achieves this representation improvement by imposing sparse regularization on the intermediate activations of a pre-trained generative adversarial network (GAN). This method enables the extraction of meaningful, sparse features from generated sentences, which can be utilized for classification, in addition to reducing the risk of adversarial examples. Evaluations under current large-scale neural text generation paradigms demonstrate improved performance, showcasing the versatility and efficiency of SparseGAN. The code for this project is available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/zhongjieLAI/SparseGAN. As the field continues to evolve, future research opportunities are identified, such as incorporating additional regularizers, sparse codes, and a comparison of different sparse methods. As an added benefit, the SparseGAN approach provides a natural defense against adversarial attacks, offering implications for neural text generation security. The idea that new life might be sparked within the solar system through combinatorial interactions between microorganisms and the various objects in interplanetary space is a fascinating but highly speculative concept.  To better assess this possibility, we examine the most promising sources of viable extraterrestrial life forms by analyzing objects in the planetary system that have the ability to carry and disperse life.  These sources include planetary comets, meteorites, and planetary surfaces.  To evaluate the possibility of interstellar panspermia, we consider comet nuclei, planetary meteorites, and outer space as potential carriers of life.  To that end, we evaluate the conditions necessary for a viable extraterrestrial life form to exist on a source, to be transferred to a carrier, to survive the journey to another star system, to be released from the carrier, and to give rise to a new life form on a destination planet.  We then use observational data to assess the likelihood of these conditions being met on Earth, on Mars, and on a comet like Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gierasimenko.  We find that while comets like Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gierasimenko are unlikely to carry viable life forms and thus are unlikely to spark new life on a planet like Kepler-62f through panspermia, Mars is a source of viable life forms that could be carried to a comet like Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gierasimenko and potentially disperse to other planets.  To that end, we propose future astrobiological research on Mars that could provide a better understanding of the possibility of interstellar panspermia.  We also suggest that astrobiological research on a sample from a comet like Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gierasimenko, which is more likely to carry viable life forms than it is to carry a life-giving effect, could yield more compelling evidence for the possibility of interstellar panspermia.  Finally, we propose a theoretical model that describes the distribution of viable life forms on a source and carrier through panspermia and interstellar dispersal.  This model is tested using data from Earth and Mars and could be applied to other planets and comets in the future.  We also explore the possibility of combinatorial life arising through the interaction of microorganisms with objects in interplanetary space and consider future directions for astrobiological research on this topic.
