Accurate population density estimates are crucial in animal research, yet traditional methods can be expensive and time-consuming. Advances in acoustic sensor technology and spatial capture-recapture modeling offer promising alternatives. However, these methods require knowledge of the home range of the animal being studied, which can be challenging to determine, especially for species that do not have well-defined ranges. In a study involving mountain lions in Colorado, a novel approach called density estimation using occurrence data (DESDO) was tested and compared with the traditional SCR method. Both methods yielded comparable and accurate density estimates with low standard errors, suggesting that DESDO and SCR can be used interchangeably. Notably, DESDO demonstrated greater sensitivity to home range estimates, implying that this species' large range may limit the effectiveness of SCR for accurate density estimation. Despite these findings, the study suggests that both SCR and DESDO can provide reliable population density data, offered in a user-friendly package called JAGUDENSITY. This package allows users to adjust data inputs and compare different modeling scenarios, facilitating the assessment of model robustness and accuracy. In the study discussed here, mountain lion density estimates ranged from 1.68 to 2.33 animals per 25 miles squared, with further analysis showing that both SCR and DESDO models were highly effective in estimating density when the study area was divided into sub-blocks, but less accurate when the entire study area was combined into a single block. Nonetheless, this latter scenario yielded the most precise and accurate density estimates. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the efficacy of DESDO and SCR in estimating population density and presents a useful package for researchers to explore different modeling scenarios and optimize study design for accurate density estimates. In the end, the study recommends the use of larger home range blocks for density estimation in mountain lion populations. In the process, the study also highlights the limitations of SCR in relation to DESDO when estimating density in species with large home ranges, emphasizing the importance of carefully considering species-specific needs when selecting modeling methods. In the context of the current study, the most suitable method was one that accounted for occurrence data, resulted in low standard errors, and was insensitive to home range estimates. Finally, the study encourages researchers to consider the applicability of SCR and DESDO to a wider range of species with varying home ranges, as well as to consider the broader utility of JAGUDENSITY as a general-purpose package for estimating population density using occurrence data. We developed a method to assess the stability of each inner network state by examining the relationships between the outer network's degree and the inner networks' degree and connectivity. We applied this stability framework to study two types of two-part networks: coupled oscillators and competitive spreading processes. It helped us uncover interesting patterns and results, including the condition under which all inner networks will have the same stability and the requirement for them to exhibit the same degree distribution. Furthermore, this framework enabled us to determine the optimal outer network structure for achieving the highest stability and to establish relationships between the outer network's degree and the inner networks' connectivity and degree. Our findings also revealed the inner networks' unique stability thresholds and how these are affected by the spread of information or oscillator coupling. We observed that the outer network's degree must be sufficient to prevent the inner networks from becoming completely disconnected or displaying alternative stable states. Testing environments are vital for ensuring software quality, but the manual process of providing input and comparing output can be time-consuming and laborious. To enhance the efficiency of testing, an algorithm has been developed that analyzes user feedback in the form of error reports. By leveraging the underlying structure of the software under test, the algorithm generates hypotheses about the source of the feedback, thereby identifying the specific program component responsible for the error. To validate these hypotheses, the algorithm creates and tests new test cases, which can include both existing and newly generated tests. In addition, the algorithm adjusts the input and expected output of existing tests to match the particular error reported. Through the execution of these modified tests, it determines whether the feedback is genuine or if it was simply a false positive prediction. If the feedback is confirmed, the algorithm applies a simple correction to the relevant program component and re-examines the outcome to ensure the change was effective. Ultimately, the algorithm provides the user with specific instructions to locate and correct the identified error. In contrast to existing approaches that simply suggest fixes, this algorithm offers a guaranteed solution by validating predicted errors and verifying the effectiveness of the proposed corrections through rigorous testing. Experiments with a real-world application revealed that the algorithm successfully pinpointed the source of nearly nine out of ten error reports, requiring on average just twenty minutes to locate and correct each error. Furthermore, it was observed that the algorithm's performance continues to improve with increased testing, thanks to the dynamic adaptation of its own accuracy through feedback in the form of checked corrections. The success of this algorithm hinges primarily on the design of the underlying software, rather than the type of feedback provided. Consequently, a similar approach can be applied to a broad spectrum of software systems following a similar modular structure. The underlying principles and methodology of this algorithm also offer valuable insights for addressing other challenging automation tasks, such as those involving difficult test case creation and costly annotations. The implementation of the algorithm is available for public use at https://github.com/Google/robot-test-automation. The associated testing environment and application for evaluating the algorithm are available at https://github.com/Google/robot-learning-environment. The experimental data gathered during testing the algorithm can be found at https://github.com/Google/robot-test-data. The associated paper was presented at the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, held in Reykjavik, Iceland, in June 2017. Within this expanded framework, an explicit and symmetric arrangement of regions can be defined to analyze the properties of roots. Specifically, when focusing on the type A context, a notable connection can be identified between the maximal root and the arrangement's central point. Moreover, both the type A and D configurations exhibit a symmetric pattern around the arrangement's peripheral roots. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the root system's structure and reveal the presence of a radial axis. The discovery of this radial axis in type A root systems also mirrors the characteristics of the Grassmannian's stratification. The research presented here builds upon the work established in the 2001 paper by Lerman and Mnev, as well as the 2012 paper by Postnikov, by expanding the core idea of a radial axis to all root systems of types A and D. The type D branch of the root system corresponds to the Euclidean building known as the wall group, which was initially identified by Tits. A key aspect of this research has been overlooked in previous studies, namely the connection between the root system's structure and the arrangement of regions, which was first introduced by Lerman and Mnev in the context of the 60th birthday collection of Dan Laksov. Our algorithm runs on multiple rounds and requires minimal initial knowledge from participants. We prove that our algorithm provides an accurate estimate of the network size, and compare it to other distributed algorithms used for size estimation. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between our algorithm's accuracy and various key factors, including the number of rounds and network connectivity. Accurate queue length estimation is crucial for safe and efficient traffic management. Traditional parametric approaches require historical data for model training, which may not be feasible in real-time applications. In response to the increasing need for nonparametric solutions, two novel methods, one based on kernel estimates and the other on moving averages, are developed here to estimate queue lengths. These proposals are designed with real-time traffic management in mind and aim to provide reliable nonparametric solutions. The proposed algorithms are tested on simulated data and real-world datasets from the Singaporean smart traffic system, with results showing they outperform existing nonparametric benchmarks, such as neighborhood estimates, in both simulation and real-world settings, according to various performance metrics including mean absolute error and root mean squared error. Furthermore, applications of these nonparametric algorithms in calculating safe time heads and stopping times during rush hours are demonstrated, showcasing their practical utility. A key advantage of these new methods is their real-time viability, as they do not require any prior knowledge of the underlying traffic dynamics. In addition, the kernels-based algorithm is discovered to be more accurate than the moving averages-based algorithm in estimating queue lengths at intersections, which is critical information for drivers navigating through busy areas during peak hours. Ultimately, this research contributes two nonparametric queue length estimation algorithms that are straightforward to implement in real-time scenarios. In addition, it highlights the significance of accurate queue length estimation in everyday driving experiences, particularly in congested urban settings with traffic signals. In such environments, where drivers face frequent stop-and-go conditions, accurate queue length information can significantly minimize delay and frustration caused by abandoned spaces at intersections during rush hours. In the worst-case scenario, incomplete knowledge of local traffic dynamics can lead to driving through an empty intersection, resulting in unnecessary stops and increased risk of accidents, particularly in settings with limited visibility, such as mountain roads. Consequently, in areas with high traffic densities, estimating queue lengths accurately can also help reduce traffic-related expenses, especially in megacities with prolonged rush hours. In the absence of accessible traffic training data, the proposed nonparametric algorithms offer a viable alternative for safe and efficient traffic management in real-world applications. In addition, these algorithms demonstrate versatility in other transportation scenarios, such as estimating stop times and detecting intersection malfunctions. In the long run, this research is expected to contribute to the development of self-driving technology, which heavily relies on accurate and nonparametric queue length estimation in various driving scenarios. In this approach, the constraint is transformed into a series of nonlinear, second-order partial differential equations for the conformal factor, which can be resolved through a non-upwind, primitive continuous scheme. Unlike conventional methods, this technique eschews the assignment of weights for the generation of source terms in the partial differential equations, instead utilizing a different method that ensures the preservation of the non-upwind property and delivers a more efficient and accurate solution. Additionally, this method allows for the direct integration of the partial differential equations over time by employing an explicit, second-order, and non-upwind numerical scheme. A key advantage of this method is that it sidesteps the difficulties associated with the convergence of the partial differential equations in the current gauge, thereby eliminating the need for the successive application of elliptic solvers and the assignment of arbitrary weights. This method has been successfully tested and validated in a variety of scenarios, including static scenarios, dynamically evolving scenarios, and scenarios with perturbations, and it is particularly well-suited for the numerical solution of the Hamiltonian constraint in the 3+1 conformal formulation. Theoretical analysis shows that the anomalous Nernst effect in LaSn$_2$ can be explained by considering both the orbital thermal fluctuations and magnetic thermal fluctuations. The contribution of orbital thermal fluctuations to the anomalous Nernst effect is constant with respect to the magnetic field, while the contribution of magnetic thermal fluctuations changes dramatically with the magnetic field, resulting in a large anomalous Nernst coefficient in LaSn$_2$. The combination of extremely small ordinary Nernst coefficients and anomalous Nernst coefficients in LaSn$_2$ leads to a clear manifestation of the anomalous Nernst effect, making it possible to study the anomalous Nernst effect in LaSn$_2$ in depth. The research on LaSn$_2$ also uncovers a mysterious temperature-dependent anomaly in the anomalous Nernst effect. The rapid advancement of materials science is largely attributed to user facilities, which provide free access to highly sophisticated tools and expertise for an expansive community of researchers. At the core of these facilities lie cutting-edge devices like synchrotron light sources, which have become indispensable tools for developing and applying sophisticated experimental techniques. As a result, researchers with outstanding ideas but limited access to advanced technology and resources can utilize these facilities to achieve breakthroughs. This achievement-to-investment ratio is a key factor in the vast success of synchrotron light sources and serves a purpose for an ongoing debate on the appropriate use of public funds for scientific research. A recent investigation at the ALS synchrotron facility in Berkeley, California, highlighted the substantial impact that research done there has on the global materials science community. It showed that the scientific consequences of research conducted at the ALS are substantial, with notable effects on the advancement of materials science, the expansion of the scientific community engaged with the facility, and the improvement of the American economy. This research provides tangible evidence to support the continued operation of the ALS and similar user facilities around the world. It also highlights the exceptional value of synchrotron light sources and urges policymakers to prioritize the maintenance and upgrade of these facilities in order to unlock the vast potential of materials science and the economy. A thorough examination of the broader implications of this research is also presented with recommendations for future policy and funding strategies. A key aspect of this research is the development of a robust methodology to assess the consequences of research conducted at the ALS, which can be applied to user facilities worldwide. This research paper establishes a significant connection between two concepts in number theory: G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycles and reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions. Within the framework of p-adic Hodge theory, it demonstrates that every reduced modulo p crystalline extension arises from a G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycle, thus extending Dawid Kiszel's findings for fields of characteristic zero to those of positive characteristic. A key method employed to achieve this connection involves utilizing narrow flat modules to represent certain cocycles, thereby facilitating the proving of this relationship. Moreover, an equivalent formulation of the result presents a direct link between l-adic etale cohomology and the set of G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycles corresponding to a given extension. This connection further enables the classification of distinct etale cohomology classes through the classification of their underlying cocycles. This research builds upon the results of Kiszel, Pollack, and Vostokov by expanding on the properties of G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycles in a broader context. Additionally, it previews the advantages of connecting these cocycles to etale cohomology, offering a promising avenue for exploring other related phenomena. Given its foundation in theoretical concepts, this research remains independent of the recent breakthroughs in analytic evidence for Sato-Tate conjectures. Nonetheless, it is anticipated that the results presented here will contribute substantially to verifying certain geometric properties of automorphism groups in number theory. In particular, it is expected to provide the necessary framework for establishing the simplicity of the group associated with a given number field through the use of etale cohomology. This simplicity can, in turn, be used to prove the irreducibility of the associated Galois representation, thus verifying a key aspect of the Sato-Tate conjectures. This achievement would, in turn, enable the establishment of an equivalence between the set of G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycles and the set of potential images of the corresponding Galois representation, thus facilitating the minimalization process. This process is crucial for ultimately calculating the number of distinct conjugacy classes of the associated group of automorphisms. This calculation is essential for verifying another key aspect of the Sato-Tate conjectures, which involves determining the size of the group of automorphisms. This size determines the density of the set of primitive directions within the set of all possible directions in the space of orbits. This, in turn, provides the necessary evidence for verifying the central conjecture of polynomials

We define a new concept called mesoscale flatness to investigate a specific type of surface in an n-dimensional space. Our analysis focuses on a hypersurface within this space that has a constant mean curvature and is confined to a small distance from a given plane. In the case where the mean curvature is negative, we demonstrate the existence of this hypersurface for any given small negative value, as well as its unique classification when the value is zero. Furthermore, when the mean curvature value is positive, we show that there is no such hypersurface within a large enough space. In contrast, a surface with a mean curvature value of zero is found to be remarkably complex, requiring an in-depth analysis that is fundamentally different from its one-dimensional counterpart. This research also explores the properties of this surface as it evolves over time, revealing intriguing patterns of growth and decay. In particular, we observe that a surface with a mean curvature value of zero will inevitably shrink to a minimal configuration known as a round point, eventually breaking into one or more round spheres that are mutually non-intersecting and have significantly small radii. In the time domain, this phenomenon is accompanied by the release of a specific amount of energy, which is directly proportional to the surface area of these spheres. Additionally, we study the relationship between this surface and a random walk process known as the Lévy flight, discovering that it follows a power law distribution as it approaches a point, as opposed to the traditional Gaussian distribution. This research was initially inspired by an examination of the properties of a specific type of random walk called the Lévy flight, which appears frequently in natural phenomena observed at various scales, from the movement of galaxies to the flight patterns of hummingbirds. This walk process is characterized by the presence of a unique scale, above which the search area becomes essentially flat, and on which the surface curvature exhibits a constant value. In the course of this study, the concept of mesoscale flatness proved to be a fundamental property that can be applied to this random walk process, revealing its intricate and complex features as it evolves over time. This research was initially presented at the 2020 annual meeting of the Society of Industrial and Applied Mathematics, applied mathematics section. A genetic algorithm is integrated into a neural network to detect damage in self-sensing composites, specifically carbon fiber reinforced polymers, by utilizing electrical resistance changes. The proposed system trains a neural network to accurately identify resistance patterns corresponding to specific damage types and sizes. To enhance performance, a genetic algorithm is employed to optimize neural network structure and weights. Utilizing a genetic algorithm leads to improved accuracy and reduces the computational time required for training the neural network. A concept called a neural network genetic algorithm is introduced, where the genetic algorithm and neural network are trained simultaneously to achieve the best results. Through analysis of the proposed method, advantages of using a genetic algorithm are revealed, including the optimization of neural network weights, the optimization of neural network structure, and the elimination of incorrect solutions. The effectiveness of using a genetic algorithm is demonstrated by the reduced error values obtained. The most favorable learning factor and migration genetic algorithm factors for the proposed method are determined by conducting an experiment with multiple factors. The results show that the neural network genetic algorithm can detect all damage types with an accuracy of 90%. The proposed method provides a framework for improving damage detection in self-sensing composites using a genetic algorithm and neural network, enabling the development of more efficient and accurate damage detection systems. The knowledge gained from this research can be applied to other self-sensing material systems involving complex pattern recognition. The proposed method is feasible due to the mutual enrichment it brings to both the genetic algorithm and neural network, and it allows for the easy integration of new damage detection methods incorporating both techniques. The feasibility study presented can be easily scaled up for larger projects, and the proposed method's advantages can be further explored in the context of real-time damage detection in real-time environments. The knowledge gained from this research can be used to improve the detection of other material system defects, such as those found in cement-based materials, metamaterials, and shape memory alloys, among others. The proposed neural network genetic algorithm framework provides a high degree of flexibility, enabling the easy integration of additional techniques and the detection of different damage types and sizes. The model can be applied to a wide range of applications, including but not limited to, the detection of concrete cracks, carbon fiber reinforced polymers delamination, and brain computer interface-based hand movement detection. The proposed method offers a promising solution for the detection of complex patterns in self-sensing materials and can be utilized in various real-world scenarios. The knowledge gained from this research is expected to contribute to the development of more efficient damage detection systems, incorporating both artificial and natural intelligence

We examine the Lotka-Volterra model, a fundamental predator-prey system, as a framework for exploring the impact of different levels of intelligence among species with varying brain-to-body mass ratios. Our mathematical analysis combines power law functions to model the dynamics of these intelligent species, thereby incorporating aspects of complexity theory and network science into the Lotka-Volterra equations. By re-expressing the system in a dimensionless form, we can identify the effects of changing brain mass on the dynamics of the system. Our results reveal a critical threshold for brain mass above which the predator or prey species exhibits a stable coexistence with its opponent. We also find that increasing brain mass can lead to a shift from alternative equilibria, such as the coexistence state, to another state characterized by the extinction of one species. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of models featuring nonlinear interactions between species. Our research demonstrates how the incorporation of intelligence, expressed through power law functions, significantly affects the outcomes of predator-prey interactions. Our findings are consistent with empirical observations of brain mass on species populations and provide a theoretical framework for predicting the consequences of changing brain mass on the dynamics of these interactions. Ultimately, this approach can be utilized to model various ecological scenarios influenced by intelligence. Our work also paves the way for exploring the impact of additional intelligence parameters on the outcomes of these interactions. Furthermore, our research highlights the broad applicability of the Lotka-Volterra model, which has served as a foundation for many complex biological systems for over eight decades. Our work demonstrates the durability and versatility of this model, allowing it to adapt to the incorporation of sophisticated traits and modern interdisciplinary ideas. We introduce a novel approach to proving a broad class of integral identities, specifically those known as $q$-polynomial identities, which are commonly used in mathematical applications such as combinatorics, representation theory, and geometry. Our method involves using geometric vectors instead of the conventional method of using algebraic structures like groups or associations. This abstract technique enables us to derive (20) different $q$-identity formulas, including notable examples like the Baclawid-Gessel-Viennot and the Macdonald identities, by breaking down these complex formulas into simpler components known as $q$-exponential formulas. We then combine these components to regain the original identities. This vector approach not only facilitates the proof of these identities but also yields a surprising $q$-exponential relation, thereby demonstrating our method's effectiveness and versatility in handling a wide range of problems. The proposed study will explore the underlying causes of the observed anomaly, which could be attributed to new physics resulting from a gauge symmetry known as little string theory. A detailed analysis shows that the J-PARC g-2 experiment has the ability to explore a significant portion of the parameter space associated with this theoretical model, specifically by investigating the behavior of a scalar field called a 'dilaton' which is linked to the symmetry of the theory. A calculation of the expected measurements indicates that the experiment can cover the relevant parameter ranges with factors ranging from 13.8 to 54.6 for different settings of the experiment. Additionally, the proposed study includes a simulation of the dilaton field's impact on the experiment's systematic errors. A proposed future upgrade to the experiment is also considered and shown to have the capability to cover the entire relevant parameter space with factors exceeding 100 for various experiment settings. The systematic error associated with the dilaton field can be minimized by improving the experiment's beam condition and correcting for systematic errors in the measurement of the muon's magnetic moment. Both experiments meet the requirements to investigate the parameter space associated with the little string theory model, which is linked to the little inflation paradigm. The research demonstrates that both experiments have the ability to explore the parameter space related to the little string theory standard model, which includes accessible ranges of energy scales and provides promising prospects for discovering new physics. Accurate brain-computer interface (BCI) decoding relies on precise electrical mapping between neural signals and intended actions. Recently, high-resolution electrocortical recordings during surgery provide valuable training data, but previous studies have focused on basic signal processing without comparing the effectiveness of different recording resolutions. In the current study, a relatively simple machine learning method was used to analyze both high-resolution electrocortical recordings from the flat cortex and simplified, spatially-weighted representations of signal features. Following training and testing on walking function data, both approaches yielded comparable results for a small set of features, but the resolution-independent method exhibited better performance at 10-fold cross-validation. Furthermore, by evaluating the algorithm's ability to accurately identify the highest correlation between local signal components and walking functions, significant discrepancies were discovered in areas associated with lower limb muscles. The resulting cortical mapping showed that the effectiveness of BCIs using electrocortical recordings is comparable whether using high-resolution recordings from the flat cortex or more aggregated representations of cortical signal features. Additionally, both methods successfully decoded important aspects of walking functions from cortical signals with moderate precision, surpassing the accuracy of conventional EEG methods that only capture broad signal patterns. The current study suggests that the effectiveness of BCIs using electrocortical recordings depends more on the specificity of feature extraction techniques rather than recording resolution. The found resolution independence and the ease of non-invasively obtaining sufficient training data make electrocortical recordings an attractive choice for developing practical BCIs. The study's novel approach to evaluating the cortical mapping of walking functions using simple machine learning methods and resolving the recorder resolution debate has significant implications for future BCI development. The accurate decoding of walking functions from cortical signals also contributes to enhancing the understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying human gait. The study's findings, advantages of its approach, and implications for future research are further discussed in the study's context. We investigate the long-term behavior of right-angled Artin groups that act on trees via a specific mechanism, where the group's action results in a minimally invariant tree. We identify the key properties of this mechanism and show that it inherently leads to a group with a finite index that acts on a tree via a combination of translations and rotations. Additionally, we determine conditions under which this group action yields a free minimally invariant tree. Moreover, we establish that any free minimally invariant tree associated with the original group is isomorphic to the tree associated with its finite index subgroup. We also explore connections between the group's action on the tree and its geometric properties, including the formation of a boundary space and the calculation of the group's growth at a specific rate. Furthermore, we establish that the finite index subgroup's growth rate is identical to the parent group's growth rate, thus providing a method for determining the parent group's growth rate by analyzing the boundary space of its finite index subgroup. Lastly, we illustrate this approach by computing the growth rates of infinite index subgroups of bounded width group functors, which are comprised of groups with a specific property that acts on trees via a combination of translations and rotations. We also examine the relationship between these subgroups and the parent group's boundary space to demonstrate that the parent group's growth rate can be classified into one of three categories based on the boundary space's geometric properties. We conclude by highlighting the limitations of our research and identifying potential areas for further study. Many real-world systems, including cultural networks and mobile communication connections, evolve over time in response to external influences. These dynamic graphs pose a challenge for machine learning models that typically operate on fixed structures. Our proposed DECENNT framework addresses this issue by utilizing time-series data to construct new features that capture the changes in graph connections. Unlike traditional approaches that focus solely on node representations, DECENNT enhances the representation of connections by introducing a new module that calculates the similarity between adjacent graphs. This module's output is connected to the features extracted from time-series data, resulting in a method that outperforms current methods in various tasks, including node classification and community detection. Moreover, DECENNT demonstrates its versatility by integrating with existing methods, such as GCN and APPA, to achieve superior performance in both low and high-resolution settings. Our code is available at this link https://github.com/zwang84/DECENNT. Despite its efficiency, DECENNT incurs a higher computational cost due to its use of graph convolutional networks. To overcome this limitation, we developed a simpler alternative called SimpleDECENNT that reduces the number of layers and channels in its architecture, leading to a DECENNT performance comparable to that of the original model at a fraction of the cost. SimpleDECENNT's code can be found at this link https://github.com/zwang84/SimpleDECENNT. Our findings have significant implications for modeling dynamic processes and complex relationships in real-world systems, and our models are applicable to various domains, including physics, finance, and neuroscience. These models can also be used as highly effective neural network architectures for classification tasks involving random graphs. Analyzing the movements of various entities within images is a challenge that requires efficient algorithms for real-world applications. Our research presents a novel approach that differentiates between the movements of biological and non-biological objects by classifying them into categories such as walking, running, falling, sinking, and floating. Our in-depth analysis of genus-one curves in algebraic geometry reveals that certain mathematical principles hold true, demonstrating the independence of geometric characteristics from the method used to compute them. We then established that this property, initially observed in one dimension, extends to higher dimensions independently of the method used to compute the invariants. We also explored applications of this property to higher-dimensional curves and discussed its relationship to the independence of geometric characteristics. Our research analyzed the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, specifically pions, kaons, and protons, in relation to their elliptic flow patterns within high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. To compare these phenomena at different collision intensities, we adjusted our data for the most productive LHC experiments: ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS. Following a standard procedure, we combined the charged hadron momentum distributions for each collision intensity by incorporating the corresponding elliptic flow values. This allowed us to identify patterns of variation in charged hadron momentum distributions across different collisions, including those involving unusual kaon behavior. Furthermore, our study revealed that pion and proton momentum distributions are roughly similar when adjusted for collision intensity, whereas kaon distributions exhibit distinct tendencies, reflecting different physical processes. We also established a unified framework combining collective motion and thermal hadron emissions, within the scope of a thermodynamic model, to interpret our findings and illustrate the resulting temperature and density variations across all collisions studied. These variations were found to be essentially unchanged, with an average increase in temperature from 340 to 400Ch, and a corresponding decrease in density from 510 to 320 times nuclear saturation density, despite the diverse outcomes of collisions at the LHC. The need for additional physical processes beyond thermal hadron emissions in kaon cases became evident in our analysis. We also discovered that charged hadron momentum distributions align with a scaling principle based on collision intensity alone, whereas distributions for pions and protons are roughly identical, while those for kaons exhibit distinct behaviors, reflecting different physical processes. We have made our research data available for the scientific community at www.fysik DP.TH.2023.03. We have also developed a computational code to combine the charged hadron momentum distributions for the most productive LHC experiments, ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS, which can be accessed at www.fysik DP.TH.2023.04. In addition, we have an answer to a long-standing question regarding the relative populations of kaon types, with our findings revealing that the ratio of K+ to K- kaons remains essentially unchanged across all LHC collisions, despite varying collision intensities, with a consistent average value of 1.52 ± 0.04, and exhibiting no significant variation with respect to collision density or energy density. Despite the discrepancy from observed neutron star masses, a meson-pion phase transition model yielded small quark star masses.  In contrast, a polytroptic mass-radius relation resulted from the Yang-Mills phase transition model, which showed quark stars having similar masses to neutron stars and exhibiting a phase transition boundary.  However, both phase transition models failed to satisfy the Buchdahl boundary condition.  A combination of the Yang-Mills phase transition model and the relativistic mean-field model, which includes hyperons, yielded a maximum quark star mass of 0.353 solar masses.  The presence of hyperons in quark stars was found to be influenced by the beta-equilibrium density gradient, which can be affected by the presence of a phase transition boundary.  The electromagnetic dissipation of quark stars during the phase transition deformation was found to result in dissipative dissipative currents and an associated heat release.  The presence of a deconfinement phase transition does not affect the quark star's overall heat content, but rather affects the heat content distribution with density.  This distribution becomes shallower in the outer regions of the star.  This phenomenon was found to result in a heat distribution that is more homogeneous throughout the star, which may influence quark star cooling mechanisms.  The presence of a deconfinement phase transition was found to accelerate quark star cooling, specifically for the Mojave model, which exhibits a phase transition boundary, and to have cooling effects that persist even after the star reaches the point of cooling reversal.  The presence of a deconfinement phase transition was found to result in the emission of electromagnetic radiation from quark stars during the phase transition deformation, which can be observed from a great distance. To leverage the metric-gaining potential of these systems, it's essential to precisely determine their initial state, particularly the compass state, which is a superposition of equally spaced knots along a rotation axis.
To achieve optimal damping measurement precision, the compass state's spatial distribution must remain unclogged by various environmental disturbances.
In this research, we investigate how accurately we can determine key damping parameters in a three-level system using the compass state, and how this metric is influenced by various quantum noise pollutants from surrounding environments.
Our findings indicate that non-uniform damping affects the compass state more significantly than uniform damping does, and that both forms of damping can be accurately determined using simple models.
Furthermore, our data reveals that both uniform and non-uniform damping rates decay at a $1/\Delta^2$ rate as the spacing between knots increases, with the rate modulated by the relevant damping parameter.

In such cases, we find that the system's ability to efficiently employ a compass state is linked to the magnitude of the detuning between relevant knots, and that this efficiency is significantly impaired by both uniform and non-uniform damping.
By analyzing the interplay between the compass state, damping processes, and various quantum noise pollutants from surrounding environments, our research provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the reliability of three-level systems with compass states in damping-based measurement precision. 
Our data can be utilized as a performance benchmark for implementing reliable compass states in various quantum engineering applications.

This research focuses on exploring a variety of estimates for harmonic functions on the basis of their growth within the framework of a specific type of Ricci solitons, which we've termed "gradient shrinking solitons with certain pointwise pinched Weyl tensor." We have successfully derived several key theorems regarding harmonic functions on these solitons, including some interesting applications of an earlier result established by Li and Shi. Notably, our findings also extend and improve upon certain growth conditions previously established by the aforementioned authors, as well as those established by Li and Wang and by Miao and Shi. Moreover, we have obtained some distinctive bounds for $n$-dimensional harmonic functions, where $n$ can be any integer greater than 2, and these bounds are specifically tailored to the characteristics of this soliton type. Finally, we have a distinct result showing that any $n$-dimensional harmonic function with a certain growth rate, where $n$ is any integer greater than 1, must be constant on these solitons, which we have proven by utilizing an approach that combines a change of metric with an application of the Cheng-Truong covering theorem. This particular result is a direct extension of an earlier finding by Li and Shi, but with a few key differences. Additionally, this research has a supplementary result that can be found in the appendix section, which may have value on its own given the current state of knowledge. This research is an expansion upon the work done by Li and Shi, as well as Li and Wang, and Miao and Shi, among others. This research has also been inspired by the gradient solitons explored by Case 3 in the paper published by Pierni, Stagnant, and Veziere. Recent research on neural networks has focused on creating faulty behavior through "backdoor attacks." However, implementing these attacks on classification tasks that change over time becomes challenging as models adapt to their environments. We successfully developed dynamic backdoor attacks that work on classification tasks that evolve, using a simple framework that incorporates label embeddings. Our results show that embedded labels can serve as triggers for backdoor attacks, achieving high accuracy rates in both static and dynamic settings. Additionally, our study found that dynamic backdoor attacks are resistant to various defenses, including retaking the training data and implementing regularized regularization. Our approach can be applied to various classification tasks, including text classification, making backdoor attacks a viable option for sabotaging software systems that change and adapt over time. Knowledge questioning is a challenging task that requires a system to pose effective questions to incorporate relevant knowledge for task performance. This approach is not supported by most existing question answering systems, which primarily focus on utilizing explicit knowledge to answer questions. To address this limitation, we introduce a method called Question-Aware Knowledge Management (QAKM), which incorporates a module that generates questions to incorporate knowledge that enhances the performance of the system on tasks like natural language inference. In our experiments, QAKM demonstrates significant performance gains on multiple natural language inference datasets, surpassing the performance of strong baselines established previously. A key aspect of our approach is the semantic-driven knowledge awareness framework, which simplifies the incorporation of knowledge by focusing on generating questions that trigger relevant knowledge for task performance, rather than directly utilizing explicit knowledge. This semantic-driven approach provides a scalable solution for incorporating knowledge in question answering systems, enabling them to pose purposeful questions that enhance the system's performance on tasks and accelerate the integration of new knowledge and datasets. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of our approach, presenting qualitative and quantitative findings, and demonstrating the versatility of QAKM by applying it to incorporated knowledge from both structured data and unsupervised relational learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chenyue1998/QAKM. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach can be applied to various tasks and datasets, leading to performance improvements across multiple evaluation metrics. Our proposed method offers a scalable and effective solution for question-aware knowledge awareness in low-cost incorporation tasks, paving the way for further research on efficient question generation strategies and methods to pose more effective questions that trigger relevant knowledge for task performance. Our findings also highlight the potential applications of our approach in incorporating high-quality multi-hop knowledge and manipulating language models via targeted questions. Our approach has the advantage of being sufficiently flexible to be combined with pre-trained models using a simple wrapper class, and we conduct an exhaustive analysis of model dependencies and provide training guidelines for fair comparison with strong baselines established previously. Our experiment results show that our approach can be applied to various tasks and datasets, leading to performance improvements across multiple evaluation metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chenyue1998/QAKM. Our approach has the benefit of being versatile and capable of incorporating knowledge from both structured and unsupervised relational learning, and our experiments demonstrate that our approach can be applied to various tasks and datasets, leading to performance improvements across multiple evaluation metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chenyue1998/QAKM.

Individual mental health treatments for offenders have shown a limited impact when it comes to reducing future crimes, prompting the exploration of a broader, more comprehensive approach - psychiatric social therapy. Originally developed in Europe, this method involves group sessions led by trained professionals with mental health issues, alongside individuals who have committed crimes and have mental health issues. The therapy's primary goal is to help participants with mental health issues who have committed crimes by reducing their future criminal behavior through a sense of community responsibility. We examined the effectiveness of psychiatric social therapy in this context, reviewing data from 1,752 Swedish offenders with mental health disorders who were convicted of serious crimes such as assault, robbery, and burglary. Following the start of their regular prison sentences, half of the participants were assigned to an additional year of psychiatric social therapy within a prison setting. Our study compared the future crimes of both groups - those who received the therapy and those who did not. The results showed that individuals who underwent the therapy had a 13% lower chance of committing a crime within the next two years following their release from prison. Moreover, the therapy appeared to lower the chances of committing specific crimes such as assault and robbery. Additionally, we discovered that the therapy had a positive effect on reducing the number of prison sentences offenders received and the overall prison time they served. The most significant positive impacts of the therapy were seen among offenders who had both schizophrenia and substance use disorders, as well as those convicted of violent crimes like murder and aggravated assault. The findings suggest that psychiatric social therapy can be a highly effective approach in reducing the future crimes of offenders with mental health issues, even those who have committed serious crimes. The research also highlights the importance of providing this therapy to such offenders within a prison setting, offering them a sense of community and responsibility for their mental health. The data and analysis used in this study are now available for other researchers to use, and the research team is open to collaborating with institutions interested in implementing this therapy in their prisons. It demonstrated the positive impact of the therapy on reducing the number of prison sentences offenders receive and the overall prison time they serve. We propose a novel framework, known as RSMIX, that integrates graph-based regularization and semi-supervised learning models using mixing processes, such as transvascular and intercellular methods, to produce physically plausible predictions. We further establish the connection between our model and several existing methods, demonstrating how it subsumes multiple prior interventions, including ReMixSeg, a previously proposed model, which it surpasses according to metric values obtained from public leaders. When utilizing MRI data from three different categories, our model shows improved performance over prior techniques in various evaluation metrics. Moreover, our model exhibits a consistent performance boost when utilizing CT data from two categories. We further provide qualitative and quantitative segmentation outcomes using real-world MRI and CT scans from various sources, demonstrating the capability of our model to segment hard-to-define structures, such as the fatty liver, and other challenging cases. We have made the proposed model, along with the code and models, publicly available on GitHub, and the related protocols are callable through our benchmark server following the MIMI protocol. To gain a deeper understanding of material properties and behavior, researchers are providing a precise mathematical description of the atomic structure within materials. This effort is enhancing predictions and explanations of physical phenomena, as machine learning models are now effectively trained on atomic structures and make reliable predictions about them. However, current methods primarily focus on representing entire crystal structures and leave underexplored the analysis of local atomic configurations. To address this, our proposed framework titled AtomicCNN utilizes graph neural networks to thoroughly examine local atomic settings by considering both short-range chemical bonds and longer-range structural patterns. The resulting features extracted from this analysis demonstrate exceptional performance in accurately identifying local defects, predicting phase transitions in carbon fullerenes, and analyzing the relationship between atomic configurations and material properties in graphene edge defects. Our data and models are openly available for other researchers to build upon. By delving into the details of local atomic structures, our work paves the way for a precise understanding and machine learning-based analysis of material defects and complex phase transitions. Our code can be found at https://github.com/AtomSim/AtomicCNN. Despite the effectiveness of our approach, issues with current materials generation methods limit the scalability to larger, real-world materials structures. To overcome this, we advise integrating the study of local configurations into training models that can generate atomic structures. This is essential for accurately modeling and confidently predicting the properties of randomly sampled materials configurations, including those found in real-world materials. By doing so, we can confidently predict the properties of randomly sampled materials configurations, even when these configurations differ from those used in the training data. Our proposed framework is an significant improvement over traditional machine learning models due to the following reasons. Third, it fails over to a coarse-grained representation of the crystal structure in the feature extraction phase. Fourth, it successfully identifies the relationship between atomic configurations and material properties in graphene edge defects. Fifth, it accurately predicts the phase transitions in carbon fullerenes by considering both short-range chemical bonds and longer-range structural patterns. Deep learning knowledge tracing models have shown significant improvements over traditional approaches, however, evaluating these models is complicated due to the lack of labeled data for knowledge tracing, which typically ranges from a few hundred to ten thousand annotations. Existing methods rely on either partial knowledge traces or ask-answer sequences to train and evaluate deep learning models. In response to these limitations, this study proposes a new approach, Knowledge Tracing Graph Labeling, which involves labeling a part of the knowledge tracing graph to train deep learning models and uses ask-answer sequences to evaluate them. The study further introduces three model-agnostic strategies, Graph Smoothing, Label Expansion, and Strategic Labeling, which are designed to enhance graph labeling for knowledge tracing. Experimental evaluations on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and associated strategies. Furthermore, the study plots a path toward extending Knowledge Tracing Graph Labeling to other educational data tasks involving student-resource interactions. The code and datasets for the study are available at https://github.com/Qianh-H/KTG-Labeling.

Given a smooth function f belonging to the domain of the second-order elliptic differential operator H, the concept of surjectivity can be characterized by the existence of a function u, such that the equation Hu = f is satisfied. In this study, we establish that the set of surjective differential operators H corresponds to the presence of a continuous integral inequality involving the Carrez norms of f and the distance function associated with the operator H. Consequently, we demonstrate that the set of surjective differential operators H is found to be compact within the space of operators acting on the Hilbert space H2(S) for compact surfaces S. Additionally, we prove that if the surface S is bounded, then the set of surjective differential operators H is shown to be compact within the space of operators acting on the Hilbert space H2(#S) for the double surface #S. Based on the integral inequality, we also establish an explicit bound for the norm of the inverse operator I/H defined on the domain of H. Furthermore, we derive an estimate of the norm of the inverse operator I/H in terms of Carrez norms for the surface S, providing an alternative proof of a result initially established by Gagliardo. Moreover, we obtain an explicit formula for the norm of the inverse operator I/H on the double surface #S, which is found to be minimized when the surface S is equipped with a specific metric. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between the set of surjective differential operators H and the geometric properties of the associated distance function d_H, demonstrating that the set of surjective differential operators H is maximally extensive if and only if the distance function d_H defines the original metric d_S on the surface S. FedBuff introduces a novel framework that enhances federated learning confidentiality by using fully private data processing, coupled with enhanced confidentiality guarantees for server nodes. To achieve this, the algorithm breaks down complex computations into manageable components, which are then efficiently outsourced to remote servers. Unlike current federated learning methods, FedBuff enables servers to process data using arbitrary deep neural networks, significantly improving scalability. Additionally, the algorithm provides robust privacy protection for server nodes by employing fully private data processing techniques. The advantages of FedBuff are demonstrated through comprehensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets using different deep learning models, showing it can be an effective solution for securing and scaling federated learning. To facilitate further research, the code and models used in this study have been made publicly available.

In the context of scheduling tasks for a single agent with side information, we investigate two scenarios: one where the agent has access to a black box providing approximate task completion times, and another with additional task duration specifications. For the first scenario, we develop a round-robin-based task allocation method that complements a cut-and-choose algorithm, resulting in a fair and approximately optimal solution in polynomial time. In comparison to using the cut-and-choose algorithm alone, this approach composes $(2r+1)$-approximate guarantees with respect to the optimal solution, where $r$ indicates the precision of available approximate side information. Additionally, this approach composes $2(2r+1)$-approximate fairness guarantees with respect to the optimal solution, where the optimal solution's fairness guarantee is defined in relation to the number of tasks and the precision of side information. For the second scenario, we establish that without additional task duration specifications, task scheduling cannot guarantee both approximate optimality and approximate fairness for any approximation factor. However, with additional specifications, we demonstrate that there exists an algorithm that provides both approximate optimality and approximate fairness guarantees for any approximation factor, specifically achieving $(2r+1)$-approximate guarantees with respect to the optimal solution and $2(2r+1)$-approximate fairness guarantees with respect to the optimal solution, where the optimal solution's fairness guarantee is defined in relation to the number of tasks and the precision of side information. Furthermore, this algorithm maintains polynomial-time complexity. A key component of these results involves the development of new techniques, including a novel extension of the round-robin method, as well as the introduction of a cut-and-choose-based algorithm that enables the composition of approximate guarantees with respect to previous solutions, which contributes to approximately optimal and fair task scheduling problems. Moreover, these results showcase the value of incorporating additional task duration specifications when scheduling tasks. A natural limitation of this work arises from its reliance on the assumption that the underlying task set possesses sufficient diversity, ensuring that no two tasks are equally difficult for the agent, although this assumption can be bypassed in specific special cases. A natural extension to this work could be the development of algorithms addressing larger and more complex scheduling problems with side information, as well as applications in practice that incorporate additional task duration specifications. From a theoretical perspective, the results presented in this research paper highlight the importance of fairness in relation to approximation factors, demonstrating that neither approximate optimality nor approximate fairness can be guaranteed for any approximation factor in the scenario without additional task duration specifications,

UGC 8839, a highly inclined spiral galaxy, exhibits a remarkably symmetrical HII region distribution, despite experiencing interactions with other galaxies. A comprehensive analysis of 23 HII regions within UGC 8839 was conducted, allowing for an in-depth examination of their properties. The findings reveal that the HII regions are concentrated near the galaxy's center and display a distinct, two-tiered diameter distribution, with a notable absence of large-scale HII regions. This absence is particularly striking when compared to notable spiral galaxies like NGC 2403 and NGC 5236 (Pinwheel Galaxy), and it's possible this phenomenon is influenced by the presence of massive, early-type galaxies with which UGC 8839 has interacted in the past. The analysis of the HII regions' radiative flux places UGC 8839 within the same parameter range as other spiral galaxies, and the detection of both an optical and a radio continuum continuum continuum in the galaxy suggests the presence of a massive young star cluster that could be associated with a particular HII region. A massive central black hole is also hypothesized based on the observed absence of a central bulge and the presence of the massive young star cluster. The analysis of the HII regions' ages reveals a broad spectrum, with many regions younger than 10 million years, and the investigation of metallicity levels suggests they are within the same parameter range as other spiral galaxies, although there is evidence of slightly enhanced levels within the galaxy's center. The investigation into the possible causes of the galaxy's symmetry, considering both its mass distribution and the impact of its starburst history, is also explored. The comprehensive examination of UGC 8839 adds a new perspective on the characteristics of HII region populations in spiral galaxies, particularly those that have experienced interactions with other galaxies. The unique features of this galaxy also present a fascinating case study of the consequences of such interactions on its structural and chemical evolution. A lattice QCD study using the stochastic source method and an almost exact solver yields precise calculations of pion properties, specifically the mass squared and decay constant, in a wide quark mass range, covering both the light and heavy quark domains. Our calculations take place in a $16^3$ lattice with a spacing of one twosuperior and feature quark masses twenty times lighter than the highest acceptable limit, where quark composition does not significantly impact the pion mass. Our results also include considerations of quark composition, which can influence pion masses in proportion to the mass variations, and result in a slight drop in mass over a wide range of quark masses, albeit primarily linear. Furthermore, our research supports previous findings that the ratio of decay constant to pion mass exhibits minimal change with quark mass. Our extensive dataset enables detailed analysis of pion mass ratios in different quark mass ranges, providing a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between these physical properties and quark composition. Our lattice QCD results comprise 24 distinct data sets, each representing a specific quark mass configuration, and cover a significant range of quark masses, from those equivalent to current experimental settings to those weighing several times more than the strange quark mass. Our calculations of pion mass ratios also extend into the heavy quark domain, a realm less explored in previous studies. Our research demonstrates that lattice QCD calculations can accurately capture the effects of quark composition on pion masses using a stochastic source method, which originate from fluctuations in the quark fields rather than the lattice discretization itself. By utilizing an almost exact solver, our results are minimized by hypercubic fluctuations, which are negligible with our $16^3$ lattice layout. Our data sets are categorized based on the mass ratios of different quark combinations, which include ratios of light to heavy quarks, as well as quark masses weighing two, three, or four times more than the light quark mass. Our research finds that the ratio of decay constant to mass in the heavy quark composition scenario exhibits minimal change with quark mass, whereas the mass ratios in the light and medium quark mass ranges showcase a linear decrease with quark mass. Our study has undertaken considerable computational efforts to achieve precise results, involving approximately 340,000 CPU hours on 512-core Xeon IvyBridge nodes, and yielded a comprehensive understanding of pion properties across a broad spectrum of quark masses. Some T Tauri stars exhibit extreme and brief spikes in rotation, which may be caused by a rapid increase in mass accretion rates. However, a problem arises in attempting to explain the evolution of diskless T Tauri stars based on mass accretion rates, as it fails to account for the peaks and valleys in data. A new approach is presented that takes into consideration variable mass accretion rates, which can result in stars like V883 Mon, with rapidly rotating cores and thick dust disks. Using this approach, the new sample of diskless T Tauri stars with variable mass accretion rates was analyzed, revealing a stronger correlation between the stars' ages and the timescales of their mass accretion fluctuations rather than average mass accretion rates. Consequently, the argument that some T Tauri stars stop accreting and spin down over time was refuted, and the process by which they lose mass through wind was proposed as the explanation for the observed correlation. Additionally, the analysis provided lower and upper limits for the mass loss and mass accretion rates in these stars. Furthermore, an examination of previously discarded data revealed 13 new candidates for diskless T Tauri stars with rapid rotation, which were likely mistaken for other types of pre-main sequence or massive young stellar objects due to incorrect interpretations of their characteristics. Finally, the possibility of stars like V883 Mon being a crucial link between low-mass T Tauri stars and Be stars was explored, with possible pathways to this transition state proposed, including both internal and external factors. The research on V883 Mon, along with the new understanding of variable mass accretion rates in T Tauri stars, the examination of other candidates, and the possible future evolution of these stars were all addressed in this study. The relationship between mass accretion rates and the disappearance of disks in low-mass young stellar objects remains a subject of debate, with the classic model relying on a direct correlation between the two, while the new approach shows that this relationship is more complex, involving variable mass accretion rates and different timescales for diskless T Tauri stars. The new perspective on the evolution of these stars also raises several questions about the balance between mass loss through wind, mass accretion from disks, and stellar rotation, as well as the possible triggers for the sudden stops in mass accretion fluctuations that mark the beginning of the diskless stage. Offline learning for multiple agents is challenging due to the limited information available about individual agents' behaviors. Our Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework addresses this issue by assuming that many agents follow the same underlying policy and that the underlying policy and relevant individual features share the same structure. Through a carefully designed neural network architecture, SIT facilitates fast policy learning and feature inference for individual agents from observed trajectories. Unlike current offline methods that focus on learning from individual data in isolation, SIT leverages shared knowledge across agents to improve the effectiveness of offline learning. Experimentally, our method demonstrates significant improvements in policy learning when compared to existing techniques and showcases the benefits of shared knowledge in dynamic scenarios. Additionally, SIT reveals a natural connection to state sharing in multi-agent settings, thereby providing a theoretical contribution to the field. Overall, our method offers a pioneering approach to offline learning for multiple agents that is both practical and theoretically sound. The investigators demonstrate that the amount of single-particle entanglement contributes significantly to the quantum steering present in symmetric two-quantum-bit systems. The protocol's performance can be further improved by using a more efficient cryptographic algorithm or more powerful hardware. The proposed scheme provides a high level of security against various attacks and malicious behaviors in vehicular networks. V392 Persei, a known Algol-type binary system, underwent an unusual transformation in 2018: it began to operate as a classic nova and switched to a 2.77 day circular orbit.  Prior to this change, the system had a slight orbital eccentricity, with an orbital period of 1.80693 days.  V392 Persei's spectrum indicates it has a white dwarf companion at a temperature of approximately 13,000 Kelvin.  During its nova phase, a white widow was observed around the system.  A search for radio and X-ray emissions from the nova was unsuccessful.  Current observations suggest that the nova's ejection phase is restricting disk accretion, and as a result, the secondary star is no longer being eclipsed during the system's primary phases.  As a result, the orbital period is expected to increase as a result of the reduced mass accenting on the secondary star.  This phenomenon has been observed during the Carin-Nagel gap phase in some binary systems.  Furthermore, as the secondary star moves further away from the white dwarf, the nova's light curve will transform once again, returning to its pre-nova state within the next 10,000 years.  In the circular orbit, the mass transfer rate from the secondary star to the white dwarf will decrease even further, preventing the white dwarf from reaching the necessary accretion level to detonate a supernova, and instead the white dwarf will continue to grow in mass until it reaches a decision point where it either reaches the necessary accretion level to detonate a supernova or it reaches the necessary mass to detonate a supernova through gas compression.  This process is expected to result in a Type Ia supernova similar to V4334 Sgr, however it will occur in the next 10,000 years or so, as a result of the reduced mass accenting on the secondary star.  Another possible outcome is that the white dwarf will continue to grow in mass at a rate of 10^-8 solar masses per year, until it reaches a Chandrasekhar limit and detonates a Type Ia supernova in about 50,000 years. By coupling adjacent layers through a common medium, researchers have shown that non-trivial surface currents can arise at the boundaries of the lattices, despite the absence of an external drive. Furthermore, the surface currents are found to be robust in both bosonic and fermionic systems, demonstrating the generality of this phenomenon. In this study, we take a multi-layer setup with multiple coupled layers to exhibit surface currents in various boundary regions, thereby demonstrating the wide applicability of this robust phenomenon. We further investigate a proposal for a two-layer optical lattice with a hexagonal geometry to generate robust surface currents in bosonic systems, and predict the associated robust surface currents in various boundary regions. Moreover, we outline the experimental realization of a hexagonal optical lattice using a pseudo-monolithic crystal array, and discuss the expected robust surface currents in this setup. Notably, the surface current robustness can be distinguished from fake currents generated by an external drive, and we outline a possible approach to achieve this differentiation. This study paves the way for the creation of robust surface currents in bosonic and fermionic systems using a multi-layer optical lattice setup. To mitigate frequency stability issues, power grids employ various tools, including redispatch and must-run units. The design of redispatch markets involves allocating incentives to encourage generators to adjust their output. However, existing models lack consideration for the peer-to-peer trading that occurs between generators within the same submarket, leading to inefficiencies. We present an all-or-none order design for redispatch markets that takes into account the submarket-specific electricity prices and generator costs, and ensures that the redispatch agreement pays a risk-free rate equal to the expected revenue from peer-to-peer trading. This approach results in a more efficient grid operation with reduced procurement by the grid operator, and we further show that this new design is at least as efficient as the existing model. To facilitate implementation, we develop an algorithm to compute the risk-free rate, and explore scenarios involving multiple submarkets and grid operators. Numerical experiments using real data demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of this novel design. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of redispatch markets that account for peer-to-peer trading, and provides a practical solution to grid operators seeking to improve the stability of the power grid. In particular, this work is relevant to operators in regions with high renewable energy integration, such as Germany and California. It also offers an efficient order design for other multi-agent systems involving complex, interconnected agents. This research paves the way for further investigation into innovative redispatch market designs, and highlights the need for considering peer-to-peer trading when addressing frequency stability challenges. This approach has been made publicly available as a part of the MATLAB-based PPA framework, which is accessible at this link https://github.com/yiyanggaoyang/PPA-framework. Moreover, additional numerical experiments and simulation scenarios are accessible at https://github.com/yiyanggaoyang/Additional-experiments. It is worthwhile to note that while the risk-free rate approach was initially proposed in a previous work, the design of the all-or-none order for redispatch markets presented in this research is an significant extension of that earlier idea. Additionally, we establish an equivalence between the direct product of a nilpotent Lie algebra and its universal enveloping algebra, using an explicit isomorphism that is detailed. This isomorphism enables us to reproduce the symmetric bilinear form associated with Kirillov's measure and, in turn, enable us to determine when this measure is positive-definite. Furthermore, this isomorphism allows us to establish that the measure defined by Frenkel and Pressing on the dual space of a nilpotent Lie algebra is equivalent to the measure derived from Kirillov's measure. This research is an expansion of the results presented in the author's doctoral dissertation at the University of Queensland. The growing complexity of x-ray scattering experiments demands more efficient phase retrieval methods to effectively recover the lost phase information from measured intensity data, particularly when attempting to reconstruct the energy spectra of x-ray energies above 20 keV. Existing approaches, subject to single-wedge Abel transformation limitations, are not sufficient to handle the complexity of modern synchrotron radiation experiments. To address this challenge, we developed a non-Abel inversion method that uncovers the x-ray energy spectra with precision, surpassing the accuracy of traditional methods, especially for low-intensity signals in the higher energy range. Utilizing a fundamental data set from the SPring-8 storage ring, our algorithm demonstrated improved performance in energy spectrum reconstruction compared to conventional methods, showcasing its effectiveness in overcoming the limitations of single-wedge experiments. The code developed as part of this research is openly available for other researchers to utilize. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have also published the code openly. The updated phase retrieval algorithm and accompanying code are available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/HiDes-Lab/SAXS-Phase-Retrieval. This study introduces a novel numerical approach that leverages the power of deep learning to enhance the efficiency of a multiple-scale numerical method for modeling blocking fractures network. Unlike traditional single-scale models, this approach can capture the complex behavior of multiple-scale blocking fractures through a mixture of fractional continuous and discrete models. Specifically, the approach simplifies the solution process by breaking down complex blocking fracture interactions into fundamental blocking-fracture-block and blocking-fracture-pore interactions. Though this model includes challenging spatial operators, it is made solvable by introducing a series of approximate solutions that gradually refine the solution through a series of nested power series expansions. Although this approach results in a sequence of solution approximations that progressively improve the accuracy, it requires the development of a complementary numerical method that can provide an initial guess for each approximation. This numerical method is, in turn, an efficient deep learning-based solution that utilizes a carefully designed neural network architecture to enhance solution accuracy by incorporating directional information. The performance of this model is demonstrated through the simulation of a classic blocking fracture problem, known as the Fatt-Berg, where it shows the ability to accurately capture the blocking fracture's impact on the flow field by modeling a range of blocking fractions from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-0}$. Furthermore, results from this study indicate that it can efficiently solve the Fatt-Berg problem by achieving a blocking fraction variance of less than $10^{-3}$ within $10^{6}$ degrees of freedom in as little as $2$ hours on a standard desktop computer. The performance of this model also shows that it can replicate the same level of accuracy as the continuous Beier model, known for its rigorous mathematical formulation, using an order of magnitude smaller number of degrees of freedom. The efficacy of this model is also demonstrated in a realistic blocking fracture network simulation, a real-world application that models the complex behavior of multiple-scale blocking fractures network in a fractured porous media, a scenario that typically involves millions of degrees of freedom but is now achievable in just a few days on a standard desktop computer. The code associated with this study is available at https://github.com/AD-FEL/DeepBlockFractures. The future direction of this research involves further optimizing the current model to handle even larger and more complex blocking fracture networks by exploring alternative neural network architectures and numerical methods that can provide more accurate initial guesses for the solution.
