In the context of hypothesis selection, utility functions play a crucial role in informing decisions, but their impact depends heavily on how hypotheses are represented. When hypotheses are expressed as probability distributions, utility optimization is challenging due to the need to consider both distribution properties and the uncertainty inherent in them. To address this challenge, we consider a framework where the utility of a hypothesis is evaluated based on the expected utility of its associated distribution, utilizing a functional decision theory approach that takes into account the precision of the distribution. To accommodate varying levels of precision, we take a robustness perspective, leveraging the notion of ambiguity functions that capture different robust utility preferences, to make hypothesis selection more resilient to implementation errors. By leveraging the ambiguity function framework, we can incorporate prior knowledge about the distribution of expert opinions, thereby reducing robust uncertainty and improving the robustness of our utility computation. Through this integrated framework, we can balance the trade-off between being robust and capturing valuable information from the distribution of expert opinions, thereby making informed decisions about hypotheses in the face of significant uncertainty. We demonstrate the effectiveness and practical applications of this method in a real-world scenario involving real-valued estimates, and also examine the theoretical properties of the ambiguity function framework, including the behavior of its components and the relationship with other relevant measures, such as the Shannon entropy and coherence. Notably, we show that the ambiguity function can be seen as a measure of non-commutative entropy, thereby establishing a connection with established concepts and providing insights into its behavior. We also explore the relationship between the ambiguity function and other measures of uncertainty and information, including the non-equivalent forms it can take and the measures that capture its key properties, such as the robustness of an agent's utility preferences. Finally, we outline possible avenues for future research, including the consideration of multiple experts with inconsistent opinions, the incorporation of hard knowledge to guide the robustification process, and the development of more efficient utility computation methods. We also discuss the broader implications of this research for utility theory and decision-making under uncertainty, particularly in the presence of ambiguous or Robustly Pareto efficient (RPE) probabilities. For a deeper understanding of text, identifying discourse markers and their connection to the surrounding context and other elements of the text is essential. To facilitate this progress, we present a large-scale Indian language dataset called DiscSense, comprising 13,000 sentences in English with annotated discourse markers and semantic relations. This dataset surpasses existing datasets in terms of scale and diversity, and we find it to be effective in modeling discourse relations even without using explicit labeling for these relations. To further facilitate progress, we launch a challenge to detect discourse markers in Indian languages. These languages have limited resources and have never been subjected to discourse analysis before. With DiscSense, we achieve notable results in discourse marker detection and relation modeling, and our findings demonstrate the importance of part-of-speech tagging, integrating multi-task learning and a detailed analysis of features. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates versatility in applying it to other tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis. We anticipate that DiscSense will serve as a significant step towards the understanding of Indian languages and the integration of discourse knowledge with deep learning models. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Vidsen/DiscSense. The competition rules and dataset are available at https://www.aicovid.org/discsense. The top submissions are featured in a companion paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04066. We are presenting a discourse-aware neural network called DANN at the technical competitions of the conferences NACL 2022 and IJCAI 2022, where it secured second and third place respectively in the DiscSense challenge. DANN integrates a rich representation of text by incorporating both deep learning and conventional features, and employs a self-correction mechanism to enhance the accuracy of discourse relation classification. In addition, we investigate the importance of part-of-speech tagging in this process, and integrate multiple task learning to boost the performance, particularly in the detection of discourse markers. We also explore a detailed analysis of features that can be utilized in this model, and discover that it can be applied to other tasks like text classification and sentiment analysis. Notably, our approach demonstrates a significant improvement in the performance of the model when only partial annotated data is available. To facilitate the widespread adoption of DANN, we have launched an open-source code at https://github.com/linguodan/DANN. We have successfully tested DANN on multiple Indian languages and achieved notable results in relation classification and marker detection, and have also tested it on English text and achieved comparable results with the current state-of-the-art approaches

We investigate the geometric characteristics of the factorized objective in matrix optimization, specifically the geodesic convexity of the natural embedding of the matrix manifold. To this end, we examine the convexity and smoothness of the factorized objective function under specific regularity conditions. Our findings reveal that the factorized objective functions do not maintain their geodesic convexity and smoothness properties on general matrix manifolds, such as the set of positive definite matrices or Gaussian manifold. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that they do exhibit these properties on the manifold of diagonal positive semi-definite matrices, which enables us to establish the uniqueness of the geodesic convex cutter in this specific case. Furthermore, we develop a generalized proximal gradient method tailored to the factorized objective functions on the manifold of diagonal positive semi-definite matrices, which we subsequently apply to solve a cutter-based matrix selection problem efficiently. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the geometric characteristics of the factorized objective functions and provides a novel algorithm for solving a matrix selection problem, which has implications for improving the efficiency of matrix selection methods such as the Nyström method. Additionally, our work identifies the limitations of current algorithms derived from the convex relaxation framework, which rely on the assumption of geodesic convexity and smoothness, and demonstrates that these algorithms do not efficiently select a subset of the most informative entries in the off-diagonal blocks of a matrix array, which is common in many real-world applications. Finally, our results demonstrate that our proposed method is superior to the existing algorithm based on convex relaxation in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness, as validated by comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on various real-world data sets and synthetic matrix arrays, which reflect typical patterns of real-world data, including both low and high dimensional cases. These results are further enhanced when the proposed method is combined with the cutter-based matrix selection method. The code for our research is available publicly on GitHub, which includes the generalized proximal gradient method, the cutter-based matrix selection method, and the corresponding numerical experiments. The code has been designed to be highly flexible and adaptable to various real-world data sets and synthetic matrix arrays, which enables other researchers to easily replicate and extend our results in the future. The code has the potential to be applied directly in real-world scenarios and provides a valuable resource for other researchers working in the field of matrix optimization, machine learning, and signal processing, among others. Our analysis focuses on the Hamming distance between solutions generated and an equilibrium point during the learning process. Our results show that the Hamming distance in individual learning converges to a stable equilibrium at a faster rate than in the other learning approach. Furthermore, our observations indicate that in the social learning case, the Hamming distance fluctuates extensively and eventually becomes stuck at a larger distance from the equilibrium point. Our research also examines the convergence rates of the Hamming distance and binary distance under both learning conditions and finds that the rates are significantly higher for the binary distance. Our proposed models can be applied to scenarios beyond fixed population sizes and provide a theoretical framework for understanding the co-evolutionary dynamics of genetic algorithms. This knowledge can be used to develop more efficient genetic algorithms by optimizing the learning processes. Our results also highlight the limitations of current co-evolutionary dynamics research and identify the need for future studies on various parameters and learning processes. Neural networks are susceptible to subtle errors caused by hardware malfunctions, leading to compromised performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a method called Uniform Quantization Checking to enforce consistent data representation across layers in neural networks, ensuring the absence of subtle data corruption. Unlike existing approaches, our method does not require uniform range restrictions for input values and can handle various quantization schemes, without significant performance degradation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by conducting thorough checks on six neural network models, subject to different quantization levels, and show that it effectively prevents subtle data corruption caused by inaccurate model predictions, including both performance metrics and anomalous classification results. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient, as it only requires approximately 10 times the usual computational resources needed for model training. Human-assisted evaluation of our method on real-world datasets reveals that it successfully identifies noisy annotations with an accuracy of over 90% in many cases. We have made our code and model checkpoints available for public use.

Recently, the generalization of the Jordanian twist was formulated and the corresponding star product was derived for a specific Lie algebra. This paper extends those findings to all bosonic semi-simple Lie algebras and demonstrates that the proposed generalization encompasses multiple simple Jordanian twists, including the fundamental one. Additionally, the underlying mathematics is clarified and previous formulations are compared to the current framework. A notable connection between the original and elevated generalizations of the Jordanian twist is established, thereby unveiling a hierarchical structure amongst them. The paper also addresses the concept of simplification of the generalization and explores its relationship to the original simple Jordanian twist, thereby demonstrating that all such twists possess the identical impact on the classical limit of an AdS5 boundary condition. The paper's primary focus lies within the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, particularly within the Glueball sector of the ${\cal N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. The proposed generalization successfully replicates the earlier obtained results, which included the power law slope of the glueball mass spectrum and the thermal free energy in perturbation theory, when considering the simple collective field method. The paper's additional contributions include the evaluation of universal thermal masses for glueballs in two distinct scenarios and the determination that the Witten or Maldacena-Popescu-Susskind (MPS) boundary condition, which yields the glueball mass spectrum, is invariant under both the simple and general Jordanian twist transformations. The paper's findings on the generalization of the Jordanian twist lead to a novel interpretation of the simple collective field method as a sort of "self-dual" solution within the context of the AdS5 space-time. The paper also presents the results of contrasting the generalization with other established approaches, such as the "humped" potential proposed by Lemos and Mitchell. Compared to other named entity recognition tasks, learning the tags for common language names like "John" and "Paris" proves to be a challenging task, especially when working with limited data. Existing approaches, largely based on neural network models and supervised training, have shown limitations in handling sparse entity tags for languages with few resources. This paper introduces a novel framework called EntitySense, a supervised learning method that employs a self-supervised strategy within the neural network itself to enhance performance. EntitySense is composed of two primary components: the first is a simple embedding model that identifies patterns in written text, and the following is a reverse lookup model that associates the learned embeddings with corresponding entity tags. By connecting the output of the embedding model to the input of the reverse lookup model, the paper shows that EntitySense gains significant performance gains in low-resource settings. Furthermore, EntitySense demonstrates its versatility by adapting to other named entity recognition tasks. Our proposed approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple assessments, including the RACE dataset with a score of 84.1%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chenyuhong/HRED-Entity-Sense. Our research indicates that named entity recognition in language-independent tags resembles language identification, and our best model achieves a score of 96.2% on the RACE dataset. Our work also highlights the challenges and potential solutions involved in learning sparse entity tags in language-independent form. Our proposed EntitySense framework provides a foundation for further innovation in this area. Our research further reveals that learning entity sense embeddings is feasible and can be beneficial for other natural language processing tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. We introduce an original approach to determine if one regular expression is contained within another using Brzozowski's operator, thereby developing a decision-making process for this query that is based on symbolic evaluation. This process involves converting the regular expressions into Brzozowski's automata forms and then utilizing the subset-like congruence relation to determine if the language of one automaton is a subset of the language of the other, which can be accomplished through a symbolic execution of the automata and the application of a subset-testing function to the resulting subset-testing problem. We demonstrate that the Brzozowski operator facilitates this decision-making process by contributing to the subset-testing problem as a function that respects the subset-testing relation, effectively transforming the problem into a form that can be solved using existing tools, such as Verilog and ABC, and thereby leveraging the capabilities of hardware description languages and Boolean satisfiability solvers for the resolution of this problem. By incorporating Brzozowski's operator, we are able to derive a decision-making process for this query that is more efficient, as measured by the number of symbolic steps required, compared to an alternative approach based on Glushkov's operator, and we have results from empirical evaluations of this decision-making process. These empirical results reveal that the regular expression containment checker yields faster step counts when evaluating contained relationships, with observed reductions in the number of steps required of 14.75 times, 5.75 times, and 3.5 times for randomly generated expressions, regular expression patterns, and XML schema expressions, respectively. We also provide a regular expression containment checker that is fully functional and test the checker using existing benchmarks, including GROOVE and XBEAR, with results showing that the checker is able to match the performance of alternative checkers, such as Lefebvre's checker, which is based on a different approach, and fail to match the performance of a checker based on Antimirov's operator, but only because that checker also uses Brzozowski's operator and thus shares similar performance characteristics. The increasing use of CPU-based systems in safety-critical applications restricts the availability of deep learning for these platforms. Our research focuses on a fundamental component of a robot's system, its visual inertial odometry (VIO). To enhance efficiency, we examine how to modify a popular and accurate VIO algorithm to function on CPU hardware. Our primary contribution involves developing a fast, deep learning-based VIO algorithm (DL-VIO) by reconfiguring a conventional VIO implementation to serve as a training dataset. This approach allows DL-VIO to benefit from the strengths of both deep learning and conventional methods. To further optimize DL-VIO for CPU systems, we experiment with different CPU-optimized neural networks and various optimization techniques. Our results show that by combining a simple neural network with optimization methods and utilizing the 2D case, we can significantly improve CPU-based VIO performance. Our proposed DL-VIO algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art approaches like LOST and SE-SAM when implementing VIO on CPU hardware. Our research also includes a comprehensive evaluation of various VIO datasets to ensure the consistency and generalizability of our findings. Our code is available for public use at this link: https://github.com/chaosrobotics/dlvio. Our proposed algorithm has the potential to enhance the integration of learning-based VIO with inertial sensors by addressing the data efficiency challenges it currently faces. In our investigation, we analyzed three-dimensional Weyl semimetals with multiple Weyl points, specifically focusing on systems that exhibit a particular arrangement where four Weyl points share the same energy eigenvalue. We established a comprehensive framework by combining a trio of techniques: the energy-axis theorem, a novel application of the integer theorem for vector fields, and a direct analysis of energy eigenvalue differences. Utilizing these methods, we demonstrated that such systems possess a unique topological characteristic - what we term "square-root topology" - which results in a non-trivial connection between their bulk and boundary properties. By comparing the results from a direct analysis of energy differences and those obtained using the energy-axis theorem, we uncovered a surprising discrepancy. Finally, we demonstrated that the disintegration of a single Weyl point is associated with a topological inaccuracy, which we linked to a real-space picture involving a atomic orbital framework. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the unique topological properties of atomic frameworks, particularly in relation to the energy eigenvalue sharing phenomenon observed with conical intersections of molecular potential energy surfaces. Moreover, our results are relevant to various three-dimensional solid-state and periodic atomic systems. Our square-root topology proposal can be applied to a wide range of materials, including TaAs, PbTaO$_3$, and Sr$_2$Ta$_3$O$_9$. Our investigation highlights the distinct features of high-order Weyl semimetals and reveals the intricate topological connection between their bulk and boundary properties. In the process, we developed a comprehensive understanding of the intrinsic properties of atomic frameworks, encompassing multiple Weyl points at the same energy eigenvalue, which share a common energy eigenvalue difference, and demonstrated that the topology of these systems is more complex than previously described. In the case of TaAs, our findings indicate that the bulk of the material can be accurately described using a single Weyl point model, whereas the boundary exhibits a complex Weyl-aragonita-like geometry. By contrast, the PbTaO$_3$ and Sr$_2$Ta$_3$O$_9$ bulk materials contain multiple Weyl points that meet the required conditions for square-root topology, while their boundary properties display Weyl-aragonita-like geometry. We propose that the energy eigenvalue sharing phenomenon, conical intersections in molecular potential energy surfaces, and square-root topology are related to a general atomic framework property, which we have come to understand through our investigation of three-dimensional Weyl semimetals

A study on edge finite elements demonstrates their effectiveness in solving a data completion problem by restoring missing data in a partially observed function when the observation map corresponds to an edge element gradient. We begin by outlining the characteristics of a valid edge element model and then examining the stability and accuracy of these elements in solving a data completion problem. Compared to the smoothness of the original function, we determine the optimal choice of edge elements that yields the best possible regularization term in the restored function. Furthermore, we theoretically show that the accuracy of the restored function improves with a higher order element type, such as bubble elements. Through numerical experiments, we also evaluate and compare different edge element models, including standard, continuous, and discontinuous elements, in solving a nonlinear algebraic data completion problem. Our results demonstrate that using continuous edge elements yields the smoothest restored function among the tested element types. Additionally, we provide a practical example of using edge elements to recover a sinusoidal function from noisy data. Our data completion algorithm and numerical experiments are implemented using the free and open-source software FEnSi. We also provide the modifiable source code for public use. Our research contributes to a broader understanding of edge element models and their applications in solving real-world data completion problems. Our findings and numerical methods can be useful for a wide range of problems involving the recovery of missing data from partially observed gradients. We also invite readers to access our research and associated software package for use in related projects. We are confident that our research, software, and associated data will find useful applications in various fields, such as the recovery of missing data from partially observed gradients, the development of numerical methods for solving PDEs with boundary conditions, and the creation of educational tools for teaching finite element methods. Teaching a student model to make accurate decisions by combining knowledge from multiple instructors is known as knowledge amalgamation. The primary challenge with knowledge amalgamation arises when data relating to student model decisions is unavailable, as it necessitates end-to-end training without feedback. To address this issue, we present an innovative strategy called Saliency-Aided Knowledge Amalgamation (SKA). The SKA framework identifies the most crucial tasks for the student model to focus on during training by analyzing the model's performance on related tasks without feedback. This is achieved by introducing a new task that serves as a directive for the student model, crafted using readily available knowledge. We demonstrate through comprehensive experiments that SKA effectively allocates learning resources to the most crucial tasks by prioritizing the most crucial information for the student model. As a result, SKA leads to a student model that is not only more accurate than traditional methods but also adapts efficiently to new tasks with minimal training data. Furthermore, we uncover interesting findings on SKA's performance in contexts with incomplete or misleading guidance. Our research on SKA highlights a novel approach to knowledge amalgamation that offers a wealth of possibilities for further exploration. The SKA code can be accessed at this link: https://github.com/Chenyue89/SKA.

Researchers examined the impact of dry etching silicon using different gases on carrier concentration in both etched silicon and adjacent oxide layers. For each etching method, varying the etching time and carrier concentration was also investigated. Notable differences in carrier concentration resulted from using different etching gases on silicon, with values ranging from -1 x 10^17 to 3 x 10^17 cm-3 in silicon and -1 x 10^20 to 3 x 10^20 cm-3 in oxide layers, depending on etching time. Conclusive evidence showed that carrier concentration in etched silicon remains higher than in adjacent oxide layers, even after stopping the etching process. This indicates that residual etching products can lead to high carrier concentrations in both silicon and oxide layers. Additionally, a comparison using quantum confinement model revealed that carrier concentration in oxide layers is higher than in etched silicon only when the oxide layer thickness is less than 4 nm. Furthermore, investigating the solubility of etching products in heat-treated silicon and oxide layers showed that carrier concentration in both materials can be significantly reduced by thermal treatment. Specifically, heat treatment at 1000°C for 30 minutes resulted in carrier concentrations less than 1 x 10^16 cm-3 in both silicon and oxide layers. This study provides valuable insights into the behavior of etching products in both silicon and oxide layers, and its findings are crucial for developing surface passivation methods using thermal oxidation. Additionally, it offers a fundamental understanding of the quantum confinement effect in oxide layers and silicon wafers. This knowledge can be applied to enhance the performance of silicon solar cells by improving passivation and reducing carrier concentration in both silicon and oxide layers. This research also provides a dry etching method evaluation tool that can be utilized for optimizing etching processes used in various silicon manufacturing processes, including the production of silicon wafers with high surface passivation and reduced carrier concentration. This is especially important for the production of high-performance silicon wafers with tight specifications, such as those required for photovoltaic cells used in high-efficiency silicon solar panels. A planetary interior-underlying model incorporating a two-way interaction with surface and atmospheric processes suggests that the cycling of material between a planet's interior and atmosphere could significantly impact atmospheric evolution over time. Through computational simulations, we examined how a planet's rotation rate, magnetic field, and atmospheric composition are influenced by the recycling process. As the model shows signs of non-linearity when considering changes in rotation rate and magnetic field, we believe it may have implications for the theory of terrestrial planet formation and evolution. Furthermore, by applying the model to simulation data of giant planet atmospheres, it demonstrates the importance of interior-atmospheric interactions on atmospheric circulation patterns and the formation of baroclinic waves. Ultimately, this study provides a framework for understanding the complex relationships between a planet's interior, atmosphere, and magnetic field through the lens of recycling processes. It also offers a potential explanation for the observed discrepancies between simulation results and actual data from giant planets, highlighting the value of this model as a tool for interpreting existing observational evidence and guiding future spacecraft missions.

Our recent paper provided an error-correcting perspective on rank metric codes, 
noting that these codes fail to accurately detect many errors, particularly at high rates. 
To address this issue, we proposed an algorithm that identifies the most probable number of errors and approximates it. 
This approximation enables the construction of a systematic decoder for rank metric codes, 
especially useful for codes with rates greater than 1/2. 
In contrast, codes with rates below 1/2 typically face fewer decoding challenges. 
As such, our proposed method primarily targets high-rate codes. 
However, it's worth noting that our algorithm can be applied to codes with rates below 1/2, 
albeit with some modifications that are less efficient in terms of the number of attempts required. 
Our analysis and proposed solution extend beyond the scope of our initial research, 
and they also expand on a previous idea discussed in 'Code Based Cryptography' by Courteau et al.. 
Our error estimation algorithm has additional implications for the security assessments of code-based cryptographic schemes, 
particularly in predicting the maximum number of attempts needed to guess the correct number of errors. 
This, in turn, can be used to determine the number of ciphertexts required to break a scheme with a given probability, 
as well as the time necessary to break it with a given number of ciphertexts. 
Our research also highlights the potential uses of our algorithm in improving the efficiency of existing code-based schemes, 
such as McBride's signature scheme and Lee-Bouillard's key encapsulation mechanism. 
Finally, our error estimation algorithm provides a decoder for the 2-out-of-N threshold scheme, 
which, to the best of our knowledge, has never been shared publicly before. 
Our proposed solution and related discussions contribute to a better comprehension of the underlying issues and potential solutions in the field of code-based cryptography. 
With this research, our primary goal is to lay the groundwork for the development of more efficient code-based cryptographic schemes, 
particularly in high-rate code scenarios, and to establish a foundation for future applications and research in this area.

In 1976, Gelfand and MacPherson introduced the concept of a combinatorial differential manifold to facilitate the integration of algebraic geometry and analysis. They established a natural correspondence between these manifolds and systems of parametric equations. Subsequent work revealed that this framework effectively captures the topological and differential properties of smooth mappings. Our study builds upon Gelfand and MacPherson's framework by demonstrating that combinatorial differential manifolds can be employed to analyze the local structural characteristics of smooth mappings cross a family of mappings from a parameter space to a target space. In the process, we develop an approach to determining the germiantion categories of such mappings by examining the combinatorial structure of associated graphs. Furthermore, our results provide a natural extension of Gelfand and MacPherson's findings to the level of mapping germs. In the special case where the target space mappings are restricted to algebraic curves, our approach enables us to classify the combinatorial structure of such mappings based on a key invariant - the number of real intersection points it exhibits for a given value of the parameter. The peculiar supernova SN~2020jfo has been studied in depth using data from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope at the Haleakala Observatory in Hawaii, spectra from the Telesco reflectance near Naples, Italy, and a spectroscopic observation from the South African Astronomical Observatory. Initially misidentified as a Type Ia supernova, SN~2020jfo, which exploded on January 18th, 2020, is now believed to be a Type Ib/c supernova with a combination of both Type Ib and II features. The analysis of SN~2020jfo's spectrum shows the presence of helium-absorption lines, a lack of hydrogen, and the appearance of cobalt and iron lines, along with a stronger nickel to iron ratio than typical for these explosions. Although the exact distance to SN~2020jfo is unclear, estimates suggest it could be 9 to 60 million light years, based on its absolute magnitude. If this range holds true, SN~2020jfo would be one of the most distant supernovae ever observed with a spectroscopic signature of helium, cobalt, and iron lines. If it is indeed a nearby supernova, SN~2020jfo's nickel to iron production ratio is higher than the solar value, and its elemental abundance profile shows a significant lack of elements like oxygen, silicon, and magnesium. If it is a distant supernova, the abundance profile is more typical of Type Ib/c supernovae, and it is unclear why the spectrum shows both Type Ib and II features. Although the exact cause of SN~2020jfo's unusual characteristics remains a mystery, it is believed that it could be the result of a supernova that occurred in a massive star that had a low metal content, and was covered in helium with little to no hydrogen. If this theory holds true, SN~2020jfo would be a significant discovery in the field of supernova research. It is also possible that SN~2020jfo could be a supernova that occurred in a binary star system, where the companion star accelerated the helium star to the point of collapse through strong winds and mass transfer, resulting in a mixture of both Type Ib and II features. If this is the case, it would be the first time such a phenomenon has been observed. Overall, SN~2020jfo remains a supernova enigma that continues to pose significant scientific questions. It is hoped that further research will help unlock the secrets of this unusual explosion.

We present a novel approach to interpreting cross-like images formed by lobster-eye optics, leveraging the azimuthal rotation angle to dissect the image and a adjacent mirrorized duplicate. This allows for the separation of an image into distinct segments based on the position of its features within the optic system. By applying this method to images of a pinhole array and a Talbot-Lau setup, we demonstrate how this approach reveals the spatial distribution of X-rays and the phase shift occurring during propagation through the system. Notably, this technique enables the direct visualization of the azimuthal component of the complex contrast, a concept previously theoretical but now demonstrated through actual data processing. By combining this approach with a simulation-based model, we can recover both the original image and the azimuthal component of the complex contrast from cross-like images. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated across various beamline configurations and optic systems, and the associated data processing is made available through a software package. This research paves the way for novel applications in X-ray imaging and metrology. Furthermore, due to the proposed method's versatility, this work is seen as a foundation for exploring similar techniques with other types of optics and X-ray imaging modalities. The associated data and software are available at https://github.com/PSI-2023-LobsterEye. Accurate prediction of halo masses in the early universe relies on correctly identifying dark matter halos from cosmological simulations. A density-based model that operates independently and maps density fields to halo masses has shown superior performance compared to model-based approaches that directly track dark matter trajectories. Whether this model's halo mass prediction reliability is consistent across various cosmic conditions remains to be studied. In this research, we tested the efficacy of the density-only model under conditions with abnormally rapid universe expansion, controlled by the epsilon factor, using the $N^3T_3$ cosmological simulation framework. Our findings show that even in scenarios with extreme cosmic conditions, the original density-only model accurately predicts halo masses with a high success rate, maintaining a 1-sigma mass estimation error of approximately 0.1. Furthermore, no significant difference in the model's performance was observed when the simulation model included an initial random fluctuation among halos, despite this leading to changes in halo mergers and growth. We observed the model's resilience even when the mean halo mass spectrum transformed significantly. Our results confirm the density-only model's versatility and stability in halo mass predictions across various cosmic environments. Furthermore, our study provides a precise evaluation of the model's performance in conditions with extremely rapid universe expansion, facilitated by the $N^3T_3$ simulation framework, involving high-resolution, high-density observations of the early universe. These findings are applicable to future large-scale cosmological simulations featuring complex halo evolutions and diverse halo mass spectra. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the underlying physical processes governing halo mass predictions from density fields, especially in extremely dilute halo mass regimes. This is the first study to extensively examine the reliability of a density-only model in scenarios with very rapid universe expansion, facilitated by the $N^3T_3$ simulation framework, involving high-resolution, high-density observations of the early universe. A key challenge in using structural learning methods like Graph Neural Networks is the cost of labeling data. To tackle this issue, we develop a method that leverages partial labeling to efficiently create labeled data. By strategically labeling only a subset of nodes with the desired class and using the graph structure to determine the labels for remaining nodes, our approach significantly reduces labeling expenses. To achieve this, we introduce a novel neural network model that incorporates a node's labeling potential based on its local features and relationships with neighboring nodes. By modeling the potential for each node as a probability distribution, we utilize a softmax function to connect it with the input from neighboring nodes, effectively creating a node-specific learning process that can be trained using Neighbor-Attention Neural Networks. When applied to large graphs representing molecular structures, our method demonstrates a significant reduction in labeling costs and data sizes required for model training, resulting in improved performance when evaluating models based on precision in predicting node labels. Furthermore, our method shows comparable performance to models using full labeling, achieving an accuracy of 97.5% on predicting molecular properties with respect to certain attributes, while reducing labeling costs by 10 times. In addition, our method succeeds in scaling models to large graphs representing real-world molecular datasets, overcoming the limitation of full labeling to smaller, substructure-level models. Redistributions of all code and datasets are free and can be used for non-commercial purposes, requiring explicit permission for commercial use. All molecular datasets used in this research are publicly accessible, while the underlying data sources are listed in the supplementary materials. The simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation from neutron star mergers offers unprecedented insights into these crucial events. Although a gamma-ray satellite is needed to initiate multi-messenger investigations, future satellite missions will likely focus on X-ray observations of mergers. To guide future research, we explore the characteristics of neutron star mergers detected by X-ray satellites in the context of future gravitational wave observations. Using the Liquid Megaton detector's sensitivity to binary neutron star mergers, we identify potential targets for X-ray observations and investigate the properties of post-merger neutron star tails, ejecta velocities, beaming, and cosmic ray connections. Furthermore, we investigate the expected counts for future satellite missions, such as the X-ray Multi-Messenger Unit on the Enhanced X-ray Timing Array, for both optimized and general-purpose observations of low-mass binary neutron star mergers. If future satellite missions focus on the optimal fields for lowest-ejecta-mass mergers, we forecast the detection of up to 0.4 events per year, resulting in one satellite-detected event every 2.5 years. If future satellite missions observe the entire sky for all binary neutron star mergers, the predicted detection rate would increase to 4 events per year, leading to the detection of one event every 6.25 years. Nonetheless, even with optimized observations, the majority of binary neutron star merger events will continue to be detected primarily through gravitational waves, and satellite-based X-ray observations are expected to complement rather than replace future generation ground-based facilities. The predicted detection rates for satellite-based X-ray observations of neutron star and black hole mergers in the context of future gravitational wave observations highlight the significance of simultaneous gravitational and X-ray wave observations of these events. This knowledge will be invaluable for allocating time on future satellite missions for the optimal fields of view and for the development of joint analysis tools that can fully exploit the multi-messenger properties of these crucial events. Furthermore, the characteristics of neutron star mergers detected by X-ray satellites in the context of future gravitational wave observations can be used to assess the effectiveness of future satellite missions in the era of decimal-Hz gravitational waves. Ultimately, the ability to observe the same event through both gravitational and X-ray waves will present opportunities to reconcile any discrepancies between the two-dimensional pictures painted by these two phenomena. This knowledge will also facilitate a deeper understanding of the matter that forms during and after these crucial events. This research explores the consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic on the diversity of urban encounters and community resilience in three diverse cities: Bogota, Nairobi, and Seoul. A comprehensive review of existing literature served as a foundation, which was then supplemented by original data collected through online surveys among urban residents in each city. The results show that the pandemic led to a significant decrease in the diversity of urban encounters in all three cities. This decline was more pronounced in the short term and varied over time in each city. Furthermore, decreased diversity in encounters was linked to lower community resilience in all three cities. A key finding reveals that digital connections played a crucial role in maintaining the diversity of urban encounters, particularly in the long term. Therefore, this study suggests that diverse urban encounters are essential for community resilience and that efforts are needed to support this diversity, especially through digital channels, in post-pandemic urban recovery initiatives. The research mentioned above can be built upon to further examine the relationship between diverse urban encounters, community resilience, and digital connectivity in the post-pandemic era. Around a young and massive star, a circumstellar disk forms, where objects such as planets, or planetesimals, migrate, potentially destabilizing the inner disk. Our research examined the effects of migrating objects on the stability of the inner disk for a star like Vega using numerical simulations of a disk with a large temperature contrast and migrating objects the size of Mars. We conducted multiple simulations with varying migration speeds and directions to observe the inner disk dynamics. Notably, we discovered that objects migrating inward can create a stable, quasi-thermal equilibrium region at the inner disk, while objects migrating outward lead to a unstable, turbulent region. Additionally, we found that the distribution of dust particles becomes skewed towards the side of the star farthest from the migrating objects, which could explain the asymmetrical polar dust fields observed around some stars like Sirius. Furthermore, the simulations agree with observations of vibrational H2 and [FeII] emission in disks like those around Vega and Beta Pictoris, suggesting that migrating objects may be responsible for these features. Finally, our results also suggest that massive stars with disks lacking polar dust fields may be lacking in migrating objects, and such a deficiency could be a crucial factor in planet formation. Our simulations provide a possible explanation for the unusual geometry of polar dust fields and provide a framework for interpreting the variety of inner disk dynamics revealed by high-resolution spectroscopy. Our research demonstrates that migrating objects in circumstellar disks could be a crucial factor in understanding the dynamics of the inner disks around young and massive stars. Our simulation data is available for public access through the MaxPlanckDust website. Our future plans involve conducting simulations with more complex migration patterns and objects the size of planets. Our initial study focuses on objects the size of planetesimals to distinguish their effects from those of larger objects like planets, which would require more sophisticated simulations using numerical codes like NGA. Our research aims to contribute to a better comprehension of the varied geometries observed in polar dust fields around massive stars with disks. Our simulation results can be visually experienced in the MaxPlanckDust website's interactive environment, where users can manipulate parameters such as the speed and direction of migration, the temperature contrast, and the mass of the star. Our website also provides access to the FSPS-spectrum simulations of the H2 and [FeII] emission for different models. To validate our method, we have results that match those found by Cligod, along with additional periodic solutions. This research also compares solutions obtained using the Trevenen-Hughes transformation with those found using the Hirota method. Current implementations of the model, however, rely solely on input data characterizations, neglecting the influence of broader contextual information. This paper investigates the impact of contextual factors on the model's performance when detecting manifold anomalies, in the context of identifying fake news. Our key finding reveals that incorporating contextual information into the score network enhances its ability to discriminate between genuine and fabricated news. This information can originate from various sources related to the anomaly itself, or even its generated counterpart. Our research demonstrates that the model excels at learning the underlying dynamics of contextual information and the anomalies it describes. This knowledge learning capability of the model truly reflects the inductive nature of diffusion models. We investigate the dynamics of a many-body system subject to an external force that varies over time, using the curriculum learning framework to explore the interplay between its geometric properties, hysteresis, and thermal behavior. In this approach, we gradually introduce the system's complexities, starting from simple, interconnected components. Our findings reveal that the curvature effect, a measure of the system's complexity, influences its entropy and hysteresis in distinct ways, depending on whether it is changing over time. Furthermore, we observe the emergence of hysteresis and a slowdown in the system's thermalization in response to the curriculum learning structure. To illustrate this concept, we apply it to a linear chain composed of interacting nodes, and demonstrate that the curvature effect can be reversed through the application of an opposite force, potentially "unlearning" the system. Ultimately, this research provides a novel perspective on the curriculum learning framework, revealing its connection to the system's geometry, hysteresis, and thermal dynamics. Moreover, it presents a non-equilibrium approach to studying the curvature effect and hysteresis, with implications for understanding complex dynamics in multifaceted systems.

To address the challenging problem of L1-PCA on real symmetric matrices, specifically when the underlying distribution is rotationally invariant, researchers have proposed various methods to tackle both large and small-scale data sets. Although these strategies have achieved successful results, they generally require the application of circular convolution that significantly increases computational costs. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel two-block formulation of the invariational L1-PCA problem that is feasible with an efficient algorithm, particularly for large-scale data sets. A gradient-based method is also proposed to solve this two-block formulation, and it is demonstrated that this method yields an equivalent solution to the original problem. Additionally, the researcher provides a sample-based formulation that enables the application of its algorithm to solve the two-block formulation using subgradients. This paper also establishes the convergence and rotational invariance of its method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both solution accuracy and computational efficiency. The researcher's efficient algorithm has been publicly available since February 2020 at the following website: https://www.cba.hku.edu.cn/Professor_Dong/resources.html. This website also provides the code for testing on synthetic and real-world datasets. Moreover, new datasets that were not previously available are provided to support the evaluation of future algorithms proposed for solving the rotationally invariational L1-PCA problem. This paper is an extended version of a paper that was previously published at the 2020 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS). This extended version includes additional experimental results, a more comprehensive literature review, and a newly proposed sample-based formulation. Moreover, the researcher's efficient algorithm has been improved to facilitate the solution of larger-scale data sets. Compared to traditional approaches, neural network-based natural language processing models yield better performance, yet it is crucial to ensure the accuracy of their annotations by detecting inconsistencies. We propose a method to achieve this guarantee through consistent annotation prediction, leveraging the availability of detailed annotations for certain tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. Our theoretical investigation focuses on an otherwise unchanged clean copper (111) surface and explores the behavior of zero-spectral-weight regions around the K and $\Gamma$ points in the surface band structure. We find that the spin-orbit interaction causes a shift in the positions of the sharp peaks of YSR states, especially in areas with magnetic adatoms or dimers, where some peaks become negative and some peaks split in pairs. In addition to the spin-orbit effect, the Kondo screening of magnetic adatoms or the exchange interaction with a magnetic dimer also influence the YSR states, causing some peaks to vanish and others to shift in frequency. Notably, the presence of a zero-bias peak at the $\Gamma$ point is possible if there is sufficient distance between the Fermi level and the bottom of the copper sp band, but this is disrupted by the presence of adatoms or a dimer. Finally, the absence of a zero-bias peak at the K point is explained by the appearance of a gap in the copper surface band structure along the direction connecting the K and $\Gamma$ points. If the spin-orbit interaction is strong enough, the zero-bias peak at the $\Gamma$ point breaks up into two peaks that are mirrored about the $\Gamma$ point. This behavior has not been observed experimentally to date. While the spin-orbit interaction causes a shift in the peaks of YSR states, it does not affect the magnitude of the zero-bias peak at the $\Gamma$ point or the absence of a zero-bias peak at the K point. Consequently, the presence of zero-spectral-weight regions around the K and $\Gamma$ points in the surface band structure remains a robust phenomenon governed by the copper surface band structure itself, unaffected by local magnetic impurities. Moreover, the magnitude of the zero-bias peak at the $\Gamma$ point is found to be independent of temperature, in contrast to earlier proposals. Additionally, the magnitude of the zero-bias peak at the $\Gamma$ point is found to be extremely sensitive to minor adjustments in the copper surface band structure, offering an exciting possibility for modifying zero-bias peaks through strain or substitutional impurities. Our study suggests that the term "zero-bias peaks" should be used with caution in the future and recommends using the more precise term "zero-spectral-weight regions". Research involving a rotating Hele-Shaw cell with a water-filled membrane chamber has yielded surprising results when it comes to the behavior of surfactant liquids. Depending on the speed of rotation, three distinct states can exist - a stable, symmetric state and two asymmetric states that can switch in a sudden, discrete jump. To understand the dynamics of these asymmetric states, researchers are examining how membrane tension affects their stability. For low rotation speeds, the asymmetric states that form are oriented at 60 degrees to each other, and controlling membrane tension has no impact on their stability. However, at higher speeds, the membrane tension's influence becomes significant, and the stability of the 90-degree asymmetric states can be precisely controlled by adjusting the tension, thereby demonstrating the pivotal role that membrane tension plays in these dynamics. Notably, when the rotation speed is very high, the asymmetric states that form can be either very large or very small, and in the latter case, they have a unique relationship - their combined size always equals a fixed amount that is determined by the speed of rotation and the properties of the membrane. The discovery of a fixed relationship governing the small asymmetric states' sizes and the speeds at which they appear suggests they are actually "snakes" that share characteristics with the stable, symmetric state, and are a part of a broader range of rotation speeds where only the symmetric state can exist. The findings of this research could have far-reaching implications for the understanding of complex dynamics in other systems that involve similar relationships between forces and shapes. The methods used in this study have also led to a better comprehension of the interaction between two powerful forces - surface tension and shear stress - within the membrane chamber. The influence of surface stress, which was previously underappreciated, has been revealed through the explicit manipulation of the asymmetric states' stability. The discovery that the membrane's own properties play a significant role in the behavior of the asymmetric states it contains has driven the development of a new model that takes into account the intricacies of the membrane itself. The previous model, which ignored the membrane's properties, is shown to be inaccurate and not representative of the actual dynamics observed in the Hele-Shaw cell. The new model's success has been validated through the accurate simulation of all the rotating membrane's states and dynamics. The development of this model has also led to the recognition that the relationship between the shear stress and surface tension forces within the membrane chamber is non-linear and unpredictable, and cannot be accurately described by a simple sum of the two forces in isolation. A recent proposal to modify the model by adding a viscosity term has led to a model where the Hubble parameter varies with time and may be used to explain different phases of the universe. This paper builds upon that model by replacing the exponential function with a power law in the density function, leading to a model where the density of the universe decreases over time and can be potentially used to describe the present universe. By applying the viscosity model to the power law density model, we find that the shape parameter 'p' affects the viscosity coefficient 'γ' and the Hubble parameter 'H'. Furthermore, the power law density model results in a linear relationship between the density of the universe and the square of the viscosity coefficient 'γ'. This model can be tested using observational data for the viscosity coefficient 'γ' and the shape parameter 'p'. If validated, this model may help in understanding different phenomena of the universe, such as the formation of structure, the acceleration of its expansion, and the variation of the gravitational constant. This paper also presents numerical solutions to a system of differential equations that define the model and provides an approach to calculate the total mass of the universe using the viscosity model. This research proposal can be further developed by investigating the cosmological implications of the viscosity model, analyzing the latter stages of the model, and exploring its application to different scenarios of the universe. This approach can be an alternative to conventional dynamic models and helps in addressing the challenge of developing physically based dynamic models for the density of the universe. The XENON1T collaboration searched for evidence of dark matter produced through interactions between dark matter and quarks within the $J/\psi$ system. By reanalyzing a data set for $J/\psi$ decaying into invisible particles, we were able to reduce the limit on dark matter nucleon scattering cross sections by a factor of five for certain low-mass dark matter scenarios. Additionally, our study identified potential contributions from backgrounds such as elastic scattering of $J/\psi$ off nuclei or the conversion of $J/\psi$ into dark matter and additional standard model particles, which could be tested with upgraded experiments. Our new limit on the scattering cross section of dark matter with a mass of 1.60 GeV, for example, is 1.5 x 10^-26 cm^2 at 90% confidence, and our findings highlight the significance of considering rare hadron decays in dark matter searches involving $J/\psi$. Our approach to analyzing the $J/\psi \to \gamma + \text{invisible}$ process also offers a versatile method for exploring dark matter and additional light particles that could be present in models of dark matter or other hadron interactions. Our research paves the way for future experiments that can capitalize on the high sensitivity to light dark matter and light, actively convertible particles using $J/\psi$ decays. Our code is available for others to use, and we encourage further investigation into the physics uncovered in this study. Our initial limit settings can be found in the code's README file, and subsequent limits can be obtained by running the code as demonstrated in the tutorial. Any new limits obtained using the code should be compared to our current limits and cited in any resulting publications. The code utilizes the DarkSUSY package that is widely adopted in dark matter research. Our research presents the MFSSA algorithm, a novel and efficient method for approximating the solution to a wide class of alternating direction convex optimization problems. Our main contribution involves deriving a non-asymmetric gap inequality, which can be used to yield the theoretical convergence rate of the MFSSA algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of MFSSA in various practical applications, including the analysis of temperature curves, remote sensing images, and the estimation of time-dependent linear models. Our empirical results show that MFSSA achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, such as Julia-ATD, PROXSD, and AD3, in terms of recovery accuracy, model selection, and computational time. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for the MFSSA algorithm and illustrate its practical utility in modeling real-world data. Our analysis focuses on the long-term behavior of this random walk as the number of steps increases without bound. We find that its asymptotic direction can be determined by a scalar parameter 'b' that is derived from the second moments of the steps. Our proof utilizes a stochastic version of the argument principle to apply the Wiener-Hopf factorization method. This approach allows us to establish the asymptotic direction of the random walk by analyzing the roots of a polynomial whose coefficients are the normalized second moments of the steps. We also investigate relationships between 'b' and existing metrics that characterize the asymptotic behavior of the random walk. Furthermore, we examine scenarios that result in 'b' changing sign and the implications this has for the asymptotic behavior of the random walk. Our study also compares 'b' with the Banister-Durrett parameter 'd' in discrete models and the Cox process gap distribution in continuous models. Our research on the BDB process reveals that its asymptotic direction is directly related to the average of its step sizes. Our results in this specific case can be viewed as extending upon previous research by Cox and John (1989) and Durrett and Schmitt (1991). This study introduces a novel W-shaped network to achieve enhanced performance in identifying cell nuclei in cervical cancer images. Our proposed framework modifies the standard UNET architecture by incorporating two parallel branches in the depth feature extraction stage, effectively doubling the network's depth while maintaining computational efficiency. Unlike conventional methods that apply image rotation as a data augmentation technique, we developed a more efficient method by creating a pair of models that process images and their rotations separately. This strategy allows us to evaluate the confidence in our predictions by calculating the consistency between an image and its rotation, which we use as a guiding factor for selecting the most credible prediction among the pair. This approach is superior to using a model that processes both an image and its rotation through a single network, which we used as a baseline for comparison. Our proposed approach has several advantages, including enhanced performance, increased robustness, and the ability to produce more reliable predictions by eliminating ambiguous detections. This approach demonstrates outstanding performance in detecting cell nuclei in images from the ACDC dataset, achieving scores of 73.6% in the diagnosis task and 79.1% in the segmentation task. This represents a significant improvement over the baseline method, which performed at 68.3% and 76.5% respectively. This method's efficiency and effectiveness make it suitable for use in challenging real-world applications. The code for this research is available publicly on GitHub at https://github.com/HuangBiao2019/WNET. This code includes example use cases, tutorials, and explanations of the underlying technology. With slight modifications, this code can be used for automatic detection of cancerous lesions in fundus images from the DIABETES dataset, which is another important application of medical image analysis. The current study formulates and proves the Geometric Whigard-Selberg Conjecture for a specific context of rank-one twists of local gamma factors, which concerns representations within the odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups. This achievement implies the equivalence of two representation categories, leading to a specific twist of local gamma factors that is equivalent to a standard version, with a specific rank that can be determined. This rank meets the expectations proposed by the Geometric Whigard-Selberg Conjecture for all representations, unlike the approach taken in previous studies which was only valid for certain specific cases. The investigation also explores the twisted local gamma factors with rank one, which are connected to the standard version by means of an isomorphism, and these are found to be a subset of the Bessel models. Moreover, the study identifies the possible ranks of the twisted local gamma factors, which can arise from the automorphisms of the field at hand, and determines the twisted delta function, denoted as delta_w, as being equivalent to the standard delta function, denoted as delta, but with an altered normalization, i.e., delta_w = w^{-1} * delta, where w is defined as the global cube root of the field's characteristic, and has consequences for the resulting Bessel models. By interpreting Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized examples of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), we provide a new perspective on their underlying mechanics. Our analysis shows that training these networks is equivalent to learning the node representations in a particular graph, specifically for CNNs - a grid-based graph, and for fully connected networks - a complete graph. We demonstrate that these black holes' entropy values align with those predicted by the dual conformal field theory, using the bulk gravity analysis. In particular, we find that the entropy of these rotating hairy black holes matches the sum of their individual components' contributions, in accordance with the Chern-Simons theory for pure gravity. This matching holds true for both the linearized and non-linearized Chern-Simons theory for pure gravity, even when the rotation parameters exceed a certain limit where the linearized approximation is valid. In addition, we find that the entropy of these rotating hairy black holes also complies with the holographic principle, expressed as an entropy density function that is a function of density rather than a direct function of the rotation parameters. This behavior is distinct from that seen with the rotating standard black holes within Einstein gravity. This result indicates that the entropy of these rotating hairy black holes cannot be explained by a single Cardy formula but rather requires a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. This conclusion holds true for both the linearized and non-linearized Chern-Simons theory for pure gravity. A significant issue in the development of reliable artificial intelligence systems involves ensuring the correctness and safety of their underlying software logic. This task is made more challenging by the increasing use of artificial intelligence tools for generating pseudocode, as these systems may produce logics that are incorrect or pose risks to the systems they are part of. To address this problem, an approach is proposed that utilizes a unique and restricted form of pseudocode called 'logical pseudocode' that is grounded in first-order logic, making it possible to establish the accuracy and safety of generated code through formal mathematical proofs. A key distinction between 'logical pseudocode' and traditional pseudocode lies in their respective purposes, as pseudocode is primarily used for explaining the functionality of software to others, as opposed to providing a precise, formally provable representation of that software. To illustrate the advantages of 'logical pseudocode', an example is given that shows how an incorrectly implemented logic could be identified and corrected following a data security breach caused by an unauthorized data transfer. Furthermore, an intuitive, graphical 'logical pseudocode' representation is presented, along with a practical application for creating and examining such pseudocodes in the context of artificial intelligence-driven software development. This research is an initial step towards a broader goal of developing tools that can automatically generate 'logical pseudocodes' from source code, with the ability to identify and fix flaws in that code. As the simplicity and readability of pseudocode make it an ideal choice for explaining complex software to others, it is essential to utilize a form of pseudocode that is both accurate and safe from a logical standpoint. By utilizing a form of pseudocode that is grounded in first-order logic, it becomes possible to establish the correctness and safety of artificial intelligence-generated pseudocode through the use of formal mathematical proofs. This is achieved by limiting the pseudocode to a set of rules that avoids the use of ambiguous language, ensuring that the underlying software logic is both free from errors and secure from common threats caused by flawed logic. This research demonstrates how such a restricted form of pseudocode can be effectively created, examined, and modified, along with a practical application for artificial intelligence-driven software development, as a crucial step towards developing tools that can automatically generate 'logical pseudocodes' from source code and identify flaws in that code. This approach is advantageous as it facilitates the development of reliable artificial intelligence systems by providing a means to ensure the accuracy and safety of the underlying software logic through formal mathematical proofs, even in the presence of significant uncertainties caused by artificial intelligence-driven software development. This represents the first instance in which a one-pass approach is successful in creating a coreset for $k$-means without requiring the employment of a separate data structure to monitor mean values and distances. Our coreset is subsequently used to create an efficient two-round clustering solution. Furthermore, our one-pass algorithm incorporates modifications to enable the creation of a coreset for a related problem, in a different context. Additionally, we present enhancements to our initial result, including a more efficient coreset creation algorithm utilizing $O(\kappa^2 \log \n)$ coordinates, and we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of this new approach to a range of geographic clustering problems. These achievements build upon our initial research published in the conference paper 'Efficient High-Dimensional Mean-Based Coresets Using Sketches' presented at the 20th annual conference of the European Skilled Computing Research, 2021. In complex decision-making scenarios, breaking down a large grid world into smaller sub-environments, or superstates, can significantly simplify agent navigation by reducing the size of the state space. Our study explores the benefits of this approach in a common and challenging scenario where one agent pursues multiple evaders among a grid of nodes. By testing various superstate methods and different node distance metrics, our results show that this strategy can lead to more efficient pursuit paths and improved evasion strategies by dynamically changing the sub-environments based on the agents' current positions. Furthermore, we found that the most effective superstate partitions vary greatly depending on the specific scenario, highlighting the importance of incorporating dynamic flexibility into the superstate framework. To facilitate easy implementation and testing of this approach, we have made the code for our study publicly available. Our research also reveals potential limitations and future directions for enhancing the superstate approach in pursuit-evasion scenarios. Additionally, we discovered that the optimal superstate partitioning strategy itself is a challenging problem that is difficult to solve exactly, yet easy to approximate, by providing a simple and efficient heuristic solution. Our extensive simulations have been designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the superstate approach in pursuit-evasion scenarios. Our data is fully reproducible, and our code is openly shared to facilitate further customization and research of this heuristic solution and related topics. Our research and associated data offer valuable insights into the dynamic partitioning of grid worlds for optimal decision-making in challenging multi-agent scenarios. In 1936, G. E. Moore delivered a lecture where he strengthened Godel's first incompleteness theorem by showing that any sufficiently powerful formal system that is capable of describing itself must contain a statement that is neither provable nor refutable within the system, yet has a counterpart among the system's valid statements that can be accessed through intuition. Twenty years later, Y. S. Sokal translated this concept into the language of logic by creating a system of sentences that are neither provable nor refutable within the Peano axioms, yet are derivable through intuition-based reasoning that adheres to the principles of first-order logic. Building upon Sokal's work, we simplify and expand upon his findings by utilizing the concept of relativized truth and a corresponding inductive definition system. We demonstrate that the resulting system, despite being inherently self-referential, does not violate the principles of the Diagonalization Lemma, the Axiom of Choice, or the Law of Excluded Middle, thereby validating the effectiveness of its components. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the system's self-referential nature and Rosser's modification of Godel's second incompleteness theorem. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the concepts of formalized arithmetic, the consistency of which remains an unproven assumption within the realm of mathematics. Despite the inherent self-referentiality of the system, we show that it can be viewed as a manifestation of the set of valid statements within the Peano axioms, thereby providing a logical framework for understanding the underlying principles of Godel's first incompleteness theorem. Moreover, we discover that the system's components are compositional in nature, thereby enabling the automatic generation of self-referential expressions for any given formal system. Consequently, we can utilize this capability to establish a direct connection between the system and the concept of metalanguage, as defined by R. Carnap, thereby demonstrating the generality of our findings beyond the confines of the Peano axioms. Ultimately, our work demonstrates that the underlying principles of Godel's first incompleteness theorem are fundamentally rooted in the self-referential nature of language itself, rather than the formal systems that utilize it. Additionally, we reveal that the associated consequences encompass a broader spectrum of mathematical concepts, including the principles of consistency, solvability, and decidability. Lastly, we believe that our research provides a compelling argument for reevaluating the long-held assumption of the consistency of the Peano axioms within the realm of mathematics

This research extends Hadamard's three circles theorem to a higher dimensional context, where it takes the form of a significant property of monogenic functions. It demonstrates that when a monogenic function is defined on a specific type of convex body in Dirac-Helmholtz space, it exhibits the same behavior predicted by Hadamard's three circles theorem if it maps lines to lines and preserves angles. Furthermore, we establish that Hadamard's theorem holds for any monogenic function on this type of convex body, providing a more general statement. Moreover, we investigate specific cases of convex bodies, including balls and polyhedra, and show that Hadamard's theorem applies to them as well. Additionally, we introduce the concept of a direct image of a monogenic function and use it to develop the three circles theorem for Riemannian monogenic functions on higher dimensional convex bodies. This leads to an interesting connection to the well-known result by Jorgens about the equality of area and perimeter in the plane. Lastly, we also examine the case where the monogenic function is defined on the ball in Dirac-Helmholtz space and establish that it satisfies Hadamard's three circles theorem if it has a specific growth rate. This growth rate condition allows us to extend the result by Fejer, who proved that the monogenic function that is harmonic in the ball and satisfies certain boundary conditions must be constant, to the case where the ball is in the higher dimensional Dirac-Helmholtz space. This extends his result to higher dimensions and provides an alternative proof. This also leads to the conclusion that any monogenic function that is harmonic in the ball and satisfies the condition of having a specific growth rate must be constant. This further implies that we can define a monogenic function on the ball in the higher dimensional Dirac-Helmholtz space if and only if it is constant. This generalizes the result by Alexander, Eschbach and Hahn to higher dimensions and provides an alternative proof. This also leads to the conclusion that we can define a monogenic function on the ball in the higher dimensional Dirac-Helmholtz space if and only if it is constant. This generalizes the result by Jorgens to the higher dimensional Dirac-Helmholtz space. This paper introduces a novel Wasserstein GAN framework, specifically a conditional version, that generates posterior samples that are beneficial in various imaging applications such as super-resolution and de-noising. Instead of focusing on approximating the data distribution, this GAN model approximates the conditional distribution of data given certain attributes or labels, which it achieves by minimizing a modified Wasserstein distance. However, this approach encounters the challenge of identifying the optimal target posterior distribution, which is already a complex problem in its own right. To resolve this issue, we propose a straightforward yet effective solution that involves approximating the target conditional distribution using the original GAN and a second GAN that mirrors the inverse relationship, which it does by flipping the roles of data and labels. This paper also explores regularized versions of both the conditional and unconditional GANs and discovers that they produce more realistic and diverse synthetic samples by constraining the learned distributions to stay within predetermined boundaries. Moreover, we demonstrate that this GAN model and its regularized variants exhibit comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in various tasks, including image classification, facial attribute manipulation, and the generation of synthetic financial news. This method also comes with the added benefit of providing feature representations that are equivalent in quality to those produced by conventional GANs, which it achieves without sacrificing synthetic sample generation performance.
