This paper explores the concept of fractional linear subspaces that remain unchanged under the action of a fractional differential operator. Our analysis focuses on the Caputo fractional derivative and develops methods for determining invariant subspaces of given dimensions. We establish that only one-dimensional invariant subspaces exist with respect to the Caputo fractional derivative, unlike its Riemann-Liouville counterpart, which does not support any invariant subspaces. We then investigate the capabilities of combining fractional and integer-order derivatives to enlarge the set of invariant subspaces. To accomplish this, we examine systems defined by the sum of a fractional differential operator and a constant matrix, determining conditions under which this system has invariant subspaces of any desired dimension. Our results demonstrate that only one-dimensional invariant subspaces are capable of withstanding the Caputo fractional differential operator, whereas the Riemann-Liouville fractional differential operator allows for the existence of invariant subspaces of any desired dimension. This contrasts with linear integer-order systems, whose viable invariant subspaces are limited by their order. We also investigate the capabilities of combining fractional and integer-order derivatives to expand the set of invariant subspaces. This combines the advantages of both the Caputo and Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives, enabling the existence of invariant subspaces of any desired dimension, albeit at the cost of system generality. This research paves the way for further exploration of fractional order systems with regard to their controllability and observability properties. Furthermore, our results highlight the significance of selecting an appropriate fractional derivative model, as this affects the systems' invariance properties, thus requiring careful consideration in control system applications. We anticipate these findings contributing to the development of controllability and observability theories for fractional order systems. This is particularly important for such systems, which often exhibit sensitive and complex behaviors in response to control inputs, as evidenced by recent examples and scenarios discussed in the paper. This leads to a key conclusion: the careful selection of fractional derivative models is necessary to ensure the system's stability, as well as its controllability and observability, as demonstrated by concrete numerical examples. This underscores the practical significance of our theoretical contributions, thereby addressing the paper's research objectives. Observations of the millisecond pulsar PSR B1133+16, spanning 29 years, have yielded detailed information about the scattering materials surrounding it. A comprehensive analysis of both the positional data and the scatter broadening of the pulse period reveals the distribution of scattering screens along the pulsar's line of sight. Twenty individual scattering screens were resolved and found to be located at a distance of 1.86 plus or minus 0.01 kiloparsecs from Earth. The small distance indicates that the pulsar is likely embedded in a molecular cloud and offers a unique opportunity to investigate the interaction between a pulsar and its surrounding environment. The large spacing between the inner and outer edges of the scattering distribution, 0.56 to 3.56 kiloparsecs, is exceptionally large for a pulsar at this distance and may be influenced by a dish-shaped distribution of particles. The observed scattering frequencies are consistent with a dish-shaped distribution, although the evidence is not yet sufficient to rule out other explanations. The large distance of some screens may be related to the pulsar's motion, specifically the radial component of its proper motion, which could be influencing the scattering distribution by creating a barrier to screens located closer to Earth. The observed scattering patterns can be used to model the distribution of the pulsar's surrounding environment and the pulsar itself, with estimates suggesting a pulsar wind dot product of approximately 10 to the power of twenty-seven erg per second and a spin-down luminosity that is largely composed of magnetic field energy, indicating the pulsar is old enough to have formed the surrounding environment. The detailed information about the scattering distribution also enables the conversion of pulse period broadening to scattering measure, which can be compared with other pulsars and is influenced by the spin period and spin period derivative. This comparison shows a stronger relationship with the spin period derivative than with the spin period itself and may be related to the pulsar's evolution, although it is more likely the result of other influences such as the presence of neutron star winds. To better capture speech's complex, long-periodic patterns, a deep neural network called a cascaded recurrent resonance network is proposed, consisting of multiple stacked sub-networks with distinct frequency focuses. Unlike traditional single-path approaches, this structure divides the frequency spectrum into manageable chunks, allowing each sub-network to concentrate on specific, overlapping periodic components, and combining their outputs to capture the entire spectral range. Theoretical analysis and a speech generation task using a cascaded network with 4 sub-networks, demonstrating improved performance compared to a conventional long short-term memory (LSTM) based solution, are presented in this paper. Evaluations show that the cascaded model achieves a 19.6% reduction in perplexity and a 1.4% boost in sentence-level F-score at 4.5 bits per model, relative to the LSTM baseline. Furthermore, the paper explores various design options for this novel architecture, including sub-network size, pooling methods, and initialization techniques, and provides theoretical formulations to guide these optimizations, including explicit frequency mappings and initialization strategies, and presents additional experiments leveraging these designs. The cascaded network's code is made available as part of this paper.

Identifying the source of audio within a complex real-world environment is a difficult problem due to the variety of audio present and the imprecision of many sound source classification systems. To address this challenge, a new and comprehensive dataset called VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) has been created, consisting of 20 distinct sound categories that are commonly found in real-world environments and can be classified using a unified framework. This dataset stands out from existing sound classification datasets, which are generally focused on specific categories such as music genres or animal sounds, and often include broad categories like VGG-Sound that require additional sub-categorization. VGG-SS has several advantages over other datasets, including publicly available code and models for both training and inference purposes, and data annotations that can be utilized for training machine learning models. When put to use, this dataset demonstrated improved performance compared to other sound classification datasets, including VGG-Sound, and provides a versatile option for integrating multi-label classification and has the capability to handle unlimited categories. The code and data for VGG-SS are both available at https://github.com/vgg/vgg-sound-source. This dataset is particularly suited for evaluating sound source classification models that are capable of handling a wide range of categories and complex, long-duration audio clips. The current version of VGG-SS is tailored for English-speaking populations, although the framework it is based on has the flexibility to accommodate other languages and non-verbal sound classification tasks, such as identifying animal sounds. The development of VGG-SS was made possible through a combination of automatically annotated data obtained from YouTube, together with human evaluations to validate and refine the results. The need for human evaluations was necessitated by the challenges encountered with simply using machine learning models to accurately classify sound within complex audio clips. The VGG-SS dataset consists of 5,500 human-validated audio clips, which were further expanded into 200,000 audio clips via strategic selection of clips with the greatest variation in their sound sources, resulting in a comprehensive set of 1.5 million annotations following human evaluation. The advantages of VGG-SS are attributed to the unique design of its classification framework, which incorporates multi-label classification and has the capability to handle unlimited categories, making it a versatile option for the sound source classification community. This paper introduces Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), a novel hyperbolic convolutional neural network, which enhances existing hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) in representing node features. Our research finds that hyperbolic GCNs already achieve superior performance over Euclidean GCNs, especially in modeling complex graphs with narrow diameters. Nonetheless, hyperbolic GCNs face challenges in mapping wide-diameter graphs, which can lead to loss of essential information in the feature representation. To address this issue, LGCN is designed with a wide-diameter learning strategy and a novel convolutional layer, dubbed the Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Layer. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate LGCN's superiority over current hyperbolic GCNs for both small-diameter and wide-diameter graph learning tasks. An approach is developed to establish the observability inequality for the solution, which is shown to hold if the observation and observation points satisfy a certain rank condition. This condition essentially ensures that the solution can be distinguished from its integral of the square of its gradient. This result is crucial for achieving stable reconstruction of the diffusion coefficient using a minimization method based on a Tikhonov functional. As a result, we can demonstrate that this optimization method yields a stable solution when applied to noisy data. Furthermore, we can determine the minimal amount of data required to achieve a specific level of stability. An example is provided to illustrate the application of this approach to a specific problem. Additionally, we observe that for a problem where the unknown diffusion coefficient varies with time, achieving stable reconstruction requires significantly larger amount of data compared to the case without time variation. An existing result from the literature is also proven in the appendix of this study. It demonstrates that if the observation period is sufficiently long, the optimal cost of solving the inverse problem approaches the cost of solving the direct problem, despite the presence of noise, as the number of observations increases without limit. This result is significant because it implies that the benefit of extending the observation period ultimately comes at a cost due to the associated increase in the order of the resulting inverse problem. This advantage/disadvantage ratio can be characterized by a non-negative integer that determines the rate at which the optimal cost decreases as the number of observations grows. It is worth noting that this integer is a measure of the ease with which the inverse problem can be distinguished from its perturbations. In an linearized gravity theory, the inclusion of a mass term leads to an apparently inconsistent equation of motion, but the inconsistency can be resolved by adopting a suitable gauge and interpreting the degree of freedom as that of a coupled particle-field system rather than a isolated particle and field. In this paper, we illustrate how the mass term affects the degrees of freedom in linearized gravity through the example of a de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in order to define the linearized gravity correctly with respect to a mass term, the background spacetime requirements need to be strengthened to require that the spacetime has a smooth curvature in the linearized sense rather than in the weak sense. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mass term leads to an instability in the linearized gravity equation of motion, specifically the growth of the energy of the particle degree of freedom with respect to the background spacetime. This result is analogous to the prediction made by the AdS linear instability theorem within a linearized AdS gravity theory. For quantum equilibrium states on a lattice system, four types of Hamiltonian dynamics have been identified: scaling, extending, proper, and trivial dynamics. This study aims to classify the dynamics of individual quantum equilibrium states, specifically for classical Fermi gases in the thermodynamic limit, by analyzing the behavior of the system's Hamiltonian as the system's size increases. It is shown that the properties of the dynamics are determined by the system's Hamiltonian and can be classified based on the asymptotic behavior of the system's energy per degree of freedom. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the dynamics is scaling for ground state equilibrium states, whereas the dynamics is proper for excited equilibrium states, provided the system's energy remains within a certain limit as it grows. Additionally, it is found that the dynamics is trivial for the uniform Fermi gas in any of its equilibrium states, whereas the dynamics is extending for a system with a gapless edge region. It is also proven that the edge region's width scales inversely with the square root of the system's size. This research provides explicit expressions for the dynamics of a uniform classical Fermi gas, which can be used to determine the properties of the dynamics of more general, near-uniform systems. It is also demonstrated that the dynamics of the uniform Fermi gas is extending, in contrast to its discrete lattice counterpart. This study has implications for the long-time behavior of time-evolved quantum equilibrium states and suggests that the edge region decays within a linear time, whereas the bulk region remains stable for an exponentially long time. It is also shown that the edge region's width can be controlled through a choice of dynamics. This research has been expanded upon in recent studies for both classical and semi-finite Fermi gases in various dimensions. It has also been applied to the study of the dynamics of edge regions in one-dimensional chains and for non-equilibrium state ergodicity. It has further been used to investigate the dynamics of a gapless edge region for a three-dimensional Fermi surface in the laboratory setting using the example of the Rb108 atomical sample case. It has also been used to investigate the dynamics of a quasi-one-dimensional Fermi momentum distribution function. It has also been used to investigate the dynamics of quantum equilibrium states in chains with defects and for systems in contact with a quasi-free Fermi sea reservoir. A common analogy to explain negative temperature relies on water temperature examples, but it's more effective to use a two-level system as an illustration, which can maintain and supply negative temperature indefinitely.  Here, we choose a laser spike scenario to fill a two-level system with negative temperature, and we demonstrate how to calculate the associated uncertainty through the quantum Fisher information.  Notably, our findings reveal that the maximum achievable uncertainty, and thus the depth of the negative temperature, are limited by the number of photons excited in the laser spike, which is itself constrained by the pulse duration.  In contrast, the initial negative temperature's lifetime is primarily influenced by the spontaneous emission caused by the quantum channel between the levels, offering a practical criterion for evaluating the durability of negative temperature in this specific scenario.  Our numerical analysis confirms the existence of a stable negative temperature phase in two-level systems, also known as atoms in the radiation field, with a duration proportional to the number of photons excited during the pulse.  Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between the duration, depth, and uncertainty of negative temperature in two-level systems.  This knowledge can be further extended to more complex systems, like nitrogen-vacancy centers, spin ensembles, and trapped ions, among others, which all share the same general characteristics.  Our results also highlight the limitation of achievable frequency estimation, as well as other time-dependent quantities, when only a single pulse is employed, offering valuable insights for future experiments aiming to achieve negative temperatures with various two-level systems.  In those cases, the accessible time windows and the associated durations, as well as the corresponding frequency estimation uncertainties, can be predicted based on the available parameters.  Ultimately, our analysis emphasizes the crucial role that spontaneous emission plays in the formation and maintenance of negative temperatures in two-level systems, presenting a practical criterion for evaluating the durability of negative temperatures in these systems. We introduce a minimal dark sector to extend the standard model, incorporating a scalar and a fermion whose vacua maintain dark parity symmetry when the scalar mass equals the fermion mass. We then develop a type-one neutrino mass generation mechanism based on the "leptonic charged Higgs" scenario, where the scalar mediates the interaction between the fermion and heavy neutrinos through dark parity symmetry. The resulting code allows for three neutrino mass spectrum patterns: massive, quasi-degenerate, and nearly massless. We examine the parameter space to determine the stability of the vacuum and dark parity symmetry, investigating constraints from the electroweak precision test, the observed neutrino mass, the effective number of relativistic species, and the relic density of the fermion. Furthermore, we explore the possibilities for detecting the fermion through searches for exotic Higgs decay, heavy neutrino oscillation, direct detection, and indirect detection in the dark sector. We also identify possible dark matter candidate fields within this scenario, which require additional assumptions about the dark sector. We demonstrate that the minimal dark sector model exhibits inherent self-consistency and predictability, and we emphasize the importance of distinguishing between the active neutrino mass generation and the dark matter neu,trino sector. We propose the LHC and its upgrades, as well as future colliders and neutrino experiments, as ideal platforms for testing this model and exploring its underlying physics. We also outline the necessary theoretical and simulation improvements required to validate the reliability of the code and the generated neutrino spectra. We make the code publicly available at https://github.com/dark-neutrino/dark-neutrino. We conclude that a type-one neutrino mass generation mechanism based on the "leptonic charged Higgs" scenario, incorporated within a minimal dark sector, presents a compelling explanation for the neutrino mass spectrum, while offering prospects for detection across various fronts, from high-energy physics to cosmology. We suggest that this model can be refuted or confirmed through a combination of existing and future experiments, which could potentially uncover further mechanisms of neutrino mass generation. A comprehensive theoretical analysis of the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides is presented, with a focus on understanding how interaction effects and crystal field splitting influence this behavior. This research explores the LDA+U method's limitations in capturing the spin-orbit coupling's variability among these materials by comparing it to experimental data and DFT+HT results. It is demonstrated that the relationship between the spin-orbit coupling and crystal field splitting is parabolic, and the associated effective $g$-factor also exhibit a nonlinear response to this change. The study further reveals that the spin-orbit coupling's standard interpretation is constant across all $d$-orbital sites, and it is shown that the site-dependent behavior is actually a direct result of the crystal field splitting's influence on the $d$-orbital hybridization. These findings provide a clear understanding of the spin-orbit coupling's origin in these materials, offering valuable insights for interpreting the results of other theoretical and experimental methods. Additionally, the effective spin-orbit coupling's energy scales with the charge transfer energy, which is especially significant for understanding the Marsanti et al. experiment's results. The research presented in this study has implications for the interpretation of magnetic anisotropy in these materials, with the effective anisotropy energy related to the spin-orbit coupling and the crystal field-induced $d$-orbital anisotropy. Consequently, the precise determination of the effective spin-orbit coupling is crucial for predicting the stability of antiferromagnetic phases in these materials, which are notoriously difficult to calculate using other methods. The study provides a useful framework for assessing the accuracy of other methods used to calculate the effective spin-orbit coupling in these materials, which is a critical aspect given the diverse range of results currently available. The research's findings are demonstrated using concrete examples of transition metal oxides, with a focus on explaining the underlying physical mechanisms governing the effective spin-orbit coupling's behavior. The methodology used involves first-principles calculations within the LDA+U and DFT+HT frameworks, as well as the analysis of experimental data from various sources. The study's scope is limited to transition metal oxides with $d$-orbital configurations, which includes a wide range of materials with both localized and itinerant electronic properties. However, the research presented provides a universal framework for understanding the effective spin-orbit coupling's behavior, which can be applied to a broader range of materials and systems sharing similar electronic properties. This study explores the potential of generative models to create new, pathologic anatomical structures by manipulating the underlying representations, and investigates how varying latent codes affects the consistency of generated images with real-world data. We test this concept on two medical image datasets: MIMIC CXR and Pancreatic T2-weighted MRI images. Our experiments demonstrate that by adjusting latent codes, the model can either maintain the consistency of generated images with real-world data or produce new anomalies, depending on the code change. However, we observe that code changes often result in images that are neither consistent with nor anomalous, indicating that the model has difficulty maintaining the complexity of anatomical structures when generating new ones. We propose a method to enhance the robustness of these models by incorporating an auxiliary classifier that helps preserve the accuracy of the model when it is pushed to its limits. We also demonstrate that by distilling the model on a smaller generator using our proposed method, we can transfer the knowledge it has learned on large datasets to those that are much smaller. Dimensionality reduction techniques are widely used to facilitate the analysis of complex data by projecting it onto a more manageable two-dimensional space. Despite significant progress in such methods, selecting the ideal combination of features for visualization remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with extensive sets of possible features. To address this challenge, we developed ViDaExpert, a interactive visualization tool designed to facilitate the exploration of multidimensional data by employing decision trees to prioritize the most significant features and thereby direct the visualization. By integrating decision trees with a range-based weighting system for feature importance, ViDaExpert is capable of creating informative visualizations of complex data, even in the presence of numerous irrelevant features. Furthermore, the tool provides a meaningful arrangement of points in two-dimensional space, which can be employed for classification purposes or simply for visual inspection. We demonstrated the effectiveness and versatility of ViDaExpert by applying it to three distinct datasets with different characteristics. The source code of ViDaExpert is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/andersonmoro/ViDaExpert.
